We study the impact of increasing input-dependence in the steering edit, moving from a difference of means to a destination retrieved per query --- the mean of the $k$ stored states nearest the query, inside the requested class --- in which the two baselines are endpoints: at $k$ equal to the class size the retrieved rule \emph{is} the class-conditional difference of means. We measure input-dependent steering on six substitution corpora that vary in whether the edit changes a word or a clause, and on an external benchmark, and find that input-dependent steering outperforms fixed-direction steering when the destination varies within the class. Retrieval wins at every layer of every substitution corpus in two models, and the level of input-dependence needed governs how to apply it: word-level edits are best made in the first tenth of the network from a few neighbours, clause-level edits at any depth from the class mean. Where the class already determines the answer the class mean suffices and retrieval only matches it, though a fixed direction still fails there. Four quantities computed from the states alone identify the regime in which the edit should be applied.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that an activation steering edit should depend on the input only when the target varies within the requested class, and shows that retrieving a per-query destination from nearest stored states beats fixed-direction steering in that regime.
AI.motivation: Contrastive Activation Addition applies one fixed direction, the difference of class means, to every input, so it cannot capture within-class variation in the required displacement that no rule reading only the source state can express.
AI.method: The destination is retrieved per query as the mean of the k stored states nearest the query within the requested class, with the fixed class-mean difference as the k-equals-class-size endpoint; the method is tested on six substitution corpora that vary between word-level and clause-level edits, plus an external benchmark.
AI.result: Retrieval wins at every layer of every substitution corpus in two models; word-level edits work best in the first tenth of the network using a few neighbours, while clause-level edits work at any depth from the class mean; when the class already determines the answer the class mean suffices and retrieval only matches it, and four quantities computed from the states alone identify where to apply the edit.
AI.conclusion: The required degree of input dependence can be measured from the states before any rule is fitted, which tells practitioners when and how to apply steering edits.

title: TactiNavi: Serving and Revising an LLM Game Coach with Explicit Strategy Conditions
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure
summary: A deployed LLM coaching agent answers requests whose correct response depends on player state and game version, so advice that is right for one player can be wrong for the next. We describe TactiNavi, the serving system behind the LLM coach of a commercial open-world game, which makes strategy applicability an explicit artifact shared by offline compilation, online execution, failure diagnosis, and release. An offline compiler turns versioned game evidence and expert guidance into strategy packages with explicit prerequisites, the serving plane evaluates those prerequisites as three-valued conditions over structured player state and records decision traces, and a control plane uses the resulting condition-rule dependencies to validate revisions on held-out traffic before release. In a retrospective evaluation of 1,122 logged coaching turns from three deployment periods, condition-bearing packages raise correctness from 57.9% to 82.0% over atomic facts and reduce strategy misapplication under changed player state from 18.1% to 10.4%, while trace-based claim verification reaches 86.4% precision at a median reply latency of 2.07 s. The deployment also showed that most apparent fixes are generation noise, because an unchanged-system rerun recovers 38.4% of failing turns and only one of 15 shipped revision units passes the release checks retrospectively. We distill these results into lessons on treating applicability as a first-class serving object, sizing traces for later diagnosis, and building the null model into the release path.

AI.tldr: TactiNavi is the serving system behind an LLM game coach in a commercial open-world game; it makes strategy applicability an explicit, versioned artifact that is compiled offline, evaluated online as three-valued conditions, and checked by a release control plane.
AI.motivation: The correct coaching advice for an LLM agent depends on player state and game version, so advice that is right for one player can be wrong for another.
AI.method: An offline compiler turns versioned game evidence and expert guidance into strategy packages with explicit prerequisites; the serving plane evaluates these prerequisites as three-valued conditions over structured player state and records decision traces; a control plane uses condition-rule dependencies to validate revisions on held-out traffic before release.
AI.result: In a retrospective evaluation of 1,122 logged coaching turns from three deployment periods, condition-bearing packages raised correctness from 57.9% to 82.0% over atomic facts and cut misapplication under changed player state from 18.1% to 10.4%; trace-based claim verification reached 86.4% precision at a median latency of 2.07 s; an unchanged-system rerun recovered 38.4% of failing turns, and only one of 15 shipped revision units passed the release checks retrospectively.
AI.conclusion: Treating applicability as a first-class serving object, keeping traces sufficient for later diagnosis, and building a null model into the release path are practical lessons, since many apparent fixes turn out to be generation noise.

title: Reducing Logprob Without Causal Verification: Diagnosing SAE-Based PII Suppression in LLMs
comment: Accepted to Findings of AACL-IJCNLP 2026
summary: SAE-based feature-level interventions to suppress PII leakage in LLMs are primarily evaluated by log-probability reduction. We show that this criterion cannot distinguish feature specific suppression from a magnitude artifact: a direction-agnostic effect of sufficiently large activation perturbations. Across 36 (model, layer, PII type) cases, we compare selected SAE feature interventions with coherencematched random direction controls using logprob and rank-aware metrics. While 17 cases (47%) appear successful under logprob-only evaluation, only 1 case (2.8%) passes our multimetric framework. The rest reveal two failure modes: random directions outperform selected features, and feature selection collapse across PII types. These results indicate that existing evaluations cannot verify whether interventions target causal pathways of PII leakage. A 9,000 run causal mediation feasibility study corroborates this: the verifier separates candidates reliably, but correlation-selected candidates rarely pass it. We therefore propose a new research mission for NLP: causally grounded PII suppression through circuit-level localization and causal mediation analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that log-probability reduction cannot tell feature-specific SAE-based PII suppression apart from a magnitude artifact, and proposes causally grounded evaluation through circuit-level localization and causal mediation analysis.
AI.motivation: SAE-based feature interventions for PII suppression are usually judged by log-probability reduction, which may not reflect whether the intervention targets a causal pathway of leakage.
AI.method: Across 36 cases of model, layer and PII type, selected SAE feature interventions are compared with random direction controls matched for coherence, using logprob and rank-aware metrics, and a 9,000-run causal mediation feasibility study checks the verifier.
AI.result: 17 cases (47%) looked successful under logprob-only evaluation, but only 1 case (2.8%) passed the multimetric framework; random directions often outperformed selected features, feature selection collapsed across PII types, and the verifier separated candidates reliably while correlation-selected candidates rarely passed it.
AI.conclusion: Existing evaluations cannot verify causal targeting of PII leakage, so the authors call for a new NLP research direction built on causal mediation and circuit-level localization.

title: Kierston & KierstonBench: Simulation of Allentown, PA and Evaluation of Language Models in Crime Investigation and Surveillance Tasks
summary: Large language models are candidates for collecting and analyzing records in criminal investigations and mass surveillance. Their capability and accuracy in this work cannot currently be measured. Real deployments lack the ground truth needed to score a model's conclusions, and no benchmark evaluates these capabilities in a simulated environment. We present Kierston, a city-scale simulation engine, and KierstonBench, a benchmark that tests these capabilities against known simulated events. Kierston models approximately 125,000 residents of Allentown, Pennsylvania, generating their daily activities and the telecommunications, financial, administrative and license-plate records that surveillance and investigative systems collect about them. These records derive from a common behavioral timeline and are distributed across sources representing separate providers. Models investigate through a restricted records interface, linking observations across sources without access to the underlying simulation. The benchmark comprises 32 task families covering record linkage, routine reconstruction, incident investigation and assessment of deceptive accounts. In an evaluation of sixteen language models, most could not perform records investigation and submitted identifications the records did not support. A small number of frontier models solved most of the tasks and abstained when evidence was insufficient. In some cases these models still fell for common deceptions and assumptions, and none replaced an investigator.

AI.tldr: Kierston is a city-scale simulation of about 125,000 residents of Allentown, Pennsylvania that generates surveillance-style records, and KierstonBench is a 32-task benchmark that tests whether language models can investigate them without ground truth leakage.
AI.motivation: Language models are being considered for criminal investigation and mass surveillance, but their accuracy cannot currently be measured because real deployments lack ground truth and no benchmark covers these capabilities in simulation.
AI.method: The simulator produces daily activities and telecommunications, financial, administrative and license-plate records derived from a common behavioral timeline and split across separate providers; models investigate through a restricted records interface without access to the underlying simulation, across 32 task families.
AI.result: In an evaluation of sixteen language models most could not perform records investigation and submitted identifications the records did not support; a small number of frontier models solved most tasks and abstained when evidence was insufficient, yet some still fell for common deceptions and assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Current models do not replace an investigator, and simulation-based benchmarks can expose their failures in records investigation before deployment.

title: Where Is the Truth When AI Agents Disagree? Dependence-Aware Belief Propagation for Unsupervised Truth Discovery (Extended Version)
comment: Extended version of a short paper accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (IEEE BigData 2026). 11 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL ; code and data archive: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21294747
summary: LLM agents often give conflicting answers to the same question, and many deployed agents are variants of one base model, so their errors are correlated. We study truth discovery among such agents: inferring the true answer and each agent's reliability without labels. Classical truth-discovery and crowdsourcing estimators reward an agreeing bloc and can fall below majority vote. We propose BP-TD, which adds per-agent decorrelation weights to mean-field variational inference on a one-coin Dawid-Skene model, so that agents sharing a base model count together as about one vote. Its first iteration is exactly a weighted vote; later iterations estimate agent reliability. With 13 local agents on MMLU, BP-TD beats majority vote without any labels (0.716 vs. 0.624 on 160 questions; 0.707 vs. 0.674 on 10,000) and ranks agents by their true accuracy, which classical estimators invert. The gain depends on the pool: over 2,852 sub-pools of four benchmarks, decorrelation helps when the largest correlated bloc is weaker than the other agents and hurts when it is the strongest, and we found no label-free statistic that tells the two cases apart. Labels change the picture quickly: with 20 labelled questions, selecting the single best agent is more accurate than every aggregator we tested on MMLU, ARC and TruthfulQA.

AI.tldr: BP-TD is an unsupervised truth-discovery method for LLM agents that uses decorrelation weights so that agents sharing a base model count together as roughly one vote, and it beats majority vote without labels on MMLU.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often give conflicting answers and their errors are correlated because many are variants of one base model, and classical truth-discovery estimators reward an agreeing bloc and can fall below majority vote.
AI.method: BP-TD adds per-agent decorrelation weights to mean-field variational inference on a one-coin Dawid-Skene model; its first iteration is a weighted vote and later iterations estimate agent reliability.
AI.result: With 13 local agents on MMLU, BP-TD scored 0.716 against 0.624 for majority vote on 160 questions and 0.707 against 0.674 on 10,000 questions, and it ranked agents by true accuracy, which classical estimators invert; decorrelation helped only when the largest correlated bloc was weaker than the other agents, and with 20 labelled questions selecting the best single agent beat every aggregator tested on MMLU, ARC and TruthfulQA.
AI.conclusion: Decorrelation can improve label-free aggregation of agent answers, but its benefit depends on the pool, and labels quickly change which approach is best.

title: RAHC: Rule-Augmented Hyper-Relational Knowledge Graph Completion for Materials Synthesis
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, including references and appendices
summary: Scientific discovery depends on reusing experimental knowledge, yet records scattered across papers and repositories are often incomplete. In materials synthesis, recovering missing conditions requires reasoning about the target material and the observed context of a specific experiment. Hyper-relational knowledge graphs (HKGs) represent this context through qualifiers, but existing completion methods leave domain knowledge and experimental regularities implicit. We propose RAHC, a rule-augmented HKG framework for single-slot and joint multi-slot synthesis-condition completion. RAHC builds a traceable rule catalog from training records and retrieved literature, retrieves rules for each query-candidate pair, and separately encodes graph structure and rule evidence. Hard rules constrain candidate validity, while soft rules guide ranking. RAHC-G aggregates rules using global reliability; RAHC-Q additionally learns query-specific relevance. Gated fusion combines structural and rule representations, while tuple-conclusion rules provide cross-condition evidence for joint completion. Experiments on five materials-synthesis datasets show improvements in single-slot and joint completion under Semi-inductive and Open-Answer Inductive settings, with Semi-inductive MRR gains of up to 15.6% over MAYPL. RAHC also improves performance on the entity-disjoint ILPC'22 Small benchmark, supporting transfer to fully inductive KG completion. These results support experimental condition selection, synthesis planning, and the reuse of scientific knowledge.

AI.tldr: RAHC is a rule-augmented hyper-relational knowledge graph framework that completes missing synthesis conditions for materials experiments by using hard and soft rules from training records and retrieved literature.
AI.motivation: Records of materials synthesis are scattered and incomplete, and existing hyper-relational knowledge graph completion methods leave domain knowledge and experimental regularities implicit.
AI.method: RAHC builds a traceable rule catalog from training records and retrieved literature, retrieves rules for each query-candidate pair, and encodes graph structure and rule evidence separately; hard rules constrain candidate validity, soft rules guide ranking, RAHC-G uses global rule reliability, RAHC-Q adds query-specific relevance, and gated fusion combines the representations.
AI.result: On five materials-synthesis datasets RAHC improves single-slot and joint completion under Semi-inductive and Open-Answer Inductive settings, with Semi-inductive MRR gains of up to 15.6% over MAYPL, and it also improves results on the entity-disjoint ILPC'22 Small benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Explicit rule evidence supports experimental condition selection, synthesis planning and reuse of scientific knowledge, and it transfers toward fully inductive knowledge graph completion.

title: AgenticFinBench: Benchmarking Financial Agents on Diverse Tasks from Real-World Requests
summary: Financial agents are becoming an important class of real-world AI systems. Financial tasks vary widely in type and difficulty, and many are open-ended with no ground-truth answers. However, existing benchmarks neither capture this breadth and open-endedness nor separate grounding from correctness. To bridge this gap, we introduce $\textbf{AgenticFinBench}$, a benchmark of 230 real-world financial tasks spanning 8 categories, 2 languages, and 4 complexity levels. We also propose a reference-free evaluation framework that combines question-specific rubrics with a two-stage claim audit that detects hallucinations, defined as claims absent from the agent's trace and refuted by external evidence. This framework better matches how financial work is assessed in practice. Experiments across 18 agent configurations reveal three key findings: (1) Ignoring hallucinations can overstate agent performance: hallucination auditing lowers the baseline leader's score by 7.58 points and moves it to fourth place. (2) Harness differences explain more variation in evidence grounding than model differences (28.6% vs 8.8%). (3) Quality scores fall from 89.44 on direct retrieval to 79.18 on the most complex tasks. Case studies show that agents struggle to explain how events affect company profits or stock prices, compare financial data on a consistent basis, and justify their conclusions. By releasing AgenticFinBench, we aim to advance financial reasoning, factual verification, and agent design for more reliable responses to diverse real-world financial requests. Our project page is at $\textbf{this https URL}$.

AI.tldr: AgenticFinBench is a benchmark of 230 real-world financial tasks, paired with a reference-free evaluation that combines rubrics and a two-stage claim audit to detect hallucinations in financial agents.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks do not capture the breadth and open-endedness of financial tasks and do not separate grounding from correctness.
AI.method: The benchmark spans 8 categories, 2 languages and 4 complexity levels; evaluation uses question-specific rubrics and a two-stage claim audit that flags claims absent from the agent trace and refuted by external evidence, applied to 18 agent configurations.
AI.result: Hallucination auditing lowered the baseline leader's score by 7.58 points, moving it to fourth place; harness differences explained more variation in evidence grounding than model differences (28.6% vs 8.8%); quality fell from 89.44 on direct retrieval to 79.18 on the most complex tasks, and agents struggled to explain event impacts on profits or stock prices and to justify conclusions.
AI.conclusion: Ignoring hallucinations can overstate agent performance, and the agent harness matters as much as the base model for reliable financial answers.

title: Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression
summary: Large reasoning models achieve strong performance on challenging tasks, but their long chain-of-thought often incurs substantial inference costs by continuing to deliberate after sufficient information has been obtained. Existing reasoning compression methods primarily operate on reasoning trajectories, paying less attention to the local decision of whether further reasoning is necessary given the current state. We propose LoCo, a local preference learning method for reasoning compression. LoCo detects candidate overthinking states from the model's own traces, freezes the corresponding reasoning prefixes, regenerates shorter verified continuations from the same states, and trains on the resulting state-conditioned preference pairs with DPO. This formulation teaches the model when to continue reasoning and when to conclude, rather than simply encouraging shorter trajectories overall. We construct training data entirely from self-generated mathematical traces and evaluate LoCo on five mathematical and three code generation benchmarks. LoCo reduces completion length by 41.7\%--45.4\% on mathematics and 23.4\%--36.3\% on code, while maintaining or improving accuracy and achieving the best AUC across all code benchmarks. LoCo consistently improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off on mathematics and transfers effectively to code generation despite math-only training, demonstrating the cross-domain generality of local preference learning for reasoning compression. The code and model will be publicly released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: LoCo is a local preference learning method for reasoning compression that trains a model with DPO on state-conditioned pairs to decide when to stop reasoning, cutting completion length substantially while keeping accuracy.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models keep deliberating after enough information is available, and existing compression methods act on whole trajectories rather than on the local decision of whether further reasoning is needed.
AI.method: LoCo detects candidate overthinking states in the model's own traces, freezes the reasoning prefix, regenerates shorter verified continuations from the same state, and trains on the resulting preference pairs with DPO, using training data built entirely from self-generated math traces.
AI.result: Completion length falls by 41.7% to 45.4% on five mathematics benchmarks and by 23.4% to 36.3% on three code generation benchmarks, with accuracy maintained or improved and the best AUC on all code benchmarks; the gains transfer to code despite math-only training.
AI.conclusion: Local preference learning gives a cross-domain way to improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off by teaching when to continue and when to conclude.

title: The Pen is Mightier than the Pixel: Natural Textual Unlearnable Example for Large Vision Language Models
summary: The proliferation of Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs), trained on vast and often sensitive datasets, raised concerns regarding data privacy and unauthorized usage. Unlearnable Examples (UEs), which subtly perturb training data to mislead the models, have emerged as a promising defense method. This paper presents the first exploration of UEs specifically on LVLMs, which poses unique challenges due to their inherent multimodal nature. We propose a novel text-based perturbation method, Natural Textual Unlearnable Examples (NTUE), which can effectively mislead LVLMs by subtly manipulating the image label, establishing a shortcut between an identity of interest and a separate target, without introducing factual misinformation or affecting readability. Comprehensive experiments compared with traditional UE methods demonstrate the superior performance of NTUE. Our findings show that NTUE achieves a high success rate with a poison rate as low as 5%, underscoring its potential as a practical and robust solution for protecting multimodal data in the era of LVLMs.

AI.tldr: NTUE is a text-based unlearnable example method that perturbs image labels in the text to create a shortcut for large vision language models, protecting data without adding factual misinformation.
AI.motivation: Large vision language models trained on sensitive data raise privacy concerns, and unlearnable examples, which have been studied for image classifiers, had not been explored for LVLMs with their multimodal nature.
AI.method: NTUE subtly manipulates the image label to establish a shortcut between an identity of interest and a separate target, while keeping the text factually accurate and readable.
AI.result: NTUE reaches a high success rate with a poison rate as low as 5% and outperforms traditional unlearnable example methods in comparative experiments.
AI.conclusion: Text-based perturbations offer a practical and robust way to protect multimodal data against training on LVLMs.

title: Reconstructing Fraudulent Strategies in Online Payments via Interpretable Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: Payment fraud causes financial losses and undermines users' trust in web payment services. Although fraud detection is a critical defense for payment security, complex and diverse fraudulent behaviors can still evade detection. Generating fraud samples for data augmentation can broaden detectors' coverage of different fraud patterns. However, existing methods matching the distribution of transaction attributes alone do not ensure that generated sequences preserve the sequential relationships among transaction choices, payment feedback, and subsequent behavioral adjustments. To this end, we propose PaySeqGen, an interpretable inverse reinforcement learning framework that reconstructs fraud behavior policies from fraudsters' observed payment trajectories. We design a mechanism for constructing candidate actions to support plausible payment sequence generation while enabling exploration. The framework also learns interpretable behavioral rewards that capture fraudsters' preferences across different transaction contexts. By alternating between reward learning and policy optimization, the framework reconstructs policies that generate new fraud sequences for detector augmentation and learns interpretable rewards supporting sequential fraud-pattern analysis in real trajectories. Experiments in real-world payment scenarios at Ant International, a leading global digital payment provider, show that PaySeqGen outperforms state-of-the-art generative augmentation methods. Reward-based trajectory analysis also identifies fraud patterns of practical value, helping analyst locating suspicious segments and examine multistep fraud tactics. Evaluation in the deployed system of online payment further confirms its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: PaySeqGen is an interpretable inverse reinforcement learning framework that reconstructs fraudsters' policies from payment trajectories to generate fraud sequences for detector augmentation and learn interpretable behavioural rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing generative augmentation methods match transaction attribute distributions but do not preserve the sequential relations among transaction choices, payment feedback and later behavioural adjustments.
AI.method: The framework alternates reward learning and policy optimization, uses a mechanism that constructs candidate actions to support plausible sequence generation and exploration, and learns interpretable rewards that capture fraudster preferences across transaction contexts.
AI.result: In real-world payment scenarios at Ant International, PaySeqGen outperforms state-of-the-art generative augmentation methods, its reward-based trajectory analysis identifies practically valuable fraud patterns, and it is confirmed in the deployed online payment system.
AI.conclusion: Reconstructing fraud policies with interpretable rewards supports both detector augmentation and analysis of multistep fraud tactics.

title: Feeling of Knowing in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Post-training updates change what large language models (LLMs) can answer, but may leave their answerability judgments misaligned. We study this knowledge-judgment desynchronization through functional feeling of knowing (FoK), which supports selective generation, retrieval triggering, and model routing without implying subjective experience. We propose two trainable channels: a knowledge channel that changes answerability and a FoK channel that judges the current knowledge state. Three stages train them: on-policy supervised fine-tuning (OP-SFT) updates knowledge from corrected on-policy answers; knowledge-delta FoK training (K$\Delta$-FT) adapts judgments across intermediate knowledge states; and FoK-guided policy optimization (FGPO) trains the subsequent answer or explanation. Factual-QA experiments, cross-dataset evaluation, and three sequential updates show that explicit FoK alignment improves judgment quality on updated knowledge. MMLU and ARC-Easy separately assess capability preservation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies functional feeling of knowing (FoK) in LLMs and proposes two trainable channels, a knowledge channel and an FoK channel, trained in three stages so that answerability judgments stay aligned after post-training updates.
AI.motivation: Post-training changes what LLMs can answer but can leave their answerability judgments misaligned, which matters for selective generation, retrieval triggering and model routing.
AI.method: On-policy supervised fine-tuning updates knowledge from corrected on-policy answers (OP-SFT), knowledge-delta FoK training adapts judgments across intermediate knowledge states (K-Delta-FT), and FoK-guided policy optimization trains the subsequent answer or explanation (FGPO).
AI.result: On factual-QA experiments, cross-dataset evaluation and three sequential updates, explicit FoK alignment improves judgment quality on updated knowledge, and MMLU and ARC-Easy were used to check that capability is preserved.
AI.conclusion: Explicit alignment of the FoK channel with the knowledge state keeps answerability judgments reliable after updates, without implying subjective experience.

title: HTCE: Homeomorphism-inspired Topological Cross-Scene Experience Canonicalization and Reuse for Object Navigation
summary: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in this https URL

AI.tldr: HTCE is a homeomorphism-inspired topological method that canonicalizes and reuses successful navigation experience across scenes, retrieving structurally matched routes as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy in object-goal navigation.
AI.motivation: Successful navigation experiences recur semantically across residences even when geometry differs, but differences in region naming and observation granularity make similar routes look different as graphs.
AI.method: Feature and topology subdivisions are reduced under semantic constraints to produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures that keep anchors, branches and endpoints; subdivision-aware matching then retrieves historical approaches to guide a frozen vision-language policy.
AI.result: Canonicalization merges 17.7% to 23.6% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance, and HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting: 59.9%/31.8% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0%/31.5% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6%/16.6% on MP3D, with SR gains of up to 4.9 points.
AI.conclusion: Canonical, structure-aware experience reuse improves object navigation with a shared frozen backbone and compresses the experience index without losing performance.

title: DGC-Net: Cross-Modal Dynamic Routing with Global-Guided Compensation in Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
summary: User-generated videos, including opinion vlogs and video reviews, provide a rich source of people's attitudes toward products, services, and social topics. Understanding the sentiment expressed by speakers is important for analyzing online opinions, as transcripts alone may not capture the attitude and intensity conveyed through vocal tone and facial expressions. Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) addresses this need by integrating textual, acoustic, and visual cues. However, these cues are often subtle, noisy, and inconsistent across modalities. Existing local affective cue modeling methods typically operate within individual modalities and overlook global contexts from other modalities. This may cause cross-modal affective cue inconsistency. Hierarchical global-local fusion methods integrate global semantics with fine-grained local affective cues. However, they commonly determine the relative contributions of the two representations implicitly, preventing the global-local contributions from adapting to the sample-dependent reliability of local cues and resulting in either insufficient use of informative local cues or excessive interference from unreliable ones. To address these issues, we propose DGC-Net, a Dynamic Gating and Global-Guided Compensation Network for MSA. DGC-Net mitigates cross-modal affective cue inconsistency through cross-modal contribution-aware dynamic expert routing. This mechanism uses auxiliary global contexts to guide local expert selection. Moreover, global-guided dynamic compensation fusion alleviates sample-dependent global-local contribution imbalance while preserving global semantic as the primary anchor and adaptively incorporating expert-refined local cues. Experiments on five multimodal benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and general applicability of DGC-Net, and ablation studies verify the contribution of each proposed component.

AI.tldr: DGC-Net is a multimodal sentiment analysis network that uses cross-modal dynamic expert routing guided by global context and a global-guided compensation fusion that adapts how much local affective cues contribute.
AI.motivation: Existing hierarchical global-local fusion methods determine the contributions of global and local representations implicitly, so they cannot adapt to the sample-dependent reliability of local cues and either underuse informative cues or absorb unreliable ones.
AI.method: Cross-modal contribution-aware dynamic expert routing uses auxiliary global contexts to guide local expert selection, and global-guided dynamic compensation fusion keeps global semantics as the primary anchor while adaptively adding expert-refined local cues.
AI.result: Experiments on five multimodal benchmark datasets show the effectiveness and general applicability of DGC-Net, and ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, sample-adaptive balancing of global and local cues mitigates cross-modal affective inconsistency in multimodal sentiment analysis.

title: Amortized Nonlinear Variable Selection with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
summary: Variable selection is an important task for interpreting potentially complex systems in fields such as biology, business, and sociology. The importance of variable selection has attracted considerable attention in statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we are mainly interested in model-agnostic variable selection for identifying variables that have general nonlinear dependence on the response. We propose MambaPFN, short for Model-Agnostic Markov BlAnket selection with Prior-data Fitted Networks, which is built upon the Transformer, a building block of many popular large language models. Specifically, we consider a functional-mapping perspective on variable-selection learning, in which the Transformer is treated as a learnable mapping from a dataset to its relevant variables. To learn this mapping, MambaPFN introduces three new components: (i) a faithful, rich, and scalable scheme for generating pretraining data, (ii) an objective that targets each variable's posterior inclusion probability, and (iii) a modified Transformer architecture tailored to variable selection. Once pretrained, MambaPFN is applied to new datasets without parameter updates. Empirically, MambaPFN achieves desirable variable-selection performance in simulation studies and exhibits a scaling law---more pretraining datasets and larger models can continuously improve its performance. Applied to a Facebook comments dataset, MambaPFN selects the fewest variables and achieves the highest computational efficiency and predictive performance, improving upon the best baselines by about 20%.

AI.tldr: MambaPFN is a pretrained Transformer that performs model-agnostic nonlinear variable selection (Markov blanket selection) on new datasets without parameter updates, by estimating each variable's posterior inclusion probability.
AI.motivation: Variable selection for interpreting complex systems needs to capture general nonlinear dependence on the response in a model-agnostic way, and existing approaches do not offer a single amortized predictor for that.
AI.method: MambaPFN treats a Transformer as a learnable mapping from a dataset to its relevant variables, and introduces a scalable scheme for generating pretraining data, an objective targeting each variable's posterior inclusion probability, and a Transformer architecture modified for variable selection.
AI.result: In simulation studies it achieves desirable variable-selection performance and shows a scaling law in which more pretraining datasets and larger models continue to improve it; on a Facebook comments dataset it selects the fewest variables, is the most computationally efficient and predicts best, improving upon the best baselines by about 20%.
AI.conclusion: Amortized, pretrained variable selection can be applied to new datasets directly and benefits from scale.

title: ScamWorld: An Interactive Environment for Evaluating Web Agents Against Online Fraud
comment: 15 pages, 17 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Web agents increasingly browse, shop, and manage accounts on behalf of their users. Prior work has shown that they can be misled by adversarial content, including prompt injections and deceptive interfaces. Beyond such attacks, agents operating on the open web also encounter online fraud designed to deceive humans, including fraudulent online stores, fake investment platforms, and advance-fee schemes. How web agents respond to such fraud during task execution remains underexplored, in part because scam websites are short-lived, making systematic evaluation difficult. To address this gap, we introduce ScamWorld, an interactive environment that reconstructs reported scam websites across diverse scenarios, fraud mechanisms, and languages. Each reconstructed website reproduces documented fraud mechanisms, making relevant signs of fraud observable before the agent's final action and enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation. Through an extensive study of web agents powered by six frontier LLMs, we find that baseline deception rates range from 11% to 35% across models. Agents proceed more readily with payments than with requests for credentials or wallet information. A closer analysis of agent trajectories shows that some agents acknowledge suspicious conditions yet proceed, at times treating the user's instructions as authorisation to accept additional terms imposed by the website. ScamWorld provides a reusable testbed for systematically evaluating and stress-testing web agents against real-world online fraud.

AI.tldr: ScamWorld is an interactive environment that reconstructs reported scam websites so that web agents can be tested repeatedly against online fraud before their final action.
AI.motivation: Web agents act on users' behalf and can be misled by adversarial content, but how they respond to live online fraud has been underexplored, since scam websites are short-lived and hard to evaluate systematically.
AI.method: The environment reconstructs reported scam websites across diverse scenarios, fraud mechanisms and languages, reproducing documented fraud mechanisms so that signs of fraud are observable before the agent's final action, and it is used to study web agents powered by six frontier LLMs.
AI.result: Baseline deception rates range from 11% to 35% across models; agents proceed more readily with payments than with requests for credentials or wallet information, and some acknowledge suspicious conditions yet proceed, sometimes treating the user's instructions as authorisation to accept extra terms imposed by the website.
AI.conclusion: ScamWorld provides a reusable testbed for evaluating and stress-testing web agents against real-world online fraud.

title: Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures
summary: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work. We study a model in which individuals tend to imitate successful peers, while their independent skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI. Because each agent's skill reflects their history, non-users and AI users develop different skill distributions, which we derive exactly. Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption, high-skill state and a high-adoption, low-skill state. When agents rarely change behaviour at random, the two transitions are asymmetric. A single AI user spreads through a population of experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, whatever the timescale of skill adaptation. A single non-user, by contrast, can lead an AI-dependent population back to independent work only if they regain enough skill before returning to AI, which becomes easier the more persistent behaviours are. As AI improves, adoption can jump abruptly, and a sufficiently long increase in its benefit, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. Skill erosion thus creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

AI.tldr: The paper models how AI adoption can lock in through skill erosion, showing that history-dependent skills create bistability and hysteresis so that widespread AI use can be hard to reverse.
AI.motivation: Generative AI improves immediate performance but may erode the human skills needed for future work, and the resulting path dependence in adoption is not captured by static models.
AI.method: Individuals imitate successful peers while independent skills grow with practice and erode with AI reliance; the authors derive the skill distributions of non-users and AI users exactly and analyse transitions between the two states, including asymmetry when agents rarely change behaviour at random.
AI.result: Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption high-skill state and a high-adoption low-skill state; a single AI user spreads through experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, while a single non-user can return a population to independent work only if they regain enough skill first; a long enough benefit increase, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit returns to its initial value.
AI.conclusion: Skill erosion creates a history-dependent switching cost, so policies to reverse widespread AI adoption need to account for lost skills and not only for the benefit of the tool.

title: FourSight: Stable FP4 RL Post-Training via Sequence Filtering and Sparse Channel Compensation
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training increasingly targets low-bit deployment, with NVFP4 weight-and activation quantization (W4A4) becoming the state-of-the-practice format. However, integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch (TIM), destabilizing training. We show that these failures are concentrated rather than uniform - severely mismatched tail tokens concentrate in a few outlier sequences, while policy weights remain largely intact and quantization error concentrates in a few high-variance activation channels. Guided by this, we present FourSight, an algorithm-system co-design with two targeted solutions: TIM-aware sequence filtering that excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, and sparse precision compensation that keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while retaining native NVFP4 elsewhere. We further design a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths to minimize overhead. FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, while improving step-to-accuracy by 1.76-2.60x and staying within 2.3% of FP4 step time up to 120B-scale models.

AI.tldr: FourSight enables stable NVFP4 (W4A4) reinforcement learning post-training by filtering outlier sequences with training-inference mismatch and keeping only high-variance activation channels in BF16, with a fused kernel for speed.
AI.motivation: Integrating NVFP4 into RL degrades rollout quality and amplifies cross-engine training-inference mismatch, and these failures are concentrated in a few outlier sequences and a few high-variance activation channels.
AI.method: TIM-aware sequence filtering excludes drifted trajectories from policy updates, sparse precision compensation keeps only top-variance channels in BF16 while the rest stay NVFP4, and a fused SpliceGEMM kernel with specialized prefill and decode datapaths reduces overhead.
AI.result: FourSight sustains near-BF16 accuracy and strong FP4 deployment quality across models and engines, improves step-to-accuracy by 1.76 to 2.60 times, and stays within 2.3% of FP4 step time for models up to 120B scale.
AI.conclusion: Targeted, algorithm-system co-design can make low-bit RL post-training stable and efficient without the cost of full higher precision.

title: Artifact-to-Capability: Diagnosing Breaks in Capability Formation of Self-Evolving Agents in a Controlled Environment
summary: Self-evolving agents write interaction experience into artifacts and reuse them in later tasks. Most work supports such methods with three proxy signals: artifacts accumulate, behavior changes once they are loaded, and metrics rise. We call this signal-based evaluation. What these signals are meant to indicate, however, has not been defined. To fill this gap, we define capability formation from artifacts as five sequentially dependent properties, two of which form a checkpoint for capability formation, and introduce three-scale diagnosis, which judges these properties at the state, game, and lineage levels. In freestyle Gomoku, Reflexion, Voyager, and DGM evolve with the same base model and all show the three signals, yet each exhibits a distinct capability-formation break. Reflexion shows a legalization gain: its pass rate rises only because more of its moves are legal. Voyager shows a compositional override: components that are sound on their own combine to miss all 20 available one-move wins. DGM shows loss-only drift: after passing the checkpoint, later versions only lose passing states. These counterexamples show that signal-based evaluation cannot determine whether a capability has formed.

AI.tldr: The paper defines capability formation from artifacts for self-evolving agents as five sequential properties and shows that three signal-based metrics can hide distinct failures in Reflexion, Voyager and DGM on freestyle Gomoku.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents write experience into artifacts and are usually judged by three proxy signals, namely artifact accumulation, behaviour change and rising metrics, but what those signals should indicate has not been defined.
AI.method: Capability formation is defined through five sequentially dependent properties, two of which form a checkpoint, and a three-scale diagnosis judges them at the state, game and lineage levels, applied to Reflexion, Voyager and DGM, which share the same base model.
AI.result: All three agents show the three signals, yet each has a different break: Reflexion's pass-rate rise reflects a legalization gain, Voyager's sound components combine to miss all 20 available one-move wins, and DGM's later versions only lose passing states after passing the checkpoint.
AI.conclusion: Signal-based evaluation cannot determine whether a capability has actually formed, so agent evaluation needs to check the properties that the signals are meant to indicate.

title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
summary: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. We further introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic testing methodology, to distinguish structural symbolic induction from surface-level pattern matching on predicate names. Experiments on 30 standard ILP benchmarks show that ALBI achieves 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6), matching Popper while requiring only 1.4-1.7 iterations on average. Under anonymization, all models maintain 100% success with a moderate iteration increase (1.36-1.67 times), providing evidence of robust symbolic reasoning.

AI.tldr: ALBI replaces the ASP hypothesis generator in Learning from Failures with an LLM that proposes candidate hypotheses, while SWI-Prolog verifies them in a generate-test-constrain loop, and it matches Popper on 30 ILP benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Inductive logic programming pipelines rely on an ASP-based hypothesis generator, and it is unclear whether LLM-based induction reflects structural symbolic reasoning or only surface pattern matching on predicate names.
AI.method: The LLM proposes hypotheses from structured prompts, Prolog tests each candidate, and diagnostic feedback drives refinement; semantic anonymization within a metamorphic testing methodology checks whether models rely on predicate names.
AI.result: ALBI reaches 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6) on 30 standard ILP benchmarks, matching Popper with 1.4 to 1.7 iterations on average; under anonymization all models keep 100% success with a moderate increase of 1.36 to 1.67 times in iterations.
AI.conclusion: The results give evidence that LLM-driven ILP relies on robust symbolic reasoning rather than surface cues, since success persists when predicate names are anonymized.

title: LatentTriad: Pre-Action Risk Representations for Malicious Agent Skill Detection
comment: Preprint. Under review. 44 pages, 16 figures, 37 tables. 9 pages of main text
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly extended with reusable skills, but untrusted skill content can induce operations outside the user's task. Detecting this contextual risk requires more than suspicious-pattern matching, while dynamic analysis incurs the cost of skill execution. We find that hidden states formed during prefill contain readable information about task-operation consistency, including across held-out expression forms in controlled evaluations. Matched Operation-state interventions also affect later Boundary states and shift fixed risk readouts toward the donor label. Based on these findings, we introduce LatentTriad, which combines contextual Boundary features, group-adjusted Operation directions, and departures from benign state relationships. All branches share one prefill: detection generates no output tokens, invokes no tools, and executes no skill code. Across 5,830 skill packages from five sources and seven backbones, LatentTriad achieves 99.0-99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0-94.6% source-macro F1. A separately measured compact implementation completes prefill and detection in a median of 259-284 ms. These results connect pre-action risk readability and functional influence to execution-free skill screening.

AI.tldr: LatentTriad detects malicious agent skills before execution by reading risk signals from the hidden states of a single prefill pass, combining Boundary features, group-adjusted Operation directions and departures from benign state relations.
AI.motivation: Untrusted skills can induce operations outside the user's task, and detecting this contextual risk by pattern matching or dynamic execution is either unreliable or costly.
AI.method: The authors find that prefill hidden states encode task-operation consistency, and that matched Operation-state interventions affect later Boundary states; LatentTriad combines contextual Boundary features, group-adjusted Operation directions and departures from benign state relationships, with all branches sharing one prefill and no output tokens, tool calls or skill code execution.
AI.result: Across 5,830 skill packages from five sources and seven backbones it achieves 99.0-99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0-94.6% source-macro F1, and a compact implementation completes prefill and detection in a median of 259-284 ms.
AI.conclusion: Pre-action risk representations in hidden states support fast, execution-free screening of malicious agent skills.

title: The Platonic Brain: Representational Convergence in EEG Foundation Models
summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) predicts that artificial neural networks converge on shared representations as scale and performance increase. We test whether these predictions hold for representations of the human brain with EEG foundation models. Using EEG recordings from six participants watching a television series, together with aligned visual and language content, we tested whether EEG foundation-model representations converge within and across modalities as their embeddings become better at decoding an informative set of EEG markers. We found that EEG models with greater decodability showed stronger cross-family alignment in both local neighbourhood similarity and global structure, not consistently increasing with model parameter count. Cross-modal convergence was modality and metric dependent: greater EEG decodability was associated with stronger global alignment to language, but not consistently to vision models, while local alignment showed no consistent association. This dissociation may reflect local sensitivity to low-level sensory features, whereas global geometry may capture weaker shared semantic structure.

AI.tldr: The paper tests the Platonic Representation Hypothesis on EEG foundation models and finds that models with greater EEG decodability align more strongly with each other and with language models, but not consistently with vision models or with parameter count.
AI.motivation: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts convergence of artificial representations with scale and performance, and it is unclear whether this holds for representations of the human brain.
AI.method: Embeddings of several EEG foundation models are compared on EEG recordings from six participants watching a television series, together with aligned visual and language content, using local neighbourhood similarity and global structure metrics, with models ranked by how well they decode an informative set of EEG markers.
AI.result: EEG models with greater decodability showed stronger cross-family alignment in local and global structure, not consistently increasing with parameter count; cross-modal convergence was stronger for global alignment to language, but not consistently for vision, and local alignment showed no consistent association.
AI.conclusion: Convergence toward shared representations depends on modality and metric, and global geometry may capture shared semantic structure, while local alignment may reflect sensitivity to low-level sensory features.

title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?
summary: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.

AI.tldr: Continual AutoResearch is an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset agents on matched task streams, and finds that persistent state improves research efficiency for all five frontier agents without consistently improving final solutions.
AI.motivation: Autoresearch evaluations start each problem in a new agent session, which is costly and leaves open whether agents can retain and apply prior insights on new tasks.
AI.method: The environment covers nine task families, including synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting and tabular AutoML, and a memory ablation varies what information agents retain from prior tasks, measuring first-solution quality, research efficiency and final held-out performance.
AI.result: Persistent state improves the research efficiency of all five agents, letting them find stronger solutions sooner, but these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions.
AI.conclusion: Retaining experience and using it effectively are distinct capabilities, so continuity alone does not guarantee better research outcomes.

title: From Opinions to Commitments: Unstable Assignments and Silent Choices in AI-Mediated Proposals
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to turn citizens' opinions into collective proposals. These proposals can make assignments: who should act, what must be done, how much one should spend and by when. However, if the assignments change when the same opinions are processed again, publishing a single proposal can hide alternatives that participants never get to see. We examined this issue in four LLM mediators (three open-weight and one commercial) using opinions from DeliberationBank and Polis. For each task, a mediator drafted a proposal from thirty opinions five times, varying either the random seed or the order of the opinions. In 17% of five-run sets from the open-weight mediators and 20% from the commercial one, some runs contained assignments while others did not. Reordering the opinions changed the assignments almost as often as replacing them with opinions from different citizens. Three human annotators confirmed that the detected differences between runs were real, although the LLM judge overstated how often they occurred. Substantial variation remained under four safeguards: temperature zero, a commercial mediator, draft selection, and draft merging. The mediator's objective also shaped representation: prompts seeking agreement covered minority positions much less often than prompts asking to describe differences. A single proposal can therefore obscure choices in both the assignments it proposes and the views it excludes. We propose audits that make alternative assignments visible and disclose the objective behind each proposal.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LLM mediators turning citizen opinions into proposals can produce unstable assignments, so a single published proposal can hide alternative assignments and excluded views.
AI.motivation: Publishing one LLM-drafted proposal can hide alternatives if the assignments of who acts, what is done, how much to spend and by when change when the same opinions are processed again.
AI.method: Four LLM mediators (three open-weight and one commercial) drafted proposals from thirty opinions drawn from DeliberationBank and Polis five times each, varying either the random seed or the opinion order, with human annotators checking the detected differences.
AI.result: In 17% of five-run sets from open-weight mediators and 20% from the commercial one, some runs contained assignments and others did not; reordering changed assignments almost as often as swapping in opinions from different citizens; substantial variation persisted under temperature zero, a commercial mediator, draft selection and draft merging; agreement-seeking prompts covered minority positions much less than prompts asking to describe differences.
AI.conclusion: Audits should make alternative assignments visible and disclose the objective behind each proposal, since a single proposal can obscure both its choices and the views it excludes.

title: Meta$^2$: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Harness Evolution in Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.

AI.tldr: Meta2 learns reusable textual guidance for when and how to evolve an agent harness offline and applies it online through task-local KEEP or EVOLVE edits, reaching the highest reported performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra on two long-horizon benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Offline harness optimization yields one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to new evidence, while online evolution must reason about each intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is unavailable at test time.
AI.method: Offline, Meta2 learns a textual Meta-Skill by contrasting training rollouts under three configurations (no evolver, an evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill, and an evolver given privileged verifier information); online, an evolver combines the frozen Meta-Skill with trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness or EVOLVE it through an edit that applies to the rest of the same run.
AI.result: On Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1 Meta2 achieves 81.00% and 44.44% respectively, the highest among evaluated methods, and ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and of keeping online harness edits task-local.
AI.conclusion: Evolution guidance can transfer across tasks while harness edits stay local to each run, without any held-out verifier feedback at test time.

title: Creating Power Flexibility in Datacenters via Query Routing
summary: The growing energy requirements of large language model inference highlight the need for datacenters to support safe grid operation by providing power demand flexibility, while maintaining service for interactive workloads. This work investigates query routing as a mechanism to enable such capability by dynamically allocating queries across different language model instances without deferring requests. We develop a general analytical framework that connects query arrival rates and sequence length distributions to token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity, and power consumption of model instances. Leveraging this framework, we characterize the feasible query routing allocations and the corresponding power demand flexibilities, enabling the selection of routing strategies to achieve desired power consumption behavior. We validate our framework across four GPU platforms on language models ranging from 1B to 70B parameters, obtaining 2.8% mean absolute percentage error in estimating achievable power flexibility. We evaluate our approach on a real trace-driven simulation of a 10,000 H100 GPUs datacenter, exhibiting flexibility up to 16% of total power consumption, with 90% of the desired power reduction achieved within approximately 10 seconds. These results establish query routing as an effective mechanism for datacenter power demand flexibility and demonstrate the broader applicability of our proposed framework to datacenter level planning and orchestration.

AI.tldr: The paper uses query routing across LLM instances to give datacenters power demand flexibility without deferring requests, supported by an analytical framework validated on four GPU platforms with 2.8% mean absolute percentage error.
AI.motivation: LLM inference is energy intensive, and datacenters need to offer grid flexibility while still serving interactive workloads, so a mechanism that does not defer requests is needed.
AI.method: A general analytical framework links query arrival rates and sequence length distributions to token iteration time, request residence time, serving capacity and power consumption, which characterizes feasible routing allocations and the resulting power flexibility; it is validated on models from 1B to 70B parameters and evaluated in trace-driven simulation of a 10,000-H100 datacenter.
AI.result: The framework estimates achievable power flexibility with 2.8% mean absolute percentage error, the simulated datacenter reaches flexibility of up to 16% of total power consumption, and 90% of the desired power reduction is achieved within about 10 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Query routing is an effective mechanism for datacenter power flexibility and the framework applies to datacenter-level planning and orchestration.

title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning
comment: 38 pages, 21 figures
summary: Generating HTML from natural-language specifications is an important application of code large language models (LLMs). Despite producing renderable pages, current models often fail to ensure functionality and visual quality during actual interaction. Existing methods typically target task-specific webpage supervision, leaving demanding interactive artifact optimization underexplored. Using mini-games as a challenging testbed, we expose limitations in interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment fidelity that are obscured by shallow webpage interactions. We introduce WebCatalyst, a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework with three complementary components: a game-level GUI assessor for sustained interaction and evaluation, Visual Anchor for mitigating VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit for grounding token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, predominantly for games, WebCatalyst raises the Cookie-Bench Mini Games score from 68.8 to 75.3 and also the WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 in average rank across evaluated metrics. Further analysis shows that Visual Anchor prevents aesthetic degradation, while runtime-grounded credit assignment accelerates functional improvement. Together, our results show that improving feedback fidelity is the key to substantially advancing interactive HTML generation.

AI.tldr: WebCatalyst is a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework that improves interactive HTML generation by using a game-level GUI assessor, Visual Anchor against VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit for runtime-grounded credit assignment.
AI.motivation: Models that generate HTML from specifications often produce renderable pages that fail under real interaction, and mini-games expose limits in interaction experience, reward signals and credit assignment that shallow webpage tasks hide.
AI.method: The framework combines a game-level GUI assessor for sustained interaction and evaluation, Visual Anchor to mitigate VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit to ground token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces, trained on fewer than 1K requests.
AI.result: On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it raises the Cookie-Bench Mini Games score from 68.8 to 75.3 and WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9, outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 in average rank across evaluated metrics; Visual Anchor prevents aesthetic degradation and runtime-grounded credit speeds functional improvement.
AI.conclusion: Improving feedback fidelity is key to advancing interactive HTML generation, and runtime-grounded rewards are more effective than shallow webpage supervision.

title: Learning Behaviorally Relevant Dynamics in Multimodal Neural Recordings
summary: Multimodal neural data can enable a more complete understanding of brain dynamics underlying behavior. Modalities such as spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), and behavior capture diverse spatiotemporal aspects of brain processes, yet prior neural-behavioral models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality. By leveraging these complementary strengths, multimodal neural fusion can provide a unified, rich representation of brain-behavior processes and address the limitations of single-modality analyses. Here we develop BREM-NET, a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that integrates behavior with multiple neural modalities having distinct statistical characteristics and temporal resolutions. BREM-NET performs multimodal neural fusion during inference while separating behaviorally relevant and residual neural dynamics via a structured learning framework. In a public multimodal non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and local field potential recordings during a 2D reaching task, BREM-NET separates these two types of dynamics and learns them more accurately, as reflected in better behavior decoding, better neural prediction, and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and it retains these capabilities when neural modalities are asynchronous or suffer dropouts, which are major challenges in real-world recordings. This framework provides a new tool for studying behaviorally relevant neural computations across spatiotemporal scales of brain activity.

AI.tldr: BREM-NET is a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that fuses spiking activity, local field potentials and behaviour to separate behaviourally relevant from residual neural dynamics, and it stays robust when modalities are asynchronous or missing.
AI.motivation: Prior neural-behaviour models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality, and real recordings often have asynchronous or dropped-out modalities.
AI.method: BREM-NET integrates behaviour with several neural modalities of different statistics and temporal resolutions, performs multimodal fusion during inference, and separates behaviourally relevant and residual dynamics through a structured learning framework.
AI.result: On a public non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and LFP recordings during a 2D reaching task, it learns both dynamic types more accurately, with better behaviour decoding, better neural prediction and stronger latent alignment with behaviour, and it keeps these abilities under asynchrony and dropouts.
AI.conclusion: The framework is a new tool for studying behaviourally relevant neural computation across spatiotemporal scales.

title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
summary: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge. We present AgentAM, a large language model (LLM) agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained surrogates of spatter and melt pool geometry for SS316L through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Polynomial surrogates trained on 279 single-track simulations predict melt pool dimensions ($R^2 \geq 0.95$) and spatter volume ($R^2 = 0.83$ on test data) at any power-velocity point in the trained range, and geometric criteria assign each point a geometry-derived defect regime (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable) that matches the regime obtained from the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation. The agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. Minimum-spatter optima often sat within 10 $\mu$m of the lack-of-fusion boundary; a margin-aware optimizer moved them away from all thresholds and raised the estimated probability of remaining classified Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under an assumed 2% process drift, and from 0.72 to 0.91 when jointly sampled cross-validated geometry residuals were added. About 40-50 well-spread simulations sufficed to reproduce the defect map. To evaluate the agent layer, we introduce a 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, plus eight prompts (40 runs) on margin-aware requests. Over the 725 runs of the main benchmark the agent passed the intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts, reported the scored spatter values and defect classes faithfully and met every stated constraint in the 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.

AI.tldr: AgentAM is an LLM agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained polynomial surrogates for melt pool geometry and spatter in laser powder bed fusion of SS316L, through the Model Context Protocol.
AI.motivation: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge.
AI.method: Polynomial surrogates are trained on 279 single-track simulations, geometric criteria assign defect regimes (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable), and the agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained, margin-aware optimization.
AI.result: Surrogates predict melt pool dimensions with R2 of at least 0.95 and spatter volume with R2 of 0.83 on test data; the defect regime matches the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation; the margin-aware optimizer raises the estimated probability of remaining Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under 2% drift; the agent passed intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts and met every constraint in 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.
AI.conclusion: Natural-language agents over validated surrogates can make predictive process models usable by engineers, with margin-aware optimization keeping optima away from defect boundaries.

title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks
summary: Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor.
