We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks.

AI.tldr: JHiMA-WebRL jointly trains a task decomposer and a subtask-conditioned actor with a hierarchical extension of GRPO, so that a 14B pair of 7B models reaches 37.2% average success on WebArena-Lite-v2.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon web tasks need joint high-level planning and visually grounded execution, but modular multi-agent systems usually leave the planner untrained with respect to the actor.
AI.method: A strong teacher model builds structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories to fine-tune the decomposer and actor, and GRPO is extended with hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages to optimize both in the interactive WebArena environment.
AI.result: JHiMA-WebRL-14B achieves an average success rate of 37.2% on WebArena-Lite-v2, compared with 24% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent fine-tuned with RL on the same tasks under the same protocol, and ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer outperforms updating the actor alone.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learned role factorization with smaller models is a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic web agents.

title: The Geometry of Ignorance: Detecting Suppressed Knowledge in LLMs through Activation Fragmentation
comment: Presented at EMNLP Findings 2026
summary: Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. A reference implementation is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness, based on the geometric coherence of anon-vectors, which separates known from unknown concepts in LLMs and correlates with adversarial recovery after unlearning.
AI.motivation: Behavioural metrics can be fooled by suppression, since a model that refuses may still hold recoverable knowledge, so a reliable test of whether an LLM genuinely knows a concept is needed.
AI.method: Anon-vectors are the hidden-state differences between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase; the geometric coherence of these vectors is measured across layers in ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three families.
AI.result: All fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts; after unlearning with five algorithms, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types, though the direction of that relationship depends on attack methodology, and layer-resolved analysis shows high attack-specific correlations invisible to behavioural evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The fragmentation geometry gives a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics.

title: You don't need long context
comment: Technical report. 31 pages, 8 figures
summary: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that frequent context compaction lets frontier LLMs keep task accuracy on long-horizon and long-input tasks with short contexts, and proposes semantic state space models as an alternative to long-context models.
AI.motivation: Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier ones, by up to 7x on frontier open-weight models, which raises the question of whether long context is needed at all.
AI.method: Through frequent compaction the authors test short-context operation across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks, and also run long-horizon software engineering tasks with at most one action per context.
AI.result: Frontier models sacrifice little to no task accuracy with short contexts, and performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even with at most one action per context.
AI.conclusion: The findings question the need for long-context language models and motivate the concept of semantic state space models.

title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
summary: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that speculative decoding affects reasoning, not just speed, and trains the draft model to be rejected at critical agent decision points so that those tokens are sampled from the target model under lower numerical noise.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding is usually treated as a pure systems optimization that does not change output behaviour, but numerical noise grows within verification windows and draft acceptance can shift the output distribution of long-horizon agents after about 30 steps.
AI.method: Critical decision points are identified in agent traces, the draft model is trained to favour adversarial preferences at those points, and at inference the draft and target diverge there, so verification restarts and the critical tokens come from the target model.
AI.result: On complex agentic coding benchmarks the approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution, and it trains only 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.
AI.conclusion: Speculative decoding can act as an allocator of context precision that improves long-horizon agent accuracy, not only as an accelerator.

title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation
comment: Accepted on Conference on Optimization, Modeling, Simulation, and Analytics (COMOSA 2026)
summary: Bitcoin perpetual futures trade continuously with shallow liquidity and high price impact, making them prone to millisecond-scale flash crashes. Agent-based limit order book simulators are a natural tool for studying such events, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale. We propose a four-stage pipeline that constructs a reproducible 100 ms BTCUSDT flash-crash event panel from 66 detected events, elicits behavioral priors for four agent archetypes using an offline large language model conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, instantiates a heterogeneous limit order book simulator with the validated priors, and applies causal discovery plus counterfactual analysis to the resulting synthetic panel. Across 500 simulation runs, LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uninformative uniform priors and generate heav- ier return tails. In the frozen counterfactual analysis, reducing leverage amplification by one within-sample standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, whereas reducing directional pressure yields only a marginal change. These find- ings suggest that empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment

AI.tldr: The paper uses an offline LLM to elicit behavioural priors for agent archetypes in a heterogeneous limit order book simulator of 100 ms BTCUSDT flash crashes, reproducing crash rates far above those from uninformative priors.
AI.motivation: Agent-based limit order book simulators are useful for studying flash crashes, but their behavioural parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline builds a reproducible 100 ms event panel from 66 detected flash crashes, elicits priors for four agent archetypes with an offline LLM conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, runs a heterogeneous simulator with those priors, and applies causal discovery and counterfactual analysis to the synthetic panel.
AI.result: Across 500 simulation runs LLM-elicited priors give a crash rate of 0.176 against 0.008 under uniform priors and generate heavier return tails; reducing leverage amplification by one standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, while reducing directional pressure gives only a marginal change.
AI.conclusion: Empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment.

title: Development of tools for all-cause mortality prediction in heart failure patients: a systematic review
comment: 26 pages and 5 figures, preprint and submitted for review
summary: Heart failure is a serious medical condition associated with risk of acute deterioration, recurrent hospitalizations and high mortality making accurate mortality prediction potentially valuable for patient care and healthcare planning. Numerous prognostic models have been developed using conventional statistics (CS), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), but variation in study populations, heart failure definitions, prediction horizons and development practices may limit interpretation of applicability. We conducted a systematic review of mortality prediction models published between 2009 to the start of 2026 searching three databases (PubMed, IEEE and Scopus) for studies predicting all-cause mortality over a 1-60 months prediction horizon among patients with heart failure. Data extracted were cohort characteristics, heart failure definitions, model development, cohort size, validation practices, mortality, computational model design and reported performance. The risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Of 1516 publications identified, 56 met the inclusion criteria. Publication numbers increased over the observation period, alongside increasing use of ML/DL models and decreasing use of CS approaches. Most development cohorts (64%) were classified as Unknown/Undefined heart failure, reflecting inconsistent reporting and terminology that did not correspond with established heart failure guidelines. External validation was reported in 23% of studies. Overall, research in modeling heart failure mortality has grown alongside increasing adoption of ML/DL approaches. Greater standardization of study design and reporting is needed for meaningful comparison, reproducibility and evaluation of models for clinical application.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 56 studies of all-cause mortality prediction tools in heart failure, covering 2009 to early 2026, finds growing use of machine learning and deep learning, inconsistent heart failure definitions and external validation in only 23% of studies.
AI.motivation: Numerous mortality prediction models for heart failure have been developed, but variation in populations, definitions, horizons and development practices limits how well they can be interpreted and applied.
AI.method: Three databases (PubMed, IEEE and Scopus) were searched and 1,516 publications were screened, with 56 meeting the inclusion criteria; data were extracted on cohorts, definitions, validation and performance, and risk of bias and applicability were assessed with PROBAST.
AI.result: Publications increased over the period, with more machine learning and deep learning models and fewer conventional statistical approaches; 64% of development cohorts were classified as Unknown or Undefined heart failure, and external validation was reported in 23% of studies.
AI.conclusion: Greater standardization of study design and reporting in heart failure mortality modelling is needed for comparison, reproducibility and clinical application.

title: ReVi: Recursive Recap Video Generation
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures, 17 tables
summary: Novels tell rich stories, but their textual form cannot directly present the sights and sounds of the worlds they describe. Film adaptations offer an audiovisual experience but require substantial production effort and viewing time; film recaps are shorter but depend on existing footage. Neither route directly provides a concise audiovisual account of a novel. We therefore study novel-to-recap video generation: producing a self-contained, source-grounded audiovisual retelling directly from a novel within a fixed viewing-time budget. This task requires compressing the story while preserving causal connections, allocating sufficient time to retained events, and aligning narration with newly generated visuals. We propose ReVi, a dual-loop multi-agent framework guided by edit first, generate second. Its Inner Loop plans story content, narration time, and corresponding shots before video generation. Across novels, its Outer Loop performs recursive self-improvement by revising both the editing policy and the meta policy that governs its revision. Experiments on two evaluation sets show that ReVi improves recap quality and duration compliance over representative baselines, with human ratings and multi-round improvement results providing further support.

AI.tldr: ReVi generates source-grounded recap videos directly from a novel within a fixed viewing-time budget, using a dual-loop multi-agent framework that plans story and shots before generation and recursively revises its own policies.
AI.motivation: Novels cannot directly present their sights and sounds, and film adaptations or recaps need heavy production or existing footage, so a concise audiovisual account grounded in the novel itself is lacking.
AI.method: The Inner Loop plans story content, narration time and corresponding shots before video generation, following edit first, generate second; the Outer Loop recursively revises both the editing policy and the meta policy that governs its revision.
AI.result: On two evaluation sets ReVi improves recap quality and duration compliance over representative baselines, and human ratings and multi-round improvement results provide further support.
AI.conclusion: Planning edits before generating video, with self-improving loops, makes novel-to-recap generation more faithful and better timed.

title: Learning Directional Randers Geometry for Latent-Space Exploration
summary: Deep neural networks extract powerful latent representations from images, enabling fast and efficient downstream analysis. However, these latent spaces lack explicit geometric structure, leading to possibly poor interpolation fidelity and misleading extrapolation. Latent interpolation techniques assume symmetric transition costs which are often not the case for real world data. Their symmetric nature cannot capture directional processes, such as disease progression, where certain transitions are impossible (e.g. tumor growth dynamics or cognitive improvement in Alzheimer's disease). Although Riemannian metrics extend Euclidean geometry by incorporating curvature, they remain symmetric. We show that understanding asymmetry and not curvature alone directly addresses these problems. To do so we propose a new Finsler-Randers metric learning framework. It incorporates direction-dependent distances, thus enabling the computation of trajectories respecting monotonic sequential constraints. We demonstrate its potential for interpolation and extrapolation on controlled cross-sectional datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Finsler-Randers metric learning framework for latent spaces, using direction-dependent distances so that interpolation and extrapolation respect monotonic, asymmetric transitions such as disease progression.
AI.motivation: Latent interpolation assumes symmetric transition costs, and Riemannian metrics remain symmetric, so they cannot represent irreversible processes in which some transitions are impossible.
AI.method: A new Finsler-Randers metric is learned to incorporate direction-dependent distances, which enables computing trajectories that respect monotonic sequential constraints.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate interpolation and extrapolation on controlled cross-sectional datasets, but the abstract reports no quantitative comparison.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetry, rather than curvature alone, addresses poor interpolation fidelity and misleading extrapolation in latent spaces of directional processes.

title: From Forecasting to Feedback: Evaluating Learned Dynamics for Tokamak Control
summary: Learned temporal models are moving beyond offline forecasting toward interactive environments for decision making, yet logged-trajectory accuracy need not predict closed-loop behavior under policies optimized in the learned model. This forecasting-control gap matters in tokamak magnetic control, where coupled plasma-circuit dynamics and actuator constraints can amplify errors through feedback. Using a calibrated free-boundary Grad-Shafranov solver, we collect four datasets in a 2x2 design over physics-parameter and current-reference coverage. At matched budgets of 500, 1k, 3k, and 5k rollouts, we train 16 action-conditioned Transformers; PPO policies optimized in the 5k surrogates are then evaluated without adaptation on six reference-solver conditions. Only joint-coverage D4 shows monotonically decreasing cross-condition mean error, whereas D1 improves in distribution but degrades out of distribution. Binary completion masks substantial closed-loop differences: D2-D4 each complete 83.3% of conditions, but reach on average 99.0%, 94.7%, and 90.5% of the evaluation horizon, while their worst conditions reach 94.2%, 68.2%, and 43.2%. Policies trained with action noise complete 5/24 matched conditions, compared with 19/24 under nominal training, and have a lower mean horizon-capped episode length. Based on one trained policy per configuration and one evaluation realization per condition, the results support combining prediction error, episode completion, condition-level duration, and tracking quality.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates learned dynamics models for tokamak magnetic control and finds that logged-trajectory accuracy does not predict closed-loop performance, with only the joint-coverage dataset improving consistently across conditions.
AI.motivation: Learned models are increasingly used in interactive control, but accuracy on logged trajectories may not predict behaviour under policies optimized within the model, and coupled plasma-circuit dynamics can amplify errors through feedback in tokamak control.
AI.method: Using a calibrated free-boundary Grad-Shafranov solver, four datasets are collected in a 2x2 design over physics-parameter and current-reference coverage; 16 action-conditioned Transformers are trained at budgets of 500 to 5k rollouts, and PPO policies optimized in the 5k surrogates are evaluated without adaptation on six reference-solver conditions.
AI.result: Only the joint-coverage dataset D4 shows monotonically decreasing cross-condition mean error, while D1 improves in distribution but degrades out of distribution; D2 to D4 each complete 83.3% of conditions but reach on average 99.0%, 94.7% and 90.5% of the horizon, with worst conditions at 94.2%, 68.2% and 43.2%; action-noise training completes 5 of 24 matched conditions against 19 of 24 under nominal training.
AI.conclusion: Prediction error, episode completion, condition-level duration and tracking quality should be considered together when judging learned models for control, since one trained policy per configuration gives limited evidence.

title: A Compact Formula-Aware Spreadsheet Abstraction for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist spreadsheet users with tasks such as spreadsheet model construction, formula generation, and data analysis, yet their interaction with real-world spreadsheets remains limited by the mismatch between the structure of spreadsheets and the sequential textual representations typically provided to LLMs. We propose a compact formula-aware spreadsheet abstraction that represents large homogeneous ranges through their positions, types, R1C1 formula patterns, and selected boundary values. An efficient algorithm detects and structures these ranges before a textual serialization is supplied to an LLM. The abstraction is provided to the LLM before detailed spreadsheet content is submitted, improving the accuracy and efficiency of spreadsheet processing while reducing token consumption. We evaluate the method on 50 spreadsheet-query cases. The evaluation shows that the abstraction alone was sufficient to answer some queries. When additional spreadsheet content is required, the abstraction reduces the amount of data that must be submitted to the LLM, thereby reducing token consumption. The abstraction layer also improves the reliability and accuracy of spreadsheet processing. We conclude by discussing further techniques for combining spreadsheet static analysis with artificial intelligence to improve the reliability, accuracy, and efficiency of AI assisted spreadsheet tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a compact, formula-aware abstraction of spreadsheets that summarises large homogeneous ranges by position, type, R1C1 formula pattern and boundary values, and gives it to an LLM before the detailed content. On 50 spreadsheet-query cases, the abstraction alone sufficed for some queries and reduced the data that must be submitted, lowering token use.
AI.motivation: LLMs interact poorly with real spreadsheets because the spreadsheet's two-dimensional, formula-based structure does not match the sequential text serialisations given to models.
AI.method: An efficient algorithm detects and structures large homogeneous ranges, which are represented by their positions, types, R1C1 formula patterns and selected boundary values, and this abstraction is supplied to the LLM before the detailed spreadsheet content, with a textual serialisation.
AI.result: On 50 spreadsheet-query cases, the abstraction alone was sufficient to answer some queries, and when more content was needed, it reduced the amount of data submitted and the token consumption, while also improving reliability and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Combining spreadsheet static analysis with AI could further improve the reliability, accuracy and efficiency of AI-assisted spreadsheet tasks.

title: Physics-Informed Functional Tucker Method with RKHS Factors for Sparse Spatiotemporal Reconstruction
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Reconstructing physical dynamics from fixed sparse sensors and missing frames is a fundamental challenge in scientific research. Sparsity leaves large regions of the field unconstrained, making the inverse problem ill-posed: a model may fit the observed sensors while producing inaccurate off-sensor structures or unreliable predictions between support frames. To this end, we propose PhysFTM---a physics-informed functional Tucker model that parameterizes the Tucker mode factors in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and incorporates PDE constraints through finite-difference residuals evaluated at off-sensor collocation points. These residuals provide additional physical information in regions without direct observational supervision. PhysFTM first reconstructs continuous spatial fields at support frames via an alternating minimization scheme, optimizing the Tucker core tensor and the RKHS-based factors separately. To enable missing-frame reconstruction, PhysFTM constructs a continuous trajectory in Tucker-core space, which is decoded by the learned spatial RKHS-FTM representation to recover the full spatiotemporal field. Experiments on Allen--Cahn, Navier--Stokes, three-dimensional Heat equations, and a three-dimensional gridded Copernicus ocean reanalysis demonstrate accurate 2D/3D reconstruction under two missing-frame protocols. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PhysFTM, a physics-informed functional Tucker model whose factors live in RKHSs and which is trained with PDE residuals at off-sensor collocation points, to reconstruct sparsely sampled spatiotemporal physical fields with missing frames. It reports accurate 2D and 3D reconstruction on four benchmark systems under two missing-frame protocols.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing physical dynamics from sparse sensors and missing frames is ill-posed, since a model can fit the sensors yet be inaccurate off-sensor and between frames.
AI.method: The Tucker mode factors are parameterised in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and PDE constraints are imposed through finite-difference residuals at off-sensor collocation points. Continuous spatial fields are fitted at support frames by alternating minimisation over the core tensor and RKHS factors, and missing frames are recovered by a continuous trajectory in Tucker-core space decoded by the spatial representation.
AI.result: Experiments on Allen-Cahn, Navier-Stokes, three-dimensional Heat equations and a three-dimensional gridded Copernicus ocean reanalysis demonstrate accurate 2D and 3D reconstruction under two missing-frame protocols.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed residuals supply supervision where observations are absent, and a Tucker-core trajectory allows full spatiotemporal reconstruction from sparse data.

title: NepTTS-Bench: Native-Speaker Benchmarking and NepaliMOS for Nepali Text-to-Speech
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Dataset: this https URL ; code: this https URL
summary: Nepali TTS has reached a point where multiple systems are available, but there is no shared evaluation to compare them. NepTTS-Bench was created to address what existing automated and manual evaluation systems lack for Nepali TTS. A controlled benchmark with phonological grounding which contains 205 sentences (77 minimal pairs targeting aspiration, retroflex/dental contrasts, nasalization, gemination, and schwa deletion) which is rated by 180 speakers. There are 6,962 ratings for 10 TTS configurations and two human references. Along with this 7 ASR systems were evaluated for round-trip CER. SCOREQ was also run as an automated baseline. The key finding is that automated evaluation like SCOREQ prefers proprietary systems like ElevenLabs but native listeners prefer Piper. This is contributed by the fact that most of the systems not properly tuned for Nepali tend to show Hindi phonological behaviour and our minimal pairs are designed to surface such contrasts. We also present NepaliMOS predictor which is fine tuned on collected ratings. NepaliMOS achieves system-level rho = 0.90 on the dense panel but drops to utterance-level rho = 0.43 under leave-one-system-out evaluation. This is statistically significant and confirms that NepaliMOS captures genuine signal but cross-provider transfer is limited. A human calibration is recommended for new systems for which we release a Python evaluation package for practitioners to run the benchmark against new systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NepTTS-Bench, a phonologically grounded benchmark for Nepali text-to-speech with 205 sentences rated by 180 speakers, and NepaliMOS, a quality predictor fine-tuned on those ratings. Automated metrics prefer proprietary systems while native listeners prefer Piper, and NepaliMOS transfers poorly across providers at the utterance level.
AI.motivation: Multiple Nepali TTS systems exist but have no shared evaluation, and existing automated and manual evaluation methods do not capture Nepali-specific contrasts.
AI.method: A controlled benchmark of 205 sentences, including 77 minimal pairs targeting aspiration, retroflex and dental contrasts, nasalisation, gemination and schwa deletion, was rated by 180 speakers, yielding 6,962 ratings for 10 TTS configurations and two human references. Seven ASR systems were evaluated for round-trip CER, SCOREQ was run as an automated baseline, and NepaliMOS was fine-tuned on the collected ratings.
AI.result: 6,962 ratings were collected for 10 TTS configurations and two human references. SCOREQ prefers proprietary systems such as ElevenLabs, whereas native listeners prefer Piper. NepaliMOS reaches system-level rho = 0.90 on the dense panel but only utterance-level rho = 0.43 under leave-one-system-out evaluation, which is statistically significant.
AI.conclusion: NepaliMOS captures genuine signal, but cross-provider transfer is limited, so human calibration is recommended for new systems; a Python evaluation package is released.

title: DualClusterNet: Personalized Pattern-Space Composition for Next-POI Recommendation
comment: submitted to WWW2027
summary: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation supports personalized place discovery on location-based Web platforms. Mobility routines can recur across users while being realized at different places and adapted to individual preferences. We present DualClusterNet, a causal sequential recommender that composes two population-shared prototype dictionaries. At each observed prefix, soft routers retrieve pattern and spatial mixtures; a factorized multiplicative interaction couples them, feature-wise affine modulation adapts the shared representation, and a separate user-conditioned branch with an additive--projective gate retains individual variation. The prediction head combines this representation with a learned first-order transition term and ranks the complete training POI vocabulary. We evaluate on NYC and TKY using a training-only vocabulary and an original-final-target protocol that neither bridges unknown POIs nor substitutes earlier targets. The available single-seed results show competitive full-candidate ranking, while controlled analyses support the contribution of the compositional and personalized branches. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DualClusterNet, a causal sequential recommender for next-POI prediction that composes two population-shared prototype dictionaries with user-conditioned personalisation. It reports competitive full-candidate ranking on NYC and TKY, with single-seed results.
AI.motivation: Mobility routines recur across users but are realised at different places and adapt to individual preferences, which a single shared representation may not capture.
AI.method: Soft routers retrieve pattern and spatial mixtures from two prototype dictionaries at each observed prefix. A factorised multiplicative interaction couples them, feature-wise affine modulation adapts the shared representation, and a user-conditioned branch with an additive-projective gate retains individual variation. The prediction head adds a learned first-order transition term and ranks the full training POI vocabulary, evaluated with a training-only vocabulary and an original-final-target protocol.
AI.result: The available single-seed results show competitive full-candidate ranking on NYC and TKY, and controlled analyses support the contribution of the compositional and personalised branches.
AI.conclusion: Composing shared prototype patterns with personalised branches is a useful design for next-POI recommendation, though the evidence is from single-seed experiments.

title: Learning to read residual images for single-pixel photography
comment: first submit
summary: Continuous video scales in cost with camera count, resolution and recording duration, yet many monitoring tasks seek events rather than complete images and can operate on a compact single-pixel measurement stream. Recovering a chosen interval as video is then desirable, but at 0.24\% of the pixel count the scene correlation image looks like noise and per-clip optimization takes minutes. Correlating the residual of an estimate with the coding patterns nevertheless gives a residual image, the gradient of a centered measurement loss. Lifted through a pretrained video decoder, its agreement with the true error exceeds that of control decoders. Video-latent inversion (VLI) then outperforms frame-wise image-latent reconstruction at 1{,}000 bucket values. Measurement-Gradient-Conditioned Video Flow (MGV-Flow), trained once to read the lifted residual image with preceding frames, reconstructs five frames in 1.55\,s at 22.9\,dB median PSNR, against 398\,s and 18.1\,dB for VLI, with the largest gains in high-motion scenes. Directional fidelity ranks 30 coding configurations and selects one needing a third fewer bucket values. On a physical system, MGV-Flow outperforms per-frame reconstruction without retraining. A sliding window over the bucket-value stream yields 3.2 frames per second on one RTX~4090 and, in theory, 20 frames per second on a data-centre accelerator. Demonstrations are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MGV-Flow, a video flow model that reads a residual image lifted through a pretrained video decoder to reconstruct video from single-pixel bucket-value measurements. It reconstructs five frames in 1.55 s at 22.9 dB median PSNR, versus 398 s and 18.1 dB for the VLI baseline.
AI.motivation: Single-pixel measurement streams can support monitoring, but at 0.24% of the pixel count the correlation image looks like noise and per-clip optimisation takes minutes.
AI.method: The residual image, which is the gradient of a centred measurement loss, is obtained by correlating the estimate's residual with the coding patterns and lifted through a pretrained video decoder. Video-latent inversion (VLI) is compared with frame-wise image-latent reconstruction, and MGV-Flow is trained once to read the lifted residual image with preceding frames. A sliding window is applied over the bucket-value stream, and 30 coding configurations are ranked by directional fidelity.
AI.result: MGV-Flow reconstructs five frames in 1.55 s at 22.9 dB median PSNR, against 398 s and 18.1 dB for VLI, with the largest gains in high-motion scenes. It outperforms per-frame reconstruction on a physical system without retraining and runs at 3.2 frames per second on one RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: Residual-image conditioning enables fast single-pixel video reconstruction, and the approach is estimated in theory to reach 20 frames per second on a data-centre accelerator.

title: HyVox: Rethinking Low-Power Voice Intelligence towards Neuromorphic-von Neumann Edge Computing
summary: We present HyVox, a hybrid neuromorphic--von Neumann system for low-energy open-set speaker identification under tight energy budgets. HyVox splits the workload at the speaker embedding. A neuromorphic processor embeds the speech with sparse, event-driven computation, and a von Neumann microcontroller holds the speaker gallery and makes every decision: it scores queries by cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users by writing a prototype, with no weight update. On the neuromorphic processor, a hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA) SNN backbone learns a synaptic time constant per leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, allocating 832 neurons across fast, medium, and slow timescales. A 32-neuron spiking embedding extractor (SEE), pretrained on episodes that each enroll new speakers and reject outsiders, turns the backbone output into an embedding for speakers unseen in training; its 32 spike counts are the only interface between the two processors. To fit the chip's synapse and integer budgets, we compress the backbone 6.5x to 29.0k synapses, train it for integer bit-shift dynamics, and fine-tune it with chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). CAST trains through a differentiable replica of the chip's integer neuron update, derived from its cycle-accurate simulator, so that gradient descent optimizes the exact weights and thresholds the chip runs; it doubles the top-1 accuracy of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers. On 20 Common Voice households of unseen speakers, HyVox reaches 99.6\% top-1 and 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 members and 94.9\% and 13.2\% with 20, and the network deployed on the neuromorphic chip matches its trained model. Each inference on a 3-s window takes 0.96 s and 1.63 mJ of dynamic energy, 42\% lower latency than the fastest embedded ANN baseline and 13.5x less dynamic and 5.8x less total energy than the most energy-efficient one.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HyVox, a hybrid neuromorphic-von Neumann system for low-energy open-set speaker identification, in which a spiking neuromorphic processor produces speaker embeddings and a microcontroller keeps the gallery and makes all decisions. On 20 Common Voice households it reaches 99.6% top-1 accuracy with 2 members and 94.9% with 20, at 1.63 mJ dynamic energy per 3-s inference.
AI.motivation: Voice intelligence on edge devices must meet tight energy budgets, and speaker identification needs open-set rejection and enrolment of new users without retraining.
AI.method: The workload is split at the speaker embedding. A hierarchical temporal abstraction SNN backbone with learned per-neuron time constants is compressed 6.5x to 29.0k synapses and trained for integer bit-shift dynamics, then fine-tuned with chip-accurate spiking training (CAST) through a differentiable replica of the chip's integer neuron update. A 32-neuron spiking embedding extractor provides the only interface between the two processors. The microcontroller scores queries by cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers and enrols users by writing a prototype.
AI.result: On 20 Common Voice households of unseen speakers, HyVox reaches 99.6% top-1 and 5.5% rejection EER with 2 members, and 94.9% and 13.2% with 20 members. CAST doubles the top-1 accuracy of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers. Each 3-s inference takes 0.96 s and 1.63 mJ, with 42% lower latency than the fastest embedded ANN baseline and 13.5x less dynamic and 5.8x less total energy than the most energy-efficient one.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid design, with chip-accurate training, can match the trained model on the deployed neuromorphic chip while achieving substantially lower latency and energy than ANN baselines for on-device speaker identification.

title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
summary: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EvoMemState, a state-centric memory framework for personal LLM agents that augments persistent facts with Relational States and a request-specific Reasoning State. It reports consistent gains over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing agent memory systems store independent facts and do not model how new facts update, constrain or conflict with earlier ones, nor how facts apply to the current request.
AI.method: Ontology-guided memory state induction extracts persistent facts and builds Relational States that track validity, scope and evolving relations. RL-based state evolution internalises memory-use experience into a policy that generates a request-specific Reasoning State. State-aware reasoning combines relevant facts, their Relational States and the Reasoning State to guide the agent.
AI.result: Experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Modelling memory as evolving states rather than independent facts improves personal agents' use of long-term memory.

title: Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. To address these challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have emerged as a powerful solution, combining retrieval-based methods with generative capabilities to enhance response quality. In this study, we present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to generate responses related to stock market information. The system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to enhance the accuracy and relevance of financial text generation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we employ the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, to measure lexical and structural similarity between generated and reference texts. Experimental results on a dataset of 100 stock market-related queries demonstrate high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents. Additionally, we assess latency to evaluate the system responsiveness, achieving an average response time of 1.16 seconds. These findings confirm that our RAG model is capable of providing accurate and timely stock market insights, making it a promising approach for financial information retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a retrieval-augmented generation system for stock-market information that combines retrieval with generation. On 100 stock-market queries it reports high ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L scores and an average response time of 1.16 seconds.
AI.motivation: Traditional NLP systems for financial information struggle to keep contextual accuracy and produce relevant responses in dynamic financial environments.
AI.method: A RAG system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to generate stock-market responses. Its output is evaluated against reference texts with ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L, and latency is measured.
AI.result: On a dataset of 100 stock-market-related queries, the system achieves high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents, and an average response time of 1.16 seconds.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that the RAG model can provide accurate and timely stock-market insights and is a promising approach for financial information retrieval.

title: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering
summary: Third-party LoRA adapters introduce serious backdoor risks: malicious adapters can maintain normal task performance while embedding hidden, trigger-activated behaviors, making them difficult to detect through standard utility evaluations. Existing removal-based defenses typically sanitize backdoored models by updating, pruning, distilling, or mixing model parameters. However, these approaches are misaligned with adapter-based deployment, where the trusted base model is expected to remain frozen. In this work, we propose LoRA-Patch, a lightweight backdoor defense tailored to LoRA adapters. Our key insight is that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of a poisoned adapter relative to its trusted base model. Building on this insight, LoRA-Patch suppresses trigger-activated behaviors by realigning adapter directions through layer-wise steering, without modifying the base model weights. Extensive experiments across five backdoor attacks and three models show that LoRA-Patch effectively mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforming existing baselines while preserving benign task performance. Moreover, LoRA-Patch is computationally efficient, constructing patches within 20 seconds across all evaluated models and adapters. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LoRA-Patch, a lightweight defence against backdoored LoRA adapters that realigns adapter directions through layer-wise steering without modifying the frozen base model. It outperforms existing baselines across five backdoor attacks and three models while preserving benign performance, and builds patches within 20 seconds.
AI.motivation: Third-party LoRA adapters can hide trigger-activated backdoors while keeping normal task performance, and existing removal-based defences modify model parameters, which conflicts with adapter-based deployment where the base model stays frozen.
AI.method: The key insight is that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of a poisoned adapter relative to its trusted base model. LoRA-Patch suppresses trigger-activated behaviour by realigning adapter directions through layer-wise steering, without changing the base model weights.
AI.result: Across five backdoor attacks and three models, LoRA-Patch effectively mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforming existing baselines while preserving benign task performance, and constructs patches within 20 seconds across all evaluated models and adapters.
AI.conclusion: Directional steering of the adapter is an efficient defence against backdoored LoRA adapters that keeps the base model untouched.

title: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for empowering search agents to tackle complex information-seeking tasks. However, since acquiring external information necessitates web search, these agents are highly susceptible to various adversarial attacks (e.g., malicious information injection or stealthy context manipulation). Existing attack strategies inevitably rely on static and human-crafted templates, failing to emulate the dynamic and complex nature of real-world threats. In this paper, we propose an adversarial self-evolution framework that integrates bi-level optimization between the attacker's strategy evolution and the defender's adaptive mitigation, to expose the vulnerabilities of search agents. Specifically, we introduce the Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method to drive the directional evolution of the attack strategy population via contrastive evolutionary signals. To provide a stable environment for this continuous evolution, we further construct a controlled sandbox and design fine-grained metrics to quantify internal vulnerabilities. Extensive experiments across various multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs demonstrate that the proposed framework yields attack efficacy superior to static baselines, underscoring the urgent need to develop more robust defense frameworks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an adversarial self-evolving framework for attacking LLM search agents, in which attack strategies evolve through Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) against an adaptive defender. Its attacks outperform static human-crafted baselines across multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing attacks on search agents rely on static, human-crafted templates and do not emulate the dynamic nature of real-world threats from web content.
AI.method: A bi-level optimisation couples the evolution of the attacker's strategy with the defender's adaptive mitigation. CREO drives directional evolution of an attack strategy population using contrastive evolutionary signals, and a controlled sandbox with fine-grained vulnerability metrics provides a stable environment for the evolution.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across various multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs show that the framework yields attack efficacy superior to static baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results underscore the urgent need for more robust defence frameworks for search agents.

title: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision
summary: Restricting what a model can say is often mistaken for restricting an attacker's influence over its decision. An attacker can add text to the evidence and steer the model toward a wrong answer that still belongs to the allowed set. We evaluate seven decision models spanning hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). We present Slot Attack, a black-box attack designed for decision models that appends text assembled from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-selected incorrect option. The method relies solely on returned label probabilities, achieves success rates of 32--99\% on initially correct decisions, and identifies the effective component combinations with a median of 17--72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal this vulnerability. Models with near-identical accuracy on the sampled tasks differ by about 20\%age points in attack success. We demonstrate that an attacker can force not just one wrong answer but every available one: on about 20\% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77\% for gpt-6-luna and 98\% for GLiNER2.5; a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out. A fixed answer set constrains a decision's form, not its source; robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Slot Attack, a black-box attack on decision models that appends text built from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-chosen wrong option, using only returned label probabilities. Success rates reach 32 to 99% on initially correct decisions, and accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal the vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Restricting a model's outputs to a fixed answer set is often mistaken for limiting an attacker's influence over the decision, since an attacker can still steer the model through the evidence it is given.
AI.method: Seven decision models, including hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder, were evaluated on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). Slot Attack appends text assembled from named components and uses the effective component combinations, with a median of 17 to 72 queries per successful attack.
AI.result: Success rates are 32 to 99% on initially correct decisions. Models with near-identical accuracy differ by about 20 percentage points in attack success. An attacker could force every available wrong answer on about 20% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77% for gpt-6-luna and 98% for GLiNER2.5, and a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out.
AI.conclusion: A fixed answer set constrains the form of a decision, not its source, so robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.

title: The role of injected noise in diffusion model generalization
comment: 10 pages, 11 figures, published at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: 2nd Workshop on Principles of Generative Modeling (PriGM)
summary: Diffusion models trained on distinct datasets can produce highly similar samples when prompted with the same noise input, suggesting that they learn a generalized data distribution. We investigate the role of noise injected during the sampling process, and show that it plays an important role in making or breaking this strong generalization effect. Based on this finding we investigate the robustness of sample similarity to changes in the injected noise, and find that its impact is largest in the sampling regime where broad structure already exists but the precise identity of the sample is not yet determined.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how noise injected during sampling affects the strong generalisation of diffusion models, where models trained on different datasets produce highly similar samples from the same initial noise. It finds that the injected noise can make or break this effect, with the greatest sensitivity in the intermediate regime where broad structure exists but sample identity is not yet fixed.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models trained on distinct datasets can produce highly similar samples from the same noise input, suggesting that they learn a generalised data distribution, but the role of sampling noise in this effect was unclear.
AI.method: The authors vary the noise injected during the sampling process and measure how robust sample similarity is to changes in that injected noise, locating where the impact is largest along the sampling trajectory.
AI.result: The injected noise plays an important role in making or breaking the strong generalisation effect, and its impact on sample similarity is largest where broad structure already exists but the precise identity of the sample is not yet determined.
AI.conclusion: Sampling noise is a key factor in whether diffusion models generalise, and its effect concentrates in the intermediate stage of sampling.

title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
comment: 20 pages (8 pages main text), 4 figures, 11 tables. Accepted to the Long-Context Foundation Models (LCFM) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026, Atlanta, December 12, 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Multi-layer Indexer (MLI), which lets a layer reuse the token selection of the previous indexer layer in DeepSeek Sparse Attention so that each indexer runs concurrently with attention. It decodes faster than IndexCache at equal retention, by up to 14.5% on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at retention 1/2, without retraining.
AI.motivation: In DeepSeek Sparse Attention, the lightning indexer scan over the whole cache, rather than the sparse attention, dominates decode time at long context, and every layer's indexer must run before its attention.
AI.method: Adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer attends the selection of the previous indexer layer, removing the dependency and letting each indexer run concurrently with its layer's attention. The default realisation changes no kernel and runs inside SGLang's production decode graph, with an optional fused decode kernel on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI is composed with IndexCache and evaluated on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 and contexts from 10K to 195K.
AI.result: At equal retention, the composition decodes up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4. At 128K context and retention 1/4 it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache.
AI.conclusion: Overlapping indexer computation with attention is a training-free way to speed up long-context decoding in DeepSeek-style sparse attention, and it composes with existing cross-layer reuse.

title: Metadata-Conditioned Audio Transformers for Adaptive Respiratory Sound Classification
summary: Respiratory sound classification from auscultation recordings is confounded by heterogeneous acquisition conditions, including recording device, auscultation site, and patient characteristics, that introduce systematic variability unrelated to the underlying pathology. Although such metadata is often available, existing approaches either ignore it or rely on naïve fusion strategies that do not model how distinct metadata sources influence different components of the acoustic representation. We propose a family of metadata-conditioning mechanisms for the Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST), progressing from gated residual fusion to Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) adapted to the Transformer architecture. We further introduce two novel variants: Token-Aware FiLM (TAFiLM), which applies distinct modulation to classification and patch tokens, and Soft-Factorized FiLM (SoftFiLM), which learns soft masks to align metadata factors with disentangled feature subspaces. Experiments on the ICBHI benchmark demonstrate consistent gains across all conditioning strategies. SoftFiLM achieves 64.11% on the official 4-class task (+3.94% over the baseline) and 72.40% on the 2-class task, establishing a new state-of-the-art on the 2-class task and competitive performance on the 4-class benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes metadata-conditioning mechanisms for the Audio Spectrogram Transformer for respiratory sound classification, including two new variants, TAFiLM and SoftFiLM. SoftFiLM reaches 64.11% on the official ICBHI 4-class task and 72.40% on the 2-class task, a new state of the art on the 2-class task.
AI.motivation: Acquisition metadata such as recording device, auscultation site and patient characteristics introduces variability unrelated to pathology, and existing approaches either ignore this metadata or fuse it naively without modelling how each source affects the acoustic representation.
AI.method: The authors progress from gated residual fusion to Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) adapted to the Transformer. Token-Aware FiLM (TAFiLM) applies distinct modulation to classification and patch tokens, and Soft-Factorised FiLM (SoftFiLM) learns soft masks that align metadata factors with disentangled feature subspaces.
AI.result: Experiments on the ICBHI benchmark show consistent gains across all conditioning strategies. SoftFiLM achieves 64.11% on the official 4-class task, +3.94% over the baseline, and 72.40% on the 2-class task.
AI.conclusion: Structured metadata conditioning improves respiratory sound classification, and SoftFiLM sets a new state of the art on the 2-class task while remaining competitive on the 4-class benchmark.

title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills
comment: 27 Pages, Submitted to ICLR 2027 (Under review)
summary: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits security obligations for third-party Agent Skills while they run, using a deterministic runtime gate on outbound sends. In evaluation at the network egress boundary, it had a 0.0% overlook rate and a 0.0% overkill rate, while the compared scanners erred on both sides.
AI.motivation: A malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation in a legitimate workflow, and neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions shows whether its execution meets the user's security requirements.
AI.method: Risk models are derived from released malicious-Skill datasets, and adversarial-benign Skill pairs are built. A language model proposes task-specific security obligations from the delivery contract, each citing the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens host approvals into fine-grained allowed actions. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of each outbound send, and a deterministic decoder verifies each obligation without any language model in enforcement.
AI.result: RuntimeTickets was evaluated at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, including an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. Its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides.
AI.conclusion: Tying approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.

title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
comment: Accepted at 2026 Cyber Awareness and Research Symposium (CARS). This is the author's accepted manuscript
summary: Most malware detection research focuses on identifying whether a file is malicious before it executes. Far less attention goes to what happens after infection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behavior across 37 families, grounded in dynamic sandbox execution using CAPEv2. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships, preserving relational structure that flat feature vectors discard. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families, and a per-family behavioral fingerprint analysis characterizes post-infection activity across registry, network, process, and API dimensions. An LLM explanation layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed behavioral evidence. The full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behaviour across 37 families, using CAPEv2 sandbox traces modelled as heterogeneous graphs. A voting ensemble reaches 94.44% accuracy and MCC 0.863, and the full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan.
AI.motivation: Most malware detection research identifies whether a file is malicious before execution, whereas what happens after infection has received far less attention.
AI.method: Behavioural traces are modelled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features is compared with a flat behavioural baseline, a multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 families, and a per-family fingerprint analysis covers registry, network, process and API dimensions. An LLM layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed evidence.
AI.result: The voting ensemble achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioural baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families.
AI.conclusion: Relational graph structure of post-infection behaviour supports accurate family classification, and the pipeline, deployed as HeteroScan, can produce evidence-grounded analyst reports.

title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
comment: 18 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, this https URL. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.

AI.tldr: AIRoA-0 is a bimanual manipulation policy trained only on 16,151 hours of handheld-gripper demonstrations recorded with the open-source YUBI gripper, with no robot data at any stage. It averages a 78% success rate across ten evaluation tasks, against 27% for the strongest of four other VLA models trained on the same demonstrations.
AI.motivation: Collecting robot demonstrations requires a robot present, which limits the scale and placement of manipulation data collection.
AI.method: Demonstrations are recorded with the YUBI handheld gripper, and the policy uses only a wrist camera on each arm. It learns which regions of each wrist view matter, predicts the task stage, and decodes actions as a continuous stream, with no teleoperation, reinforcement learning or on-robot correction. The policy is embodiment-agnostic and runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper.
AI.result: Across ten evaluation tasks, A-0 averages 78% success, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same demonstrations. It runs on bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR robots, and post-training on a new task takes under four hours on one node of eight H200 GPUs.
AI.conclusion: Handheld demonstrations without any robot data can train cross-embodiment manipulation policies, and the authors release the dataset, pre-trained weights and post-training recipe.

title: Rethinking Next-Visit Diagnosis Prediction Beyond Aggregate Metrics: Retrieval--Memory Multi-Agent Adjudication
comment: 2 figures, 18 tables, and 29 pages
summary: Next-visit diagnosis prediction forecasts the diagnoses documented at a patient's next encounter, turning retrospective electronic health records into prospective clinical prediction. However, conventional aggregate evaluation obscures its multifaceted nature: distributionally, models must handle variable-size diagnosis sets and long-tailed labels; temporally, they must distinguish persistent, newly recorded, and recurrent diagnoses; and both vary with observed history depth. We introduce an evaluation framework along these dimensions and apply it to rule-based heuristics, LLM-based prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent approaches. This reveals that repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses, and that retrieval and memory exhibit distinct profiles whose relative strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones. Motivated by this, we propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework combining evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory. Using cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, it preserves shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. Across MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with four LLM backbones, LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings while remaining competitive with them on aggregate metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates next-visit diagnosis prediction with dimensions for distribution and temporal transitions and finds that repeating the last visit beats most LLM-based approaches overall. It proposes LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework that gives the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV.
AI.motivation: Aggregate metrics obscure the multifaceted nature of next-visit diagnosis prediction, which involves variable-size diagnosis sets, long-tailed labels, and the distinction between persistent, newly recorded and recurrent diagnoses.
AI.method: Rule-based heuristics, LLM prompting, retrieval, memory and multi-agent approaches are assessed along these dimensions. LONGINUS combines evidence retrieved from patient records with structured memory of the patient trajectory, uses cross-view agreement as a reliability heuristic, keeps shared predictions and adjudicates disagreements without revealing their source. It is evaluated with four LLM backbones.
AI.result: Repeating the last visit outperforms most LLM-based approaches overall despite predicting no new or recurrent diagnoses. LONGINUS achieves the best transition-specific performance among LLM-based methods in nearly all settings on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, while remaining competitive on aggregate metrics.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate evaluation is insufficient for this task, and retrieval and memory have distinct profiles whose strengths vary across temporal transitions and backbones.

title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
summary: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PianoBench, a benchmark that tests language models on reasoning about piano performances in aligned acoustic and symbolic input, derived from a dataset of over 20,000 hours of interleaved music transcripts and spoken commentary. Open-weight audio-language models reach at most 52.8%, while frontier models with chain of thought reach up to 93.2% when given transcripts as text.
AI.motivation: It is unclear which musical features multimodal language models can perceive and reason about, and broad music benchmarks do not isolate this.
AI.method: PianoBench is derived from a new multimodal, training-scale dataset of interleaved transcripts and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Its questions are paired with congruent acoustic and symbolic representations, and a no-audio control is used. Mid-training on interleaved instruction is tested on Qwen 3.5 9B Base.
AI.result: Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy and at best only modestly outperform a no-audio control. Frontier models with chain of thought reach up to 93.2% when given transcripts as text. Instruction tuning raises Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy with transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0%.
AI.conclusion: A gap exists between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about events given explicitly, and instructional videos may be an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music.
