title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
comment: 29 pages, 9 figures. Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.

AI.tldr: RoboScope Kit wraps each model as a Policy and each benchmark as an adapter around its own evaluator, with scheduling that sizes simulator workers and policy replicas separately, to speed up embodied-AI evaluation. On LIBERO-Long it runs 500 episodes 4.45x faster than the official StarVLA evaluator with equivalent success rates, and 25.04x faster on RoboTwin Easy with four GPUs.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based robot policy evaluation is slow and fragmented, since each benchmark has its own evaluator, observation layout and action convention. The baseline StarVLA evaluator leaves the GPU at 14.3% average utilisation.
AI.method: Each model is wrapped once as a Python Policy class and each benchmark once as an adapter around its own evaluator, keeping its scoring unchanged. Simulator workers and Policy replicas run as separate pools, sized from measured probes, sharded deterministically across GPU instances, and only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads are rendered. Adapters cover six benchmark families.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Long with one 48 GiB RTX 4090, 12 simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas run 4.45x faster than the official StarVLA evaluation, 2.78x faster than RLinf and 1.52x faster than vla-eval. With CUDA MPS, 16 workers sharing four replicas run 6.16x faster than StarVLA. On RoboTwin Easy with four GPUs, 500 episodes finish in 14.4 minutes, 25.04x faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Separating simulator and policy resources and sharding across GPUs substantially accelerates embodied-AI evaluation while leaving benchmark rules and scoring unchanged.

title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
summary: Reasoning substantially improves language models' ability to solve difficult problems, but long reasoning traces make these gains expensive. Efficient reasoning should express useful analysis in fewer tokens by reducing repetition and text that adds little value to solving the problem. Progress in proprietary models motivates this goal, yet their hidden scratchpads limit direct study of how it is achieved. We investigate whether open-weight models can generate less verbose reasoning by changing the form of their own earlier thoughts, without retraining. Our intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, then compares continuations from original and compact histories. Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning; a coding case study also shows less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target and compressor. These findings identify reasoning history as one way to reduce future reasoning-token use and motivate model-specific compaction policies evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether open-weight models can reduce reasoning-token use by rewriting their own earlier reasoning into compact state records before tool results are revealed, without retraining. Accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning, and in software-agent deployments compaction can reduce total spending.
AI.motivation: Long reasoning traces make strong reasoning expensive, and proprietary hidden scratchpads prevent direct study of how efficient reasoning is achieved.
AI.method: The intervention rewrites prior reasoning into compact state records before pending tool results are revealed, and continuations from the original and compact histories are then compared across the tested models. A coding case study examines repeated verification after a shared candidate solution.
AI.result: Across the tested models, accepted compact histories usually shorten future reasoning. In the coding case study, there is less repeated verification after a shared candidate solution. In software-agent deployments, compaction can reduce total spending, although task quality and rewrite-inclusive time depend on the target model and compressor.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning history is one way to reduce future reasoning-token use, and compaction policies should be model-specific and evaluated for both efficiency and retained capability.

title: Camera Radar LiDAR Fusion via Point-Cloud Projection for Multi-Task Learning
comment: IEEE International Workshop on Signal Processing Systems 2026
summary: Autonomous vehicles require robust perception systems to operate safely under diverse environmental conditions. While cameras provide high-resolution visual data, their performance significantly degrades in low-light and adverse weather. High Definition (HD) radar offers superior reliability and angular resolution under such conditions but lacks rich visual feature recognition. LiDAR, though expensive, delivers highly precise distance measurements and dense point clouds. Each sensor exhibits unique trade-offs, necessitating the development of advanced sensor fusion algorithms to harness complementary strengths while minimizing computational complexity and maintaining accuracy. In this study, the proposed fusion architecture performs early fusion by combining camera images with perspective-view point cloud data from HD radar and LiDAR sensors. The proposed model is trained to detect vehicles and segment free drivable space simultaneously. Experiments are performed on the RADIal dataset where we demonstrate that fusing point cloud data with camera images in front-view surpasses the performances of the most recent standalone and fusion models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an early-fusion architecture that combines camera images with perspective-view point clouds from HD radar and LiDAR, trained to detect vehicles and segment drivable space jointly. On the RADIal dataset it surpasses recent standalone and fusion models.
AI.motivation: Cameras degrade in low light and adverse weather, while HD radar is more reliable there but lacks rich visual features, and LiDAR is precise but expensive, so the sensors' complementary strengths need fusing with modest computational cost.
AI.method: Camera images are early-fused with perspective-view point-cloud data from HD radar and LiDAR, and a single model is trained to detect vehicles and segment free drivable space simultaneously.
AI.result: Experiments on the RADIal dataset show that fusing point-cloud data with front-view camera images surpasses the performance of the most recent standalone and fusion models.
AI.conclusion: Early fusion of camera with radar and LiDAR point clouds in the front view is an effective way to improve joint vehicle detection and drivable-space segmentation.

title: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering
summary: Small language models (<=9B parameters) can support local medical question answering (QA) while reducing privacy and latency concerns, but effective fine-tuning remains challenging. This paper compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervised fine-tuning methods: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS), which applies equal loss weighting to the full CoT-and-answer sequence, and Segment-weighted (SwS), which separately weights CoT and answer losses. We evaluate six general- and medical-domain models on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA) and free-text QA (Med-O1). Results show that neither method is universally best: on multiple-choice QA (MedQA and EMS-MCQA), SwS generally performs better, with general-purpose models benefiting most; notably, Qwen3.5-4B improves by up to 44.8% over its zero-shot baseline on MedQA. In contrast, medical-domain models show smaller or even negative gains on MCQs. On free-text QA (Med-O1), UaS performs best for nearly all models and provides consistent improvements across both model types, with the 3B Llama-3.2 model approaching the performance of much larger 7B medical-domain models. We also find that excessively long CoT generation is associated with lower performance in some models on either multiple-choice or free-text QA tasks, suggesting that limiting the CoT length during training may benefit selected models. Overall, the results show that CoT loss weighting should be matched to the task format and the knowledge already encoded in the base model, rather than using a single fine-tuning strategy for all clinical QA tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning methods for small language models on medical QA, uniform-across-sequence (UaS) and segment-weighted (SwS), and finds that neither is universally best. SwS generally helps multiple-choice QA, while UaS performs best on free-text QA.
AI.motivation: Small models of up to 9B parameters can support local medical QA for privacy and latency reasons, but effective fine-tuning of their reasoning remains difficult.
AI.method: UaS applies equal loss weighting to the full chain-of-thought-and-answer sequence, while SwS weights the chain-of-thought and answer losses separately. Six general-purpose and medical-domain models are evaluated on MedQA and EMS-MCQA (multiple choice) and Med-O1 (free text).
AI.result: On MedQA and EMS-MCQA, SwS generally performs better, with general-purpose models benefiting most, and Qwen3.5-4B improves by up to 44.8% over its zero-shot baseline on MedQA. On Med-O1, UaS performs best for nearly all models, and the 3B Llama-3.2 model approaches much larger 7B medical-domain models. Excessively long chain-of-thought generation is associated with lower performance for some models.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought loss weighting should be matched to the task format and to the knowledge already encoded in the base model, rather than using one fine-tuning strategy for all clinical QA tasks.

title: P$^2$-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors
summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P$^2$-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P$^2$-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P$^2$-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes P^2-MOPD, which treats the linear combination of student and expert parameters as one differentiable model and jointly optimises mixing coefficients and student weights under the on-policy distillation objective. At 1.7B scale it reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.
AI.motivation: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities but is costly, while task arithmetic merges parameters training-free yet stays confined to the span of the frozen student and expert parameters.
AI.method: Experts act as parameter priors, and the student remains trainable, so the merged model is not restricted to the span of the frozen parameters. The mixing coefficients and student weights are optimised jointly under the same on-policy distillation objective, across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales.
AI.result: P^2-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialisation, surpassing MOPD's final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, the 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.
AI.conclusion: Using expert parameters as trainable priors accelerates and balances multi-teacher on-policy distillation compared with MOPD.

title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
summary: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ProteoCraft, a tree-based search framework that treats protein-protein interaction design as proposal-verification search, using diffusion structure predictors for proposals and folding models for verification. It improves design quality and high-confidence yield across 14 binder-design settings, and experimentally yields an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins.
AI.motivation: Designing proteins with desired interactions is hard because of the structural complexity of molecular recognition, and structural evaluation is expensive, so the design is cast as search over a combinatorial sequence space.
AI.method: Approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors serve as proposal policies that specify where to explore, and no-gradient inference of folding models assigns values to the resulting sequences. A coarse-to-fine budget allocation first explores distinct sequence basins with multi-site edits, then applies strict single-site refinement to verified promising states.
AI.result: Across 14 de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets and four localised CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield, persisting under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective validation gives an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirms binding of a designed IFNAR2 VHH.
AI.conclusion: Proposal-verification tree search with structural gradients and folding-model verification improves computational protein binder design, with experimental confirmation for two targets.

title: Stacking-Based Weighting for Large Language Bayes in M-Open Settings
comment: 10 Pages,4 Figures
summary: Large Language Bayes (LLB) transforms a natural language problem description into a collection of candidate probabilistic programs and performs inference within each model, combining their predictions using Bayesian model averaging. While this provides a flexible framework for probabilistic inference without manual model specification, the resulting candidate model set is often misspecified in practice, and likelihood-based aggregation can concentrate on a single model, under-representing uncertainty across the sampled models. We propose a stacking-based aggregation method for LLB that selects model weights by optimizing predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood, while preserving the original language-model-driven model generation and within-model inference pipeline. Because leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable in latent-variable models, we derive a variational lower bound that yields a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective. Across real-world probabilistic inference tasks, our method achieves comparable predictive performance to Bayesian model averaging while yielding more dispersed model weights, reducing concentration on a single candidate model under misspecification.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes stacking-based weighting for Large Language Bayes (LLB), selecting model weights by predictive performance rather than marginal likelihood. It achieves predictive performance comparable to Bayesian model averaging while giving more dispersed weights under model misspecification.
AI.motivation: LLB generates candidate probabilistic programs from a language description, but the candidate set is often misspecified, and likelihood-based model averaging can concentrate on a single model and underrepresent uncertainty.
AI.method: Leave-one-out predictive quantities are intractable for latent-variable models, so a variational lower bound yields a tractable ELBO-based stacking objective. Model generation and within-model inference of the original LLB pipeline are preserved.
AI.result: Across real-world probabilistic inference tasks, the method achieves predictive performance comparable to Bayesian model averaging, and yields more dispersed model weights that reduce concentration on a single candidate model.
AI.conclusion: Stacking with an ELBO-based objective is a practical aggregation method for LLB under misspecification, reducing over-concentration on one model.

title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures
summary: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order. Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no increase in reported mental demand. Our findings show that people can recover what the system left implicit and that pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under the constraints of a changing world.

AI.tldr: In a preregistered study (N=114) of a time-critical monitoring task, participants understood underspecified machine alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones, and responded sooner. A pragmatic planner that reasons over the listener's knowledge outperformed a baseline that states problems fully in onset order.
AI.motivation: Assistive systems often state everything explicitly, spending attention on what users already know, whereas people leave out what the listener can infer; it was unclear whether people use prior knowledge to understand incomplete messages from a machine.
AI.method: The pragmatic planner, which reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge, decides what to say, when and how explicitly. It is compared with a baseline that specifies problems fully in onset order, while controlling users' prior knowledge and the time available to detect critical situations, in a preregistered study with 114 participants.
AI.result: Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and more often rated the pragmatic assistant as helpful, with no increase in reported mental demand.
AI.conclusion: People can recover what a system leaves implicit, and pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under time constraints.

title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 6 tables. Camera-ready version for the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET). Project page: this https URL
summary: Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks -- mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. Current tool-use benchmarks do not test this regime -- they expose only a handful of tools, evaluate single-step invocation, or grade multi-step behavior with subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores that penalize valid alternative trajectories. We introduce SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a large-scale benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise domain. SLATE couples (i) queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a ~1,000-tool e-commerce library, (ii) a deterministic, context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and (iii) an end-to-end task-success metric -- a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome -- that credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while remaining fully automatic and reproducible. Experiments with six open decision models and the language models they are built on, from 3B to 12B parameters, show that even the best model completes only 5.0% of the tasks, establishing SLATE as a challenging testbed for reliable enterprise tool use. We release SLATE, its simulator, and the evaluation harness at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SLATE, a benchmark for long-horizon API selection over a library of about 1,000 e-commerce tools, using a deterministic simulator and an end-to-end task-success metric. Even the best of six open decision models completes only 5.0% of tasks.
AI.motivation: Enterprises want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over thousands of internal APIs, but existing tool-use benchmarks expose few tools, test single-step calls, or rely on subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores.
AI.method: SLATE couples queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a library of about 1,000 e-commerce tools, a deterministic context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and a task-success metric under which a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome.
AI.result: Six open decision models, built on language models from 3B to 12B parameters, are evaluated, and even the best completes only 5.0% of the tasks.
AI.conclusion: SLATE is a challenging, reproducible testbed for reliable enterprise tool use, and its simulator and evaluation harness are released.

title: FlagRot: Selective Rotation for Low-Bit KV Caches
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, which 2-bit codes could shrink about sixfold if their error stays in check. The usual remedy rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. However, we observe that it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat one a new peak, and both coexist within one key. We therefore propose FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece rotated or as is, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, and rotates the query instead when reading. We further show that how often to decide follows the quantization axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head, at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits. At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. Served as a vLLM plugin, it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on the three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy. It also lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FlagRot, which stores each 32-channel piece of a KV-cache key either rotated or unrotated, whichever has the smaller calibrated attention error, to make low-bit KV caches more accurate. At 2.5 bits per value it lowers KIVI's twelve-model KL divergence from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3 and is served as a vLLM plugin.
AI.motivation: Two-bit KV-cache codes could shrink long-context memory about sixfold, but rotating keys before quantisation, the usual remedy, does not always help, since rotation can flatten a spiky piece of a key and create a new peak in a flat one.
AI.method: Each 32-channel piece is stored rotated or as is by calibrated attention error, and the query is rotated instead when reading. The decision granularity follows the quantisation axis: per-channel caches such as KIVI need one decision per head at no write cost, while per-token caches decide per key, with the choice stored in existing sign bits.
AI.result: At 2.5 bits per value, FlagRot lowers the twelve-model KL divergence of KIVI from 18.7 to 12.4 x 10^-3, below RotateKV on 9 of 12 models. As a vLLM plugin it raises RULER at 128k tokens by +2.9 points and the LongBench v1 mean by +0.4 to +1.9 points on three of four models where 2-bit KIVI loses accuracy, and it lowers the error of 4-bit integer and FP4 caches.
AI.conclusion: Selective rotation chosen by calibrated error improves low-bit KV-cache quantisation, and the best decision granularity depends on the quantisation axis.

title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding
comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables; includes online appendix. Accepted manuscript of the article published in Journal of Business Venturing Insights 26 (2026) e00682. Data, design files and code: this https URL
summary: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly advise backers on which crowdfunding campaigns to support. LLMs have known race and gender problems, and it is unsettled whether they reproduce, erase, or reverse the discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance. We ask when, and through which decision process, LLM assistants use founders' gender and ethnicity. In a pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment, seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomized quality signals and founder names, under three backer personas and a persona-free control (40,248 responses). By default, founder names barely matter: under budget-conscious and delivery-focused personas, gender and Black-name effects are statistically equivalent to zero. When the backer wants to support underrepresented creators, the models favor Black-signaled (+8.1 percentage points; positive in all seven models) and female-signaled (+5.1) founders. They do so most strongly among near-tied campaigns and for the founder who alone carries the signal, and they almost never name gender or ethnicity in their reasons. The results fit an agency account of algorithmic discrimination: an aligned assistant takes its demographic preferences from its user rather than from its training data.

AI.tldr: In a conjoint experiment with seven LLMs choosing among synthetic crowdfunding campaigns, founder names barely matter by default, but when the backer persona wants to support underrepresented creators, the models favour Black-signalled (+8.1 percentage points) and female-signalled (+5.1) founders. The authors read this as an agency account in which the assistant takes demographic preferences from its user.
AI.motivation: LLM assistants increasingly advise backers on crowdfunding, and it was unsettled whether LLMs reproduce, erase or reverse the gender and ethnic discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance.
AI.method: A pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment in which seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomised quality signals and founder names, under three backer personas and a persona-free control, yielding 40,248 responses.
AI.result: Under budget-conscious and delivery-focused personas, gender and Black-name effects are statistically equivalent to zero. When the backer wants to support underrepresented creators, the models favour Black-signalled (+8.1 percentage points, positive in all seven models) and female-signalled (+5.1) founders, most strongly among near-tied campaigns, and they almost never name gender or ethnicity in their reasons.
AI.conclusion: An aligned assistant takes its demographic preferences from its user rather than from its training data, which fits an agency account of algorithmic discrimination.

title: When Music Needs Meaning: Semantic Communication as a Transformative Enabler for the Musical Metaverse
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Accepted and Presented at IEEE International Symposium on the Internet of Sounds (IS2) Conference 2026
summary: The Musical Metaverse (MM) enables geographically distributed musicians, audiences, sound engineers, and AI agents to interact through synchronized audio, visual, kinematic, and haptic streams, imposing latency, synchronization, bandwidth, and scalability requirements that are difficult to satisfy with conventional bit-level communication. This paper argues that semantic communication, understood here as the transmission of musically meaningful information rather than raw audio-visual-haptic samples, provides a principled communication paradigm for the MM. We define the MM from a communication perspective and derive modality-specific require ments; propose a three-pillar framework for musical semantic communication comprising semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration, and cross-modal semantic synchronization; survey representative work across semantic communication, music AI and edge orchestration, identifying the gaps that prevent their integration; and propose a semantic-first reference architecture based on device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers, and cross-modal semantic synchronization. The resulting framework positions the MM as a concrete and demanding use case for 6G semantic communication.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that semantic communication, meaning the transmission of musically meaningful information rather than raw audio-visual-haptic samples, is a principled paradigm for the Musical Metaverse. It proposes a three-pillar framework and a semantic-first reference architecture, and positions the Musical Metaverse as a demanding use case for 6G.
AI.motivation: The Musical Metaverse links distributed musicians, audiences, engineers and AI agents through synchronised audio, visual, kinematic and haptic streams, whose latency, synchronisation, bandwidth and scalability needs are hard to meet with conventional bit-level communication.
AI.method: The authors define the Musical Metaverse from a communication perspective and derive modality-specific requirements. They propose a three-pillar framework of semantics extraction, semantic-aware orchestration and cross-modal semantic synchronisation, survey work in semantic communication, music AI and edge orchestration, and propose a reference architecture built on device-side semantic encoders, edge semantic routers and cross-modal synchronisation.
AI.result: The paper reports no experimental results; its contribution is a framework, a survey of gaps, and a reference architecture.
AI.conclusion: The Musical Metaverse is a concrete and demanding use case for 6G semantic communication.

title: Measure Before You Repair: An Explainable Agent for Blind Restoration of Multi-Artifact 3-D MRI
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ISBI 2027
summary: A brain MRI scan can carry an unknown mix of artifacts, so restoration has to be blind, yet most deep-learning methods are built to correct one known artifact. We present Dx-Rx, an agent in which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) measures suspected artifacts before it repairs them. To our knowledge, it is the first agent to restore whole 3-D MRI volumes, whereas earlier MRI agents restore 2-D slices. In a loop, it looks at slices of the 3-D volume, calls five diagnostic tools (noise, spike, ghosting, bias field, motion) and four restoration tools in any order it chooses, checks each repair, can return to any earlier version to change the order, and ends with a radiology-style report of its diagnostic reasons, the repairs it applied and their results. We simulated up to five artifacts on 148 whole 3-D T1-weighted volumes, at levels calibrated to radiologists' grades of real scans. An MLLM that only looked at the image, as earlier MRI agents do, removed at most 19.7 % of the artifact error. With the best of five MLLMs, Dx-Rx removed a mean 64.5 %, nearly matching the 64.6 % of the same tools given the ground-truth artifacts, which are never known for a clinical scan. With all five models, it made no volume worse and was on par with or better than an expert rule-based pipeline built from the same tools (62.3 %). Code and demo are public at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Dx-Rx, an agent in which a multimodal LLM measures suspected artifacts in a 3-D brain MRI volume before repairing them, and it is described as the first agent to restore whole 3-D MRI volumes. On 148 simulated volumes it removes a mean 64.5% of artifact error with the best of five MLLMs, nearly matching the 64.6% of the same tools given the ground-truth artifacts.
AI.motivation: A brain MRI scan may carry an unknown mix of artifacts, so restoration must be blind, yet most deep-learning methods correct only one known artifact, and earlier MRI agents restore 2-D slices and reason from the image alone.
AI.method: In a loop, the MLLM inspects slices of the 3-D volume, calls five diagnostic tools (noise, spike, ghosting, bias field, motion) and four restoration tools in any order, checks each repair, can return to an earlier version to change the order, and ends with a radiology-style report.
AI.result: Up to five artifacts were simulated on 148 whole 3-D T1-weighted volumes. An MLLM that only looked at the image removed at most 19.7% of the artifact error, while Dx-Rx with the best of five MLLMs removed a mean 64.5%, against 64.6% with ground-truth artifacts and 62.3% for an expert rule-based pipeline. With all five models it made no volume worse.
AI.conclusion: Measuring artifacts before repairing them lets an agent restore multi-artifact 3-D MRI blindly, with performance close to an oracle that knows the artifacts.

title: Characterizing Adversarial GEO via Implicit Brand Injection
comment: Preprint. Under Review
summary: Generative search engines increasingly shape how users discover products, services, and commercial entities by generating answers from retrieved web content. This creates an opportunity to influence which brands appear in these answers by modifying the content available to the retrieval system. In this work, we study an adversarial generative engine optimization (GEO) setting in which a predefined brand is added to an article through a single contextually integrated mention. The challenge is to make the mention fit the surrounding article without making the content overtly promotional, while keeping it relevant enough to be retrieved and to influence the generated answer. To study this, we introduce Implicit Brand Injection (IBI), a multi-agent framework that identifies insertion locations, rewrites the selected sentence, verifies the edit, and selects the final candidate. To evaluate IBI at scale, we construct IBIBench, which contains 1,000 web articles and 60 synthetic brands across 12 diverse domains, with both endemic and non-endemic brand placements. We compare IBI with Direct Prompting and Best-of-N with ranking under an equivalent budget, evaluating insertion quality, target-chunk retrieval, and downstream brand propagation. Compared with the baselines, IBI produces insertions that better preserve semantics and disrupt perplexity less, while improving Hit@k across all evaluated cutoffs, query regimes, and placement settings. IBI achieves up to 82.2% Hit@10 and 0.74 MRR@10, while Brand Mention Rate (BMR) and Conditional Propagation (CP) reach up to 62.7% and 75.9%, respectively. These results show that a single brand mention can increase both retrieval exposure and brand visibility in generated responses, highlighting the need for defenses against implicit content manipulation in generative search.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Implicit Brand Injection (IBI), a multi-agent framework that inserts a predefined brand into an article through one contextually integrated mention to influence generative search answers. On IBIBench it improves Hit@k across cutoffs and reaches up to 82.2% Hit@10, with brand mention rates up to 62.7%.
AI.motivation: Generative search engines build answers from retrieved web content, so editing that content could influence which brands appear, and the study examines how such adversarial generative engine optimisation can be done without making the mention overtly promotional.
AI.method: IBI identifies insertion locations, rewrites the selected sentence, verifies the edit and selects the final candidate. IBIBench contains 1,000 web articles and 60 synthetic brands across 12 domains, with endemic and non-endemic placements, and IBI is compared with Direct Prompting and Best-of-N ranking under an equivalent budget.
AI.result: IBI produces insertions that better preserve semantics and disrupt perplexity less than the baselines, and improves Hit@k across all evaluated cutoffs, query regimes and placement settings, reaching up to 82.2% Hit@10 and 0.74 MRR@10. Brand Mention Rate and Conditional Propagation reach up to 62.7% and 75.9%.
AI.conclusion: A single brand mention can increase both retrieval exposure and brand visibility in generated answers, which calls for defences against implicit content manipulation in generative search.

title: A Practical Causal Framework for Autonomous Mobile Robots: From Simulation to Real-World Human Environments
comment: Accepted in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the ``why'' behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a causal framework for autonomous mobile robots that transfers simulation-learned causal relations to the real world by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. The framework runs onboard a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baseline in complex human-shared scenarios.
AI.motivation: Causal inference could let robots make safe, efficient decisions, but collecting causal data in human-populated environments takes time, while users expect immediate operation.
AI.method: The invariant high-level causal structure is retained from simulation, and only the causal model parameters are updated with a limited set of real-world observations.
AI.result: The parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer, and the framework runs efficiently onboard a mobile robot, significantly outperforming non-causal baselines in navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Transferring causal structure from simulation and adapting only its parameters offers a practical route to deploying causal robot navigation with minimal real-world effort.

title: When Model Complexity Matters in Cross-Subject Naturalistic fMRI Prediction
comment: 43 pages
summary: Increasingly complex neural models predict blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses to naturalistic stimuli, but the predictive value of this added complexity remains unclear. We ask when pretrained stimulus representations help and how much downstream complexity is needed, with and without recent measured BOLD history. We compare linear diagnostic references and nonlinear predictors across HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10 subjects), and Algonauts 2025 (4 subjects). Under a shared offline protocol, models are fitted on training subjects and evaluated on held-out subjects viewing largely familiar stimuli, without refitting. Pretrained visual features generally improve prediction over raw pixels; for linear autoregression, this advantage becomes more pronounced over longer rollouts (recursive predictions without additional measured BOLD). Measured BOLD history provides substantial gains that generally diminish {as rollouts lengthen}. Nonlinear stimulus-only predictors can improve on linear readouts, whereas linear autoregression provides a strong history-conditioned baseline. Controls examine context length, regularization, fitting procedures, and model capacity. Regional response consistency across subjects is associated with held-out prediction accuracy, while less consistent regions tend to gain more from measured history. In paired simulations with fixed linear neural dynamics, slower hemodynamic responses generally sustain high temporal prediction correlations over longer rollouts, illustrating how the observation process can contribute to predictive persistence. Together, these findings support evaluating stimulus representations and downstream complexity separately, using history-conditioned linear prediction as a diagnostic reference under matched inputs and measurement availability.

AI.tldr: The paper compares linear and nonlinear predictors of naturalistic fMRI responses across three datasets and finds that pretrained visual features help most for long rollouts, while measured BOLD history gives large gains that diminish over longer rollouts. A linear autoregressive model with history is a strong baseline.
AI.motivation: Increasingly complex neural models predict BOLD responses to naturalistic stimuli, but the predictive value of the added complexity is unclear, and it is unknown when pretrained stimulus representations help.
AI.method: Linear diagnostic references and nonlinear predictors are compared on HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10 subjects) and Algonauts 2025 (4 subjects). Models are fitted on training subjects and evaluated on held-out subjects without refitting, with controls for context length, regularisation, fitting procedure and capacity, and paired simulations with fixed linear dynamics.
AI.result: Pretrained visual features generally improve prediction over raw pixels, and for linear autoregression the advantage grows over longer recursive rollouts. Measured BOLD history gives substantial gains that generally diminish as rollouts lengthen. Nonlinear stimulus-only predictors can improve on linear readouts. Regional response consistency across subjects is associated with held-out accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Stimulus representations and downstream complexity should be evaluated separately, using history-conditioned linear prediction as a diagnostic reference under matched inputs and measurement availability.

title: ScienceVision: Can AI Observe and Reason Like a Scientist?
summary: Scientific discovery builds on accurate observations interpreted through domain knowledge and reasoning. For scientific 3D data, this requires understanding structures and spatial relationships, from protein contacts to anatomical organization. Existing multimodal benchmarks largely evaluate text and 2D images, while scientific 3D evaluations vary in representations and protocols across disciplines, limiting cross-disciplinary comparison. To assess these foundational capabilities, we introduce ScienceVision, a cross-domain benchmark for scientific 3D understanding and reasoning through expert-level visual question answering (VQA). We construct 250 questions, with 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD, and Architecture, through a pipeline combining synthetic question generation with domain-expert review and annotation. Each task pairs a native 3D artifact with a scientific question, a specified response format, and a task-specific reference answer, requiring domain knowledge to be applied to geometric or topological evidence. We evaluate 12 models on the same questions in three settings: visual question answering with native 3D artifacts accessed through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools; the same workflow augmented with expert-inspired viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP); and visual question answering from prescribed rendered 2D images using an agent harness. All settings use the same task-specific deterministic final-answer scoring. The inspection environment supports view changes, target isolation, and slice inspection. In this main comparison, the best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores in the native-artifact workflow without additional MCP tools exceed those in the rendered-image workflow for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.

AI.tldr: ScienceVision is a benchmark of 250 expert-level visual questions over native 3-D scientific artefacts across five domains, and the best of 12 models reaches a mean score of 0.53 out of 1. Native-artefact workflows outscore rendered-image workflows for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal benchmarks mostly cover text and 2-D images, while scientific 3-D evaluations differ in representation and protocol across disciplines, which prevents cross-disciplinary comparison.
AI.method: 250 questions, 50 each from Biology, Chemistry, Medical Imaging, Mechanical CAD and Architecture, were built by combining synthetic generation with domain-expert review. Models are evaluated in three settings: native 3-D artefacts through an agent harness's file and code-execution tools, the same workflow with viewer inspection and measurement tools exposed through MCP, and prescribed rendered 2-D images, all with deterministic final-answer scoring.
AI.result: The best mean answer score is 0.53 out of 1. Mean scores with native artefacts and no additional MCP tools exceed those with rendered images for every model, by 17.2 percentage points on average.
AI.conclusion: Current models still have limited expert-level 3-D scientific reasoning, and direct access to native 3-D artefacts is more effective than rendered 2-D views.

title: Swapping the Judge Changes the Ranking: A Preregistered Study of Cross-Provider Replication in LLM-Judged System Comparisons
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Code and judge verdicts are provided as ancillary files
summary: Practitioners who compare systems with an LLM judge and have no human labels often check a conclusion by repeating it with a judge from another provider. We test how far that check can be trusted. In a preregistered study (with a disclosed post-registration reduction of the judge set), five judge models from three providers re-judged 4,000 Chatbot Arena battles (nine systems, 33 system pairs) that carry human votes, each in both response orders. Agreement with the human vote was low at the verdict level (median Cohen's kappa = 0.22), and system rankings did not survive a change of judge: Kendall's tau with the human ranking ranged from 0.17 to 0.89 (median 0.67), so the preregistered hypothesis that rankings remain stable was not supported. Conclusions replicated by two low-cost judges from different providers matched the human conclusion more often than single-judge conclusions (+0.10 precision), but the gain came from filtering out one poorly aligned judge, and replication involving that judge left a conclusion for only 35% of comparisons. Judges that agreed with humans reached a stable conclusion with no more verdicts than human votes required; the others failed to converge on 26-70% of system pairs at the sample sizes tested (up to 100 verdicts per pair). Disagreements with the human vote co-occurred across judges far more often than independence predicts, although a single human vote per battle cannot separate shared judge bias from voter noise.

AI.tldr: In a preregistered study, five LLM judges from three providers re-judged 4,000 Chatbot Arena battles, and system rankings did not stay stable when the judge changed (Kendall's tau with the human ranking 0.17 to 0.89, median 0.67). Agreement with human votes was low (median Cohen's kappa 0.22), so the cross-provider replication check cannot be fully trusted.
AI.motivation: Practitioners without human labels often check an LLM-judged system comparison by repeating it with a judge from another provider, and the reliability of that check was untested.
AI.method: Five judge models from three providers each re-judged 4,000 Chatbot Arena battles (nine systems, 33 system pairs) that carry human votes, in both response orders. The preregistered hypothesis that rankings remain stable was tested, with a disclosed post-registration reduction of the judge set.
AI.result: Verdict-level agreement with human votes was low (median Cohen's kappa 0.22), and the preregistered hypothesis of stable rankings was not supported. Conclusions replicated by two low-cost judges from different providers matched the human conclusion more often than single-judge conclusions (+0.10 precision), but this gain came from filtering out one poorly aligned judge, which left a conclusion for only 35% of comparisons. Judges failed to converge on 26 to 70% of system pairs at the sample sizes tested.
AI.conclusion: Cross-provider judge replication is not a reliable check of LLM-judged rankings, and disagreements co-occur across judges more than independence predicts, though a single human vote per battle cannot separate shared judge bias from voter noise.

title: Separating Common and Unique Directions for Data-Free Model Merging
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, and arithmetic methods have emerged as a simple yet effective way to merge models without data. However, existing arithmetic methods treat task vectors in parameter space and apply a single element-wise rule to directions that can differ in mergeability. In a shared directional basis, we find a consistent two-regime structure: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion task-dominated tail that carries disproportionate energy. These findings motivate Common--Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that separates task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately. Experiments across $11$ base models, four model families, and four arithmetic-based merging operators show that CUSD improves 42 of 44 model--operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines. Our code is publicly available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Common-Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that splits task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common part with an arithmetic operator and keeps the unique residuals separately. It improves 42 of 44 model-operator combinations, by up to 22.5% over the corresponding baselines.
AI.motivation: Arithmetic model-merging methods apply a single element-wise rule to task vectors in parameter space, although directions differ in how mergeable they are.
AI.method: In a shared directional basis, task vectors show a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion, task-dominated tail carrying disproportionate energy. CUSD separates each task vector into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with a downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately.
AI.result: Across 11 base models, four model families and four arithmetic-based merging operators, CUSD improves 42 of 44 model-operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines.
AI.conclusion: Treating common and unique directions of task vectors differently improves data-free model merging across models and operators.

title: Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection with Embedding-Space Explanations
comment: WACV 2027
summary: AI-generated images have reached unprecedented realism, while instruction-driven AI editors re-synthesize images for local changes, leaving no splice boundary to localize. Most detectors are black boxes with unverifiable verdicts and generalize poorly because adapting a backbone on the detection distribution memorizes generator-specific fingerprints that quickly become obsolete. Specialist detectors built on pure-vision representations, particularly DINOv3, generalize well across generators, but explainable methods forgo this advantage: jointly training one multimodal model for classification and language generation subjects its visual representation to the language objective. We therefore require that explanation training cannot alter the verdict. We introduce FOX, which first builds and locks a specialist DINOv3 detector, then uses its representation to guide a lightweight VLM toward forensic explanation. A joint-embedding predictor maps locked visual evidence into a frozen text encoder's semantic space, producing guidance that the VLM verbalizes on demand. FOX achieves 97.4 mean AUC across 14 unseen generators, 69.8 BERTScore on XPlainVerse, and 56.1 on LOKI.

AI.tldr: FOX is a detector of AI-generated images that first locks a specialist DINOv3 classifier and then uses its representation to guide a lightweight VLM toward forensic explanations, so explanation training cannot change the verdict. It achieves a 97.4 mean AUC across 14 unseen generators, with 69.8 BERTScore on XPlainVerse and 56.1 on LOKI.
AI.motivation: Most detectors are black boxes that generalise poorly, and explainable methods lose the generalisation of pure-vision DINOv3 specialists because jointly training a multimodal model for classification and language generation alters the visual representation.
AI.method: A specialist DINOv3 detector is built and locked. A joint-embedding predictor maps the locked visual evidence into a frozen text encoder's semantic space, producing guidance that the VLM verbalises on demand.
AI.result: FOX achieves a 97.4 mean AUC across 14 unseen generators, 69.8 BERTScore on XPlainVerse and 56.1 on LOKI.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the verdict from explanation training allows explainable AI-generated image detection without sacrificing cross-generator generalisation.

title: Improving PI-RADS Prediction and Prostate Cancer Detection from Multiparametric MRI with Anatomical Guidance
summary: Accurate prediction of Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) scores from multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) remains challenging, more so than clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) detection. Given the importance of lesion location in PI-RADS scoring, we evaluated whether incorporating prostate zonal masks improves PI-RADS prediction and csPCa detection across multiple architectures (3D ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ViT) using a large-scale internal dataset. Anatomical guidance generally improved performance across architectures, with the best results achieved by ResNet-18 with 2-zone guidance for PI-RADS prediction (QWK = 0.511) and ResNet-50 with 5-zone guidance for csPCa detection (AUC = 0.809). Fine-tuned results on external datasets further demonstrated the benefits of anatomical guidance. Furthermore, models with anatomical guidance improved the utility of model-predicted PI-RADS scores for PI-RADS-based csPCa detection (positive defined as PI-RADS>=3). Combining model-predicted and expert-assigned PI-RADS scores significantly increased the AUC from 0.711 to 0.756 (p < 0.05), suggesting that AI-derived PI-RADS scores may provide complementary information to expert assessment for csPCa detection. Overall, our findings highlight the value of incorporating prostate zonal anatomy into deep learning-based prostate MRI assessment.

AI.tldr: Adding prostate zonal masks as anatomical guidance generally improves PI-RADS score prediction and clinically significant prostate cancer detection from multiparametric MRI across 3D ResNet-18, ResNet-50 and ViT. The best PI-RADS prediction is QWK 0.511 with ResNet-18 and 2-zone guidance, and csPCa detection AUC is 0.809 with ResNet-50 and 5-zone guidance.
AI.motivation: PI-RADS prediction from mpMRI is harder than csPCa detection, and lesion location matters in PI-RADS scoring, so the authors test whether zonal anatomy helps.
AI.method: Prostate zonal masks are incorporated as guidance across three architectures on a large internal dataset, with fine-tuning on external datasets.
AI.result: Anatomical guidance generally improves performance, with the best PI-RADS prediction at QWK 0.511 (ResNet-18, 2-zone) and the best csPCa detection at AUC 0.809 (ResNet-50, 5-zone). Combining model-predicted and expert-assigned PI-RADS scores raises the AUC from 0.711 to 0.756 (p < 0.05).
AI.conclusion: Incorporating prostate zonal anatomy into deep learning MRI assessment is valuable, and AI-derived PI-RADS scores may add complementary information to expert assessment.

title: What Remains in Sight? Autoregressive Video Decoding as Representation-Guided Context Rewriting
summary: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.

AI.tldr: ReCR is a training-free method that treats autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting, selecting which generated past frames or segments to show the decoder at each step. It consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones on long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks under matched visible-token budgets.
AI.motivation: Most autoregressive video inference pipelines decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory, rather than as an explicit choice.
AI.method: At each step ReCR selects context units from the generated history using internal decoder representations, favoring units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts; the selected units are mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block.
AI.result: ReCR consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks under matched visible-token budgets; representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching support the analysis.
AI.conclusion: Improving what remains visible in the context is an effective route to more stable long-video decoding.

title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code and trial-level data: this https URL
summary: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. We show that, for retrieval, length is cheap and competition is not. On five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families), neutral filler costs nothing: accuracy stays at 0.97 to 1.00, up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Statements in the format of the evidence, placed at the same positions, drop it to 0.16 to 0.33. A single statement that gives the queried key a rival value multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and every additional rival adds to it. Inside the model, one quantity tracks the failure: the attention mass left on the evidence. Across 126,473 trials it explains up to 58% of the variance in loss; log length explains at most 8%. The masked-filler protocol behind the claim that length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU (11 to 18 points lost at 30K tokens), but fails a visible control in retrieval: masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K tokens, while the same filler left visible costs none. In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention. We release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that in retrieval, context rot in language models comes from competition for attention rather than input length: neutral filler costs little, while a rival value for the queried key sharply reduces accuracy. The attention mass left on the evidence explains most of the variance in loss.
AI.motivation: The common explanation that language models fail on long inputs because of length is challenged, since it does not separate length from competing evidence in retrieval.
AI.method: The authors test five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families) with neutral filler, evidence-format statements, and rival-value statements at matched positions, and measure attention mass on the evidence across 126,473 trials; they also run a masked-filler protocol on MMLU and a visible-filler control.
AI.result: Neutral filler keeps accuracy at 0.97 to 1.00 up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B, while evidence-format statements drop it to 0.16 to 0.33; a single rival-value statement multiplies the loss by 9 to 110. Attention mass on the evidence explains up to 58% of the variance in loss, while log length explains at most 8%. Masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K in retrieval, whereas visible filler costs none, and masked filler costs 11 to 18 points on MMLU at 30K tokens.
AI.conclusion: In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention rather than a length effect; the authors release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.

title: When the Consumer Is an Agent: Execution-Grounded Service-Level Agreements
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for the 24th International Conference on Service-Oriented Computing (ICSOC 2026), Springer LNCS. Followed by the companion artifact paper, accepted in the ICSOC 2026 Artifact Evaluation track. Replication package: this https URL
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. We introduce execution-grounded completion contracts, which treat completion as a service-level outcome. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes execution-grounded completion contracts, in which an independent control plane verifies against a deadline-bound service-state predicate whether an agent's task is complete, rather than trusting the agent's self-assessment. The approach is evaluated on a live multi-provider data service with an injected transfer delay.
AI.motivation: In asynchronous distributed services, an accepted call or an immediate state read does not show that the required state became observable by the deadline, and LLM agents that report completion themselves may be wrong.
AI.method: An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits or rejects completion, and directs recovery while the agent works; policies for placement and deletion tasks are tested with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay.
AI.result: Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions stayed consistent with later observations, all healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified.
AI.conclusion: Completion of agent-performed service tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state instead of the agent's self-assessment.

title: Agentic Path Maps: Exposing an Agent's Traversal Through the Garden of Forking Paths
summary: When an AI agent executes an underspecified task, it embeds choices that may contradict unarticulated user context and preferences. However, interrupting the user for clarification on all such decisions is untenable. How might agents communicate impactful, but unexplored, paths to the user after execution? To investigate, we first distill a design space for communicating alternative paths, supporting the generation of new systems and structuring dimensions of future study. We then measure the impact of one vital design space dimension on user comprehension: the number of alternatives displayed. Through a user study (n=48) in the data analysis domain, we find that participants rarely consider alternative paths of their own volition, but AI overreliance reduces when alternative paths are visualized for them. By revealing paths the agent did not take, we demonstrate how users can better interpret results and incorporate personal context.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how an AI agent should communicate the alternative paths it did not take in an underspecified data analysis task, so that users can notice and check the choices embedded in its results. A user study with 48 participants finds that visualizing alternatives reduces overreliance on the AI.
AI.motivation: Agents make consequential choices under underspecified tasks that may contradict unstated user context, but interrupting users for clarification on every decision is impractical, and users rarely consider alternatives on their own.
AI.method: The authors first distill a design space for communicating alternative paths after execution, then measure the effect of one dimension, the number of alternatives displayed, through a user study (n=48) in data analysis.
AI.result: Participants rarely considered alternative paths unprompted, but AI overreliance decreased when alternative paths were visualized for them.
AI.conclusion: Revealing paths the agent did not take helps users interpret results and incorporate personal context.

title: Impact of Input Resolution in Mammographic Mass Detection: A Controlled Multi-Architecture Study
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Deep-learning-based mass detectors usually downsample mammograms, trading fine image detail for lower computational cost. However, published studies cannot reveal how much accuracy this trade-off sacrifices, since they also differ in architecture, preprocessing, and evaluation protocol. In this work, we isolated the effect of input resolution in a controlled study on the VinDr-Mammo dataset, training 18 detectors at six input resolutions ranging from 512 x 416 to 1600 x 1280 pixels, for 108 model-resolution combinations. Whole mammograms were resized without cropping or tiling. For each model, preprocessing, model initialization, augmentation, and evaluation procedures were kept fixed across resolutions. Detection accuracy was evaluated by mAP50 on the 219 mass-positive images of the official test split, and 57 combinations with test mAP50 of at least 0.60 were analyzed. From the lowest to the highest resolution, median mAP50 rose from 0.626 to 0.660 and the best mAP50 from 0.670 to 0.709. The best result, achieved by DINO with a ConvNeXt-S backbone, is the highest mAP50 reported to date on mass-positive VinDr-Mammo images. Gains were concentrated in small masses: for the smallest third of lesions, median mAP50 rose by 0.074 (from 0.367 to 0.441), compared with 0.007 and 0.032 for medium and large masses. Median training time increased from 0.45 to 1.40 h, and median inference time from 23.6 to 113.7 ms per image. Therefore, higher input resolution mainly benefits the small masses that are hardest to detect, at a computational cost that remains practical.

AI.tldr: A controlled study of 18 mass detectors trained at six input resolutions on VinDr-Mammo finds that higher input resolution improves mass detection, mainly for small masses, at a practical computational cost. The best result, DINO with a ConvNeXt-S backbone, reaches a test mAP50 of 0.709, which the authors report as the highest to date on mass-positive VinDr-Mammo images.
AI.motivation: Published mammogram detectors downsample images, but prior studies differ in architecture, preprocessing, and evaluation, so the accuracy cost of downsampling cannot be isolated.
AI.method: Whole mammograms are resized without cropping or tiling to six resolutions from 512 x 416 to 1600 x 1280 pixels, training 18 detectors (108 model-resolution combinations) with preprocessing, initialization, augmentation, and evaluation held fixed; mAP50 is measured on 219 mass-positive test images, and 57 combinations with test mAP50 of at least 0.60 are analysed.
AI.result: Median mAP50 rose from 0.626 to 0.660 and the best mAP50 from 0.670 to 0.709 from the lowest to the highest resolution. For the smallest third of lesions, median mAP50 rose by 0.074 (0.367 to 0.441), versus 0.007 and 0.032 for medium and large masses. Median training time rose from 0.45 to 1.40 h and median inference time from 23.6 to 113.7 ms per image.
AI.conclusion: Higher input resolution mainly benefits the small masses that are hardest to detect, at a computational cost that remains practical.

title: GC-MoE: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with FP8/FP4 Grouped GEMM via CUDA Green Contexts
comment: 25 pages, including appendices
summary: Under expert parallelism, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers pay all-to-all token dispatch, grouped GEMMs, and a combine step in every layer. In decode each rank holds only 1-256 tokens: dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate while tensor-core utilization is inherently low. In fused operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation overlap only by sharing every SM: dispatch warps compete with TMA/MMA and epilogue warps for registers, shared memory, and issue slots; every phase shares one CTA resource budget, synchronization spans the whole SM array, and every replay ends with a workspace-clean pass and a cross-rank barrier. We present GC-MoE, an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the device into a small communication partition and a large compute partition. Each role gets its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain, so dispatch and GEMM tune independently. A three-node CUDA Graph (four on Hopper with fused shared experts) launches the dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots; a token-ring handshake starts computation on the first filled ring blocks, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier between replays. The compute partition runs operand-swapped tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts. On 8 H20 GPUs GC-MoE accelerates DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x); on 8 B300 GPUs it accelerates GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), beating Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy. GC-MoE reserves only 20 of 148 SMs on B300 for dispatch.

AI.tldr: GC-MoE is an open-source FP8/FP4 mixture-of-experts inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to run expert-parallel token dispatch and grouped GEMM concurrently on separate device partitions. It speeds up DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.2 decoding and beats Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy.
AI.motivation: In fused MoE operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation share every SM, so their resource budgets, synchronization, and per-replay barriers are coupled and cannot be tuned independently, which hurts decode with few tokens per rank.
AI.method: The device is split with CUDA Green Contexts into a small communication partition and a large compute partition, each with its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain; a three-node CUDA Graph launches dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots, a token-ring handshake starts computation early, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier; the compute partition uses tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper.
AI.result: On 8 H20 GPUs, decode of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is accelerated by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x). On 8 B300 GPUs, GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash are accelerated by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), and GC-MoE beats Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy; 20 of 148 SMs on B300 are reserved for dispatch.
AI.conclusion: Partitioning communication and computation with Green Contexts lets dispatch and GEMM be tuned independently and gives consistent decode speedups over a fused MoE baseline.

title: IntentGEO: Intent-aware Generative Engine Optimization for Recommendation
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape recommendations across chatbots, e-commerce, and user-generated content (UGC) platforms, creating demand for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to improve item visibility in generated responses. Existing GEO studies are mainly content-centric, optimizing visibility under general-purpose queries. However, a shared item description usually serves users with different needs and decision goals, resulting in its visibility gains being dependent on the request. To investigate how changing intent affects visibility, we formulate IntentGEO to evaluate shared rewrites across need specificity and decision progression. We revisit existing GEO methods and find that their visibility gains vary across user intents. More critically, learning-based prompt optimization can underperform its handwritten seed on average. Tracing these updates reveals prompt drift from explicit recommendation instructions toward generic promotional tactics. To address this drift, we propose AMO (Anchored Meta-Optimization), which preserves recommendation instructions in a fixed core while learning appended strategies from citation feedback.
