Across four domains and ten intent states, AMO improves average citation-rank gain by 35% over the strongest prior learning-based baseline and leads on nine states. Ablations show that learned additions improve on the fixed core alone and that AMO outperforms full-prompt optimization initialized from that core. It also achieves the highest gains in an agentic recommendation pipeline and, after separate adaptation, on Doubao, a commercially deployed, closed-source online assistant. These findings highlight user intent as a key dimension of GEO evaluation and support anchored adaptation across recommendation needs and decision stages.

AI.tldr: IntentGEO formalizes generative engine optimization as dependent on user intent and proposes AMO, which keeps recommendation instructions in a fixed core and learns appended strategies from citation feedback. AMO improves average citation-rank gain by 35% over the strongest prior learning-based baseline across four domains and ten intent states.
AI.motivation: Existing GEO methods are content-centric and evaluated on general queries, but a shared item description serves users with different needs, so visibility gains depend on the request; learning-based prompt optimization can even underperform its handwritten seed, with prompt drift toward generic promotional tactics.
AI.method: The authors evaluate shared rewrites across need specificity and decision progression, then propose Anchored Meta-Optimization (AMO), which preserves recommendation instructions in a fixed core and learns appended strategies from citation feedback.
AI.result: AMO improves average citation-rank gain by 35% over the strongest prior learning-based baseline and leads on nine of ten intent states. Ablations show that the learned additions improve on the fixed core alone and outperform full-prompt optimization initialized from that core. AMO also gives the highest gains in an agentic recommendation pipeline and, after separate adaptation, on Doubao, a commercially deployed closed-source assistant.
AI.conclusion: User intent is a key dimension of GEO evaluation, and anchored adaptation supports recommendation across needs and decision stages.

title: DiMuRe: Diagnosis-Guided Multilevel Recovery for Robotic Task Execution
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, including appendices
summary: Disturbances can invalidate the conditions required by a robot's next action even when much of its task program remains useful. A recovery system must therefore choose a response suited to the current state. We present DiMuRe (diagnosis-guided multilevel recovery), a framework for robot-use agents that uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA) grasping. After the original program exits, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can generate corrective code from images and execution feedback. Local verification checks the outcome of each recovery attempt. We also introduce LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for robustness and recovery under mid-execution disturbances, supporting program-based agents and VLA policies. On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local DiMuRe (program reuse and recovery skills) achieves 77.65% complete-task success, compared with 58.68% for the original program under the same physical-step allowance. Full DiMuRe achieves 81.90% with terminal replanning, an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program.

AI.tldr: DiMuRe is a diagnosis-guided recovery framework for robot task execution that chooses between reusing the original program and applying predefined recovery skills, including bounded VLA grasping, or generating corrective code with an MLLM. On the new LIBERO-Disturb benchmark it raises complete-task success from 58.68% for the original program to 77.65% (Local DiMuRe) and 81.90% (full DiMuRe).
AI.motivation: Disturbances can invalidate the preconditions of a robot's next action even when much of its task program remains useful, so a recovery system must select a response suited to the current state, and no benchmark tested recovery under mid-execution disturbances for both program-based agents and VLA policies.
AI.method: The framework uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded VLA grasping; after the original program exits, a multimodal LLM can generate corrective code from images and execution feedback, and local verification checks each recovery attempt; the authors also introduce LIBERO-Disturb.
AI.result: On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local DiMuRe reaches 77.65% complete-task success versus 58.68% for the original program under the same physical-step allowance, and full DiMuRe reaches 81.90% with terminal replanning, an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program.
AI.conclusion: Choosing a recovery response based on diagnosis of the current state improves robustness to mid-execution disturbances over reusing the original program alone.

title: Constructing a Regional Slang Lexicon for Electricity Demands via Soft-Label Bidirectional Anchoring and Active Learning
summary: Power-grid customer service increasingly relies on community social media, where customers describe outages, billing, and equipment faults in informal regional dialect. Such messages exhibit non-standard morphology, semantic drift, and out-of-vocabulary expressions that make manual lexicon construction costly and degrade conventional NLP tools. We propose a weak-supervision framework constructing a regional slang lexicon from curated dialect anchors and power-domain seed terms. Candidates are generated via Pointwise Mutual Information with soft-label bidirectional anchoring, retaining dialect-anchored terms while recording power-domain relevance as separate metadata, and are scored by combining Sentence-BERT semantic similarity with a jieba-based wordhood measure. Uncertainty-aware active learning with rule-based and retrieval-augmented LLM oracles is applied under three query strategies, and the resulting lexicon is evaluated by a higher-capability LLM calibrated against human expert annotations via Cohen's $\kappa$. On 11,177 real WeChat messages from Yuxi (Yunnan, China), the framework achieves an evaluator-estimated dialect precision of DP~$=$~1.0 with zero false positives. An ablation shows that soft-label layering retains 751\% more candidates than strict power-gating at identical precision, expanding the candidate pool from 41 to 349 terms. Human calibration ($n=46$) yields $\kappa_{\text{dialect}}=1.0$ and $\kappa_{\text{power}}=0.85$. The resulting 25--33-term lexicon, 4--5 of which are power-relevant, provides a preliminary resource for dialect-aware power-grid service NLP.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a regional slang lexicon for power-grid customer messages in the Yuxi dialect using weak supervision, soft-label bidirectional anchoring, and active learning with LLM oracles. On 11,177 WeChat messages it reports dialect precision of 1.0 with zero false positives and produces a 25 to 33-term lexicon.
AI.motivation: Customer messages to power-grid services are written in informal regional dialect with non-standard morphology and out-of-vocabulary terms, which makes manual lexicon construction costly and degrades standard NLP tools.
AI.method: Candidates are generated with Pointwise Mutual Information and soft-label bidirectional anchoring from dialect anchors and power-domain seed terms, keeping power-domain relevance as separate metadata; candidates are scored by combining Sentence-BERT similarity with a jieba-based wordhood measure; uncertainty-aware active learning uses rule-based and retrieval-augmented LLM oracles under three query strategies; a stronger LLM is calibrated against human experts via Cohen's kappa.
AI.result: On 11,177 WeChat messages from Yuxi (Yunnan), the framework reaches evaluator-estimated dialect precision of 1.0 with zero false positives. Soft-label layering retains 751% more candidates than strict power-gating at identical precision, expanding the pool from 41 to 349 terms. Human calibration (n=46) gives kappa of 1.0 for dialect and 0.85 for power relevance.
AI.conclusion: The resulting lexicon of 25 to 33 terms, 4 to 5 of them power-relevant, is a preliminary resource for dialect-aware power-grid service NLP.

title: LIRA: A More Interpretable Dynamic Loss-Informed Rank Allocation for Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large pretrained models. However, standard LoRA typically assigns a fixed rank profile despite layer- and stage-dependent adaptation needs, while recent adaptive-rank variants often rely on heuristic or first-order signals that provide only an indirect link between rank reallocation and local loss behavior. This leaves the rationale behind each rank reallocation insufficiently interpretable. Motivated by this gap, we propose LIRA (Loss-Informed Rank Allocation), a dynamic-rank LoRA method designed to make online rank reallocation more interpretable. LIRA scores each layer by the estimated magnitude of the local loss perturbation associated with its recent LoRA-factor movements under a second-order approximation, making the basis for each rank change interpretable term by term. By periodically applying DELTA (Displacement-Evaluated Loss-Trajectory Allocation), a displacement-based algorithm for LoRA rank reallocation, LIRA produces discrete effective ranks under matched budgets while remaining compatible with standard (A,B) adapters. On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, LIRA outperforms the uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines reported under this protocol; Trajectory EMA attains performance competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.

AI.tldr: LIRA is a dynamic-rank LoRA method that reallocates ranks online by scoring each layer with the estimated local loss perturbation from its recent LoRA-factor movements under a second-order approximation. It is claimed to outperform uniform LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines on RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol.
AI.motivation: Standard LoRA uses a fixed rank profile despite layer- and stage-dependent adaptation needs, and recent adaptive-rank methods rely on heuristic or first-order signals that only indirectly link rank reallocation to local loss behavior.
AI.method: LIRA scores each layer by the estimated magnitude of the local loss perturbation under a second-order approximation, and periodically applies DELTA, a displacement-based rank reallocation algorithm, to produce discrete effective ranks under matched budgets while staying compatible with standard (A,B) adapters.
AI.result: On RoBERTa-base GLUE under the La-LoRA/LoRA protocol, LIRA outperforms the uniform-LoRA and adaptive-rank baselines reported under that protocol. Trajectory EMA is competitive with Fixed-point Fisher at lower estimation cost.
AI.conclusion: Scoring rank changes by their local loss effect makes each reallocation interpretable term by term while keeping performance competitive.

title: Navigating Runtime Dynamism in Semantic Query Serving
summary: LLM-powered semantic queries increasingly combine relational processing with multiple LLM-based operators over unstructured data. Efficiently serving such queries is challenging due to runtime dynamism at two coupled levels. Across queries, dynamic arrivals and heterogeneous resource demands continuously change scheduling priorities. Within a query, heterogeneous characteristics across fine-grained input batches cause operator costs and selectivities to vary throughout execution, making a statically optimized plan unreliable. These two forms of dynamism create a circular dependency: inter-query scheduling requires estimates of remaining LLM work, while the remaining work depends on runtime plan choices whose costs become observable only during execution. We present SeqoFlow, a runtime framework that jointly adapts query plans and schedules concurrent semantic queries. SeqoFlow enumerates equivalence-preserving plan alternatives under operator dependencies and decomposes queries into fine-grained units, enabling safe plan adaptation and query preemption at batch boundaries. To support both decisions without exhaustively profiling candidate plans on the target LLM, SeqoFlow uses lightweight speculative estimation to capture runtime costs. These estimates jointly guide plan adaptation and inter-query scheduling, closing the loop between query optimization and LLM inference. Experiments across diverse query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show that SeqoFlow substantially reduces end-to-end latency compared to existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.

AI.tldr: SeqoFlow is a runtime framework that jointly adapts query plans and schedules concurrent LLM-based semantic queries, using lightweight speculative estimation of runtime costs. It substantially reduces end-to-end latency compared with existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.
AI.motivation: Serving semantic queries is hard because dynamism operates at two coupled levels: across queries, arrivals and resource demands change priorities, and within a query, operator costs and selectivities vary across input batches, so inter-query scheduling needs remaining LLM work estimates that depend on plan choices only observable at runtime.
AI.method: SeqoFlow enumerates equivalence-preserving plan alternatives under operator dependencies, decomposes queries into fine-grained units to allow safe plan adaptation and preemption at batch boundaries, and uses lightweight speculative estimation rather than exhaustive profiling on the target LLM; the estimates jointly guide plan adaptation and inter-query scheduling.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show substantial end-to-end latency reductions compared with existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between query optimization and LLM inference through runtime plan adaptation and scheduling improves the serving of semantic queries.

title: OmniST: Topology-Invariant Spatiotemporal Forecasting with Guaranteed-Coverage Uncertainty at Unseen Sensor Locations
comment: Code and experiments: this https URL . 9 tables, 4 figures. Baselines (E-STGCN, IGNNK) are faithful reimplementations, not the authors' original code
summary: Standard spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks need a fixed-size adjacency matrix, coupling model weights to a specific sensor count N; they cannot produce any output at a sensor absent from training. We present OmniST, a topology-invariant forecaster whose computation has zero structural dependency on the number of nodes, and which, composed with inductive split-conformal calibration, gives distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at arbitrary (including never-seen) sensor locations, preserving that guarantee as sensors are added or removed. Topology invariance follows from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing via a bidirectional GRU. On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019-2023), OmniST attains a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and degrades at most 1.1 percent when 40 percent of stations are removed. Its inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation (about 12 percent) and a learned kriging GNN (IGNNK, about 21 percent), and, unlike either, carry a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The guarantee holds at 90 percent or above under 30-50 percent node dropout across four real datasets over three domains (Delhi and Beijing air quality, NOAA GHCN weather, Caltrans PeMSD7-M traffic), and still holds at 325 real sensors (full PeMS-BAY). We also fix a temporal-drift failure: static conformal under-covers over time (about 0.50 late), but a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator restores target coverage (0.89 overall, 0.96 late) at the cost of wider intervals.

AI.tldr: OmniST is a spatiotemporal forecaster whose computation does not depend on the number of sensors, and combined with inductive split-conformal calibration it gives coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at unseen sensor locations. On Delhi air-quality data it reaches a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and beats nearest-neighbor interpolation and IGNNK at unseen stations.
AI.motivation: Standard spatiotemporal GCNs need a fixed-size adjacency matrix tied to a sensor count, so they cannot produce output at a sensor absent from training, and static conformal prediction under-covers when the data drift over time.
AI.method: Topology invariance comes from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention built from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing with a bidirectional GRU; inductive split-conformal calibration gives finite-sample coverage, and a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator handles temporal drift.
AI.result: On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019 to 2023), the 30-day PM2.5 MAE is 31.0 ug/m3, and performance degrades by at most 1.1% when 40% of stations are removed. Inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation by about 12% and IGNNK by about 21%. Coverage holds at 90% or above under 30 to 50% node dropout across four datasets, and at 325 real sensors. Rolling adaptive conformal restores coverage to 0.89 overall and 0.96 late, where static conformal reached about 0.50 late.
AI.conclusion: Topology-invariant forecasting combined with adaptive conformal calibration gives reliable prediction intervals at arbitrary sensor locations, at the cost of wider intervals.

title: Predicting protein structures at any folding stage from sequence
comment: 47 pages, 10 figures. The first five authors contributed equally
summary: Protein structure predictors reliably identify native conformations, but do not describe the continuum connecting unfolded ensembles to folded states. Here we present FoldScape, a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework that generates C$\alpha$ conformational ensembles at a specified folding fraction $Q$. FoldScape reconstructs three-dimensional chains through hierarchical, sliding-window regressions of one-dimensional inter-residue distances, followed by chain assembly and sampling with a rectified-flow decoder. It is trained on multi-scale coarse-grained folding trajectories and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories. Across 20 human proteins (36-857 residues), at matched sample size, FoldScape covers about an order of magnitude more of the folding coordinate than seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles, robustly across proteins, order parameters and binning choices. AlphaFold 3 better anchors the immediate native vicinity, which FoldScape does not reach, making the approaches complementary. FoldScape reconstruction accuracy remains approximately constant along $Q$, from collapsed coil to near-native globule, rather than deteriorating away from the native state. A stride-one crop-and-superpose scheme extends inference to chains several times longer than a single chain-level forward pass. We also show that training trajectories resolve mechanical unfolding at residue resolution, that elongation-conditioned ensembles exhibit reproducible continuous observables across pulling velocities, and that partially unfolded chains form geometrically coherent segments. FoldScape thus combines broad coverage of folding stages with stable reconstruction accuracy, without per-protein simulation.

AI.tldr: FoldScape is a sequence-conditioned deep learning framework that generates C-alpha conformational ensembles at a specified folding fraction Q, covering the continuum from unfolded to folded states. It covers about an order of magnitude more of the folding coordinate than seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles, and the two are complementary.
AI.motivation: Protein structure predictors reliably find native conformations but do not describe the continuum between unfolded ensembles and folded states.
AI.method: FoldScape reconstructs 3D chains through hierarchical sliding-window regressions of one-dimensional inter-residue distances, followed by chain assembly and sampling with a rectified-flow decoder; it is trained on multi-scale coarse-grained folding trajectories and all-atom mechanical-unfolding trajectories, and a stride-one crop-and-superpose scheme extends inference to longer chains.
AI.result: Across 20 human proteins (36 to 857 residues), at matched sample size, FoldScape covers about an order of magnitude more of the folding coordinate than seed-varied AlphaFold 3 ensembles. AlphaFold 3 better anchors the immediate native vicinity, which FoldScape does not reach. Reconstruction accuracy stays roughly constant along Q, from collapsed coil to near-native globule.
AI.conclusion: FoldScape combines broad coverage of folding stages with stable reconstruction accuracy and does not need per-protein simulation.

title: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation
summary: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that multi-agent debate can amplify safety risks in retrieval-augmented web applications: under social pressure, standard debate raises adoption of unsafe guidance from 0.0% to 100.0%. The proposed inference-time framework RiskTrace-Debias reduces worst-case unsafe adoption to 2.0% or less across architectures without causing over-refusal.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent debate aggregates noisy web information, but deliberation is a social process, so conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries when retrieved sources contain latent hazards.
AI.method: The authors introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six web risk categories that holds queries and evidence fixed while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry; RiskTrace-Debias is an inference-time auditing framework combining evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration.
AI.result: Isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, but standard multi-agent debate raises unsafe adoption from 0.0% to 100.0% and silences safe minority evidence. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to 2.0% or less across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, and produces verifiable provenance traces.
AI.conclusion: Social structure in deliberation can amplify latent web safety risks, and inference-time auditing can mitigate this without retraining or debate regeneration.

title: Reciprocity Can Erase Direction:tructural Boundaries and Controlled Utility of Magnetic Graph Networks
summary: Magnetic graph networks encode direction through phase, but a learned graph can erase the intended directional mechanism before prediction. We characterize this failure for support-based magnetic Laplacians. Exact identities relate imaginary energy and distance from zero phase to amplitude-weighted reciprocity. Top-$k$ selection forces complete collapse when the observed-node count satisfies $m\leq k+1$, and dense support imposes a lower bound on reciprocal-arc fraction. We then construct paired propagation examples with identical node features and symmetric amplitudes but opposite labels, giving a provable chance-level limit for direction-erasing representations. In 72 fixed neural fits, support phase achieved test AUROC 1.0000 on a unilateral ring but 0.5000 on reciprocal ring and complete supports; continuous score phase and a real directed comparator achieved 1.0000 throughout. All models solved the direction-free control. These are oracle-direction mechanism tests, not evidence of learned clinical direction. In the preserved public DeepDRiD development study, continuous phase was active but its robustness difference from zero phase was only $+0.0036$ (descriptive 95\% interval $-0.0014$ to $+0.0095$) on validation patients used for checkpoint selection. The contribution is a structural and experimental framework for distinguishing erased direction from unestablished task utility. It provides a precise circumstance in which magnetic phase preserves useful information, without asserting universal or clinical superiority.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a learned graph can erase the direction encoded by magnetic phase in magnetic graph networks, and gives conditions under which this happens. In controlled fits, support phase reaches test AUROC 1.0 on a unilateral ring but 0.5 on reciprocal rings and complete supports, while continuous score phase stays at 1.0.
AI.motivation: Magnetic graph networks encode direction through phase, but a learned graph can remove the intended directional mechanism before prediction, and it was unclear when phase preserves useful directional information.
AI.method: The authors derive exact identities relating imaginary energy and distance from zero phase to amplitude-weighted reciprocity for support-based magnetic Laplacians, show that top-k selection forces complete collapse when the observed-node count is at most k+1, and build paired propagation examples with identical features and opposite labels to give a chance-level limit; they run 72 fixed neural fits and a preserved public DeepDRiD development study.
AI.result: In the 72 fits, support phase achieves test AUROC 1.0000 on a unilateral ring but 0.5000 on reciprocal ring and complete supports, while continuous score phase and a real directed comparator achieve 1.0000 throughout. In DeepDRiD, the robustness difference of continuous phase from zero phase is only +0.0036 (descriptive 95% interval -0.0014 to +0.0095) on validation patients.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a framework for separating erased direction from unestablished task utility and identifies when magnetic phase preserves useful information, without claiming universal or clinical superiority.

title: SEAM: Situated Executable Associative Memory for a Co-located Community
summary: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.

AI.tldr: SEAM is a social app that builds a shared, situated, associative memory for a co-located community, distilling group knowledge from members' posts and replying in context; some memories act as instructions that make the system programmable by its members. A two-week deployment to 46 people and a follow-up workshop with 14 participants are reported.
AI.motivation: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals and how it is combined depends on social ties, so the authors draw on how a single mind recalls memories in response to stimuli to build a community-level memory.
AI.method: Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in an associative and situated way; some memories serve as instructions that alter system behavior.
AI.result: Deployed to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, with a follow-up workshop of 14. Members shared their days, queried the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced members to people and topics they had not encountered.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue the system points toward communities where knowledge finds people.

title: FlowTranslator: Training-Free In-Image Machine Translation with Flow-Based Editing
summary: In-image machine translation (IIMT) replaces text in an image with its translation while preserving the surrounding visual context. Existing task-specific models achieve convincing performance but require massive paired training images before and after translation. As advanced text-to-image (T2I) models have reached a practically usable level of multilingual text generation, we argue that this capability can be transferred to IIMT and present FlowTranslator. It is a training-free IIMT framework that first employs an OCR model and an LLM to generate the translation prompt, which is injected into the T2I-based diffusion model. To optimize the accurate and natural generation of translated text, we introduce two trajectory controls: Region Coupling Release (RCR) partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, while Coupling Expansion (CE) amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory. Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator achieves average PRIM BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2, respectively, substantially outperforming the strong training-based baseline UniTranslator. On the more challenging and realistic whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reaches 40.1\% exact-match accuracy and surpasses existing editing systems, some of which only address the text-rendering stage rather than the complete IIMT task. These results establish flow-based editing as a strong, fully training-free baseline for IIMT.

AI.tldr: FlowTranslator is a training-free in-image machine translation framework that replaces text in images using flow-based editing of a text-to-image diffusion model, with the translation prompt produced by OCR and an LLM. On the ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese it reaches 40.1% exact-match accuracy, and it outperforms the training-based UniTranslator on average PRIM BLEU and COMET.
AI.motivation: Existing in-image translation models need large sets of paired images before and after translation, while modern text-to-image models can already render multilingual text, which the authors argue can be transferred to this task.
AI.method: An OCR model and an LLM generate the translation prompt, which is injected into a T2I-based diffusion model; two trajectory controls are introduced: Region Coupling Release partially decorrelates target-branch noise inside the text region early in the trajectory, and Coupling Expansion amplifies the emerging edit displacement mid-trajectory.
AI.result: Under the EasyOCR read-back protocol, FlowTranslator achieves average PRIM BLEU and COMET scores of 20.6 and 57.2, substantially outperforming UniTranslator. On whole-image ScenePair photographs translated into Chinese, it reaches 40.1% exact-match accuracy and surpasses existing editing systems, some of which address only the text-rendering stage.
AI.conclusion: Flow-based editing is a strong, fully training-free baseline for in-image machine translation.

title: What Is the Influence of Task Order in Continual Learning? An Empirical Study and Order-Aware Evaluation for Motion Forecasting
comment: 13 pages
summary: Aggregate scores for continual learning algorithms rest on a distribution over task orders that is rarely stated. We formulate algorithm comparison as an expectation over a declared order distribution, which separates training variation from order variation, and apply it to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs). Task order accounts for 65\% to 91\% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90\% to 99\% of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task: the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders, the leading algorithm in current-task error and backward transfer is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up. Backward transfer depends on the order mainly through its reference term, which weights the first task most heavily, so relative improvement and final error identify different leading algorithms for displacement error. A transition-direction descriptor computed from task statistics tracks the position of the smallest task, and weighting orders by it leaves the algorithm ranking unchanged. These results call for benchmarks that declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores. The code and data are available \href{this https URL}{here}.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in continual-learning results for motion forecasting, and that most of this order effect comes from the identity of the starting task. The authors propose evaluating algorithms as an expectation over a declared order distribution.
AI.motivation: Aggregate continual-learning scores depend on a task-order distribution that is rarely stated, so algorithm comparisons may reflect order variation rather than the algorithms.
AI.method: Algorithm comparison is formulated as an expectation over a declared order distribution that separates training variation from order variation; it is applied to motion forecasting with four road-layout tasks from the INTERACTION dataset, all 24 task orders, four algorithms, and three training replicates (288 runs).
AI.result: Task order accounts for 65% to 91% of the variation in current-task error and backward transfer, and 90% to 99% of this order effect comes from the starting task, since the smallest task cannot be learned from a cold start. Beyond the first stage, the order effect is comparable to training variability. In most orders the leading algorithm is within one replicate standard deviation of the runner-up, and weighting orders by a transition-direction descriptor leaves the ranking unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Benchmarks should declare their order distribution and report order-resolved, starting-task-resolved, warm-start, and final errors alongside aggregate scores.

title: Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention
summary: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a training-free sparse attention method that clusters keys into large semantic blocks and selects blocks per query by scoring their centroids, speeding up both prefill and decoding. On Qwen3.5 hybrid models at 512K to 1M tokens it reports whole-model speedups of 1.7 to 3.0x over dense attention, with accuracy close to dense on the 35B-A3B model.
AI.motivation: Attention cost limits long-context prefill and decoding, and smaller blocks with a smaller token budget are the usual trade-off, whereas larger semantic blocks could make both selection and grouped processing cheap.
AI.method: A prompt-specific key index groups tokens from noncontiguous positions into large semantic blocks; each query selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them, and queries that select the same block are processed together.
AI.result: Including index construction and use, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention on one NVIDIA H200 are 2.3 to 2.4x for prefill and 1.7 to 2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9 to 3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval but outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B on all three benchmarks at similar latency at 512K.
AI.conclusion: Larger blocks with a larger token budget can be both faster and more accurate than smaller blocks with a smaller budget on long-context tasks.

title: Anchor: Augmented Cross-Layer Recurrent State for Long-Context Retrieval in Test-Time Training
comment: 10 Pages main paper with reference and appendix
summary: Parameter-efficient linearization turns a pretrained autoregressive Transformer into an efficient model by hybridizing sliding-window attention (SWA) with a constant-size recurrent memory. But does every layer's recurrent state contribute to long-context retrieval? Investigating an SWA and Test-Time Training (TTT) hybrid, we find that retrieval is sparse across depth, concentrated in a few anchor layers, and that the remaining states hold similar information expressed through layer-specific transformations. We exploit both observations in Anchor: TTT memory placed only at the anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation, along with demonstrated generalization to other hybrid attentions. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3-3.1x higher recall and 6.7-8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91-95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.

AI.tldr: Anchor is a hybrid of sliding-window attention and test-time training that places recurrent memory only at a few anchor layers and shares one cross-layer recurrent state across layers through learned layer-specific read maps. On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B it gives 2.3 to 3.1x higher recall than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient linearization of Transformers with sliding-window attention and constant-size recurrent memory raises the question of whether every layer's recurrent state contributes to long-context retrieval, and the authors find retrieval is concentrated in a few layers while other states hold similar information.
AI.method: Test-time training memory is placed only at anchor layers, and a cross-layer recurrent state is written once and read by many layers, each through its own learned read map that realizes a layer-specific stretch and rotation.
AI.result: On Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, Anchor delivers 2.3 to 3.1x higher recall and 6.7 to 8.9 points higher MMLU accuracy than LoLCATs with a 10x smaller recurrent state, retains 91 to 95% of the teacher's MMLU accuracy, and cuts end-to-end latency by up to 4.3x relative to softmax attention.
AI.conclusion: Concentrating recurrent memory at a few anchor layers with a shared cross-layer state gives strong long-context retrieval at a small state size, and the design also generalizes to other hybrid attentions.

title: Large Language Models for Forecasting of Electricity Price Spikes
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures
summary: Can market notices read by a large language model (LLM) improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts? We study five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. A local LLM extracted features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin were used, and a gradient-boosting model produced onset probabilities. In an out-of-sample development back-test (July 2022 to July 2024), notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model including the market operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did so almost equally and attribution to notice content was not established. A locally frozen protocol, not publicly deposited, governed a retrospective single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026. At 60 minutes, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the numeric model's Brier score was not established (H1; relative Brier skill -0.09%), so the planned comparison with rule-based features was not tested (H2). At 24 hours, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the score against a text-free control was not established (H3; +0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39], inconclusive). By the frozen wording rule the non-significant 24-hour improvement comes mainly from recalibration and cannot be attributed to notice content, although post hoc the decomposition could not separate recalibration from resolution. The 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development. With 5 onsets on 3 days and 24-hour positives in 2 of 22 three-day blocks, the holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether notices read by an LLM improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts in Australia's National Electricity Market, and finds no established improvement at 60 minutes and an inconclusive result at 24 hours. The holdout is too small, with 5 onsets, to settle a 24-hour effect either way.
AI.motivation: Market notices may carry information about price spikes, but it was unknown whether LLM-extracted features improve forecasts beyond numeric models and rule-based features that use only information visible at the forecast origin.
AI.method: A local LLM extracts features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin are used, and a gradient-boosting model produces onset probabilities for five regions; a development back-test runs from July 2022 to July 2024, and a frozen protocol governs a single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026.
AI.result: In development, notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model that includes the operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did almost as well. On the holdout, the 60-minute hypothesis was not established (relative Brier skill -0.09%), and the 24-hour hypothesis was inconclusive (+0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39]); the 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development.
AI.conclusion: The holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect, and the 24-hour improvement cannot be attributed to notice content under the frozen rule.

title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
summary: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

AI.tldr: CloakFEM is an LLM-agent framework that generates runnable finite element method programs designed to amplify solver computation, exposing computational denial-of-service vulnerabilities in FEM solvers. In the most extreme case solver iterations rise from 43 to 247,367, a 5,752.72x amplification.
AI.motivation: FEM solvers are foundational to scientific simulation, yet their susceptibility to efficiency attacks is largely unexplored, and the space of valid FEM programs is large and structured by numerical, geometric, and constitutive constraints.
AI.method: CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints, searching over seeds across three FEM stacks and 17 problem classes.
AI.result: Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM finds adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. It outperforms five generic black-box baselines and keeps an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis shows both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific vulnerability sources.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers, and runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

title: Aligning Training and Rollout Policies for End-to-End FP4 RL on Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
summary: In this work, we study end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models. Recent work on FP4 RL has introduced effective recovery recipes that restore accuracy under aggressive low-precision quantization for dense models, but we find that the same approach yields no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting. We conduct an in-depth study to understand why. Our analysis identifies the root cause in the routing mechanism unique to MoE: because the router makes discrete expert-selection decisions, training-inference policy alignment becomes acutely sensitive to whether the same recovery technique is applied symmetrically on the training and inference sides. When an asymmetric recipe is used-including the dense-model approach, which corrects only the rollout-training-inference alignment deteriorates sharply, as measured by the Pearson correlation coefficient between training and inference probabilities, and router selection matching rates. Building on this finding, we propose MoeResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe for MoE RL post-training that enforces symmetry between the training- and inference-side corrections. MoeResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision, establishing symmetric recovery as the key principle in FP4 RL for MoE models.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that a recovery recipe for end-to-end FP4 reinforcement learning on dense models gives no gain on Mixture-of-Experts models, because the router's discrete expert selection requires the same correction on training and inference sides. The proposed MoeResQ enforces this symmetry and closes much of the accuracy gap to full precision.
AI.motivation: FP4 RL recovery recipes that work for dense models yield no improvement over the naive FP4 baseline in the MoE setting, and the cause was unknown.
AI.method: The authors analyse the MoE routing mechanism and measure training-inference alignment with the Pearson correlation between training and inference probabilities and with router selection matching rates; they then propose MoeResQ, a quantization-recovery recipe that applies the same correction symmetrically on both sides.
AI.result: With an asymmetric recipe, including the dense-model approach that corrects only the rollout side, alignment deteriorates sharply on both measures. MoeResQ restores training-inference alignment and substantially closes the accuracy gap to full precision.
AI.conclusion: Symmetric recovery is the key principle for FP4 RL on MoE models.

title: Understanding Backdoor Attacks in Scene Graph Generation via Global Context Pathway
comment: Accepted by the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)
summary: Scene Graph Generation (SGG) produces structured scene representations, yet its training-time backdoor risk remains unexplored. Unlike classification, SGG exposes a pair-level attack surface that enables selective corruption of relations involving a designated object category. However, because SGG largely relies on localized evidence, globally placed triggers may face difficulty in manipulating such predictions. Recent SGG architectures increasingly incorporate global context to improve scene modeling, which may in turn facilitate such attacks. In this paper, we systematically study this backdoor risk and investigate the role of the global context pathway in backdoor behavior. Concretely, we first instantiate this attack with an effective method, and propose a three-axis evaluation protocol to characterize backdoor behavior. Experiments on Visual Genome with representative open-vocabulary and closed-set SGG models demonstrate the effectiveness of the attack. Mechanistic analyses reveal that the explicit global context pathway serves as a major carrier of the backdoor effect across the evaluated SGG models. In particular, replacing the poisoned global context representation with its clean counterpart during inference sharply suppresses the attack, yielding 100% and 97% reductions in attack success for the OvSGTR family and RelationFormer, respectively. Moreover, training-time interventions in the OvSGTR family show that suppressing trigger signals in this pathway either reduces attack success or substantially degrades utility. Together, these findings suggest that explicit global context designs may pose a backdoor risk in SGG architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper studies backdoor attacks on scene graph generation and finds that the explicit global context pathway is a major carrier of the backdoor effect. Replacing the poisoned global context with its clean counterpart at inference sharply suppresses the attack, cutting attack success by 100% for the OvSGTR family and 97% for RelationFormer.
AI.motivation: Scene graph generation exposes a pair-level attack surface that enables selective corruption of relations for a designated object category, and recent architectures add global context that may make triggers more effective, yet this backdoor risk was unexplored.
AI.method: The authors instantiate a backdoor attack with an effective method, propose a three-axis evaluation protocol to characterize backdoor behavior, and run mechanistic analyses and training-time interventions on the global context pathway in OvSGTR-family models.
AI.result: Experiments on Visual Genome with representative open-vocabulary and closed-set SGG models show the attack is effective. Replacing the poisoned global context representation with its clean counterpart at inference reduces attack success by 100% for the OvSGTR family and 97% for RelationFormer. In the OvSGTR family, suppressing trigger signals in this pathway either reduces attack success or substantially degrades utility.
AI.conclusion: Explicit global context designs may pose a backdoor risk in scene graph generation architectures.

title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). 17 pages, 7 figures, 8 tables
summary: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an attacker can steer LLM agents by planting a single fabricated hazard in retrieved content, so the agent's own harm avoidance disqualifies legitimate options, with no injected command for a detector to recognize. A corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker.
AI.motivation: Security work models retrieved-content threats as instruction injection and defends by detecting command syntax, but an attacker can instead exploit the agent's harm-avoidance reasoning, and deployed injection detectors score such payloads as benign.
AI.method: The authors define voluntary servitude, write fabricated hazards as ordinary reviews, and measure generation-stage steering across six models, ten consumer-service domains, and three attack families; they test transfer to production browser agents and to a retrieval pipeline, and evaluate a corroboration requirement in the agent's instructions.
AI.result: These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and behind a deployed injection filter they are 1.7 to 4.4x more effective. End-to-end success in the retrieval pipeline ranges from 1.0% to 57.0% depending on the retriever. With the corroboration requirement, roughly 95% of the exposure is removed against a non-adaptive attacker, and the agent still reads the planted hazard but no longer acts on it.
AI.conclusion: Agents that rely on their own harm avoidance can be weaponized through fabricated hazards, and a corroboration requirement in instructions is an effective, retraining-free mitigation against non-adaptive attackers.

title: $τ$-Rec-Books: A Disclosure-Controlled Benchmark for Requirement Elicitation in Agentic Recommender Systems
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ECIR 2027 (Resource Track)
summary: While conversational recommendation systems provide a more natural user interface, they face the challenge of progressively discovering a user's needs before they can recommend an item that satisfies them. To evaluate the ability of AI agents at this elicitation process, we introduce $\tau$-Rec-Books, a benchmark that holds each user request fixed while varying only when the user reveals their requirements: all at the start (volunteer), one at the start and the rest when asked (mixed), or some never (hidden). A hidden requirement can be found only by proposing books and inferring it from the user's accept or reject verdicts. We generate 450 tasks over a catalog of 20,000 books from Wikidata, develop a rule-based simulated user to answer the agent, and score recommendations against catalog metadata without an LLM judge. Across four agents and two search interfaces, success rates fall for every agent and interface, on average from 0.975 (volunteer) to 0.756 (mixed) and 0.283 (hidden). Mixed tasks fail mainly because agents do not ask, and when told to ask, every agent reaches at least 0.931. On hidden tasks, most failures come from agents recommending a book they never proposed to the user. When told to propose first, agents only match a simple baseline that proposes popular books, and stay well below one that uses rejection to rule out possible requirements. We release the catalog pipeline, task generator, simulated user, validators, reference agents, and all agent traces at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces tau-Rec-Books, a benchmark of 450 tasks for testing whether AI agents elicit user requirements in conversational book recommendation, varying whether requirements are revealed at the start, partly on request, or never. Success falls from 0.975 for volunteered requirements to 0.756 for mixed and 0.283 for hidden ones.
AI.motivation: Conversational recommenders must progressively discover needs before recommending, and no benchmark controls when requirements are revealed to test elicitation directly.
AI.method: Each user request is held fixed while only the timing of requirement disclosure varies (volunteer, mixed, or hidden); tasks are generated over a catalog of 20,000 books from Wikidata, with a rule-based simulated user and scoring against catalog metadata without an LLM judge.
AI.result: Across four agents and two search interfaces, success rates fall for every agent and interface, on average from 0.975 (volunteer) to 0.756 (mixed) and 0.283 (hidden). Mixed-task failures come mainly from agents not asking, and when told to ask every agent reaches at least 0.931. On hidden tasks most failures come from recommending books never proposed to the user; agents only match a popularity baseline when told to propose first and stay well below a rejection-based method.
AI.conclusion: Agents do not elicit requirements well unprompted, and the authors release the pipeline, simulator, validators, reference agents, and traces for further study.

title: SaMA: Morpho Adaptation via Asymmetric Expansion of Kronecker Product
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 61 pages, 29 figures, 25 tables. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT); Large Language Models (LLMs); Large Foundation Models
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has attracted significant attention in the parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) landscape. However, its design suffers from two fundamental limitations. First, its invariance manifold induces flat directions in the loss landscape, creating an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers. Second, its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget. In this paper, we propose Scalable Morpho Adaptation (SaMA), a PEFT method grounded in a principled generalization of the Kronecker product. By relaxing the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization, SaMA spans from low to full rank and achieves a practical rank that scales quadratically with the parameter budget, up to full-rank. Furthermore, we show that its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, making it structurally more optimizer-friendly. Empirically, SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.

AI.tldr: SaMA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that generalizes the Kronecker product through asymmetric expansion, so its effective rank scales quadratically with the parameter budget and can reach full rank. It outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning while using fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: LoRA has flat directions in its loss landscape that create an optimization bottleneck for adaptive optimizers, and its effective rank scales only linearly with the parameter budget.
AI.method: SaMA relaxes the shared-block constraint in the perfect-shuffle factorization of the Kronecker product, which spans from low to full rank, and the authors show its invariance manifold collapses to a diagonal group, which is more optimizer-friendly.
AI.result: SaMA consistently outperforms strong PEFT baselines on commonsense and arithmetic reasoning benchmarks while being more parameter-efficient.
AI.conclusion: A generalized Kronecker-product adaptation removes LoRA's rank bottleneck and is more friendly to adaptive optimizers.

title: From Watching to Steering: Enabling Human-Coding Agent Collaboration through Execution Traces
comment: 16 pages,10 figures
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled coding agents to autonomously perform complex software development tasks, yet their long-running execution remains difficult for users to inspect, understand, and steer. We present Vibetrace, an interactive trace visualization and intervention system for agentic programming built upon OpenCode. Vibetrace introduces a human-agent collaboration paradigm of Observe, Understand, Intervene, and Evolve. It (1) visualizes agent workflows as interactive execution traces for inspecting actions, intermediate states, and failures; (2) enables users to fork execution from prior steps and provide targeted corrections without restarting validated progress; and (3) distills traces and human feedback into reusable skills for continual agent evolution. On SWE-bench Verified, distilled skills reduce input tokens by 23.0% and cost by 15.5%, while improving pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0%. User studies further demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional log-based interaction.

AI.tldr: Vibetrace is an interactive trace visualization and intervention system for coding agents built on OpenCode, supporting inspection, forking from earlier steps, and distilling traces into reusable skills. On SWE-bench Verified, distilled skills cut input tokens by 23.0% and cost by 15.5% while raising pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0%.
AI.motivation: The long-running execution of coding agents is hard for users to inspect, understand, and steer, and conventional log-based interaction is less effective.
AI.method: Vibetrace follows an Observe, Understand, Intervene, and Evolve paradigm: it visualizes agent workflows as interactive execution traces, lets users fork execution from prior steps with targeted corrections, and distills traces and human feedback into reusable skills.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, distilled skills reduce input tokens by 23.0% and cost by 15.5%, and improve pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0%. User studies show improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional log-based interaction.
AI.conclusion: Making agent traces inspectable, forkable, and distillable supports human-agent collaboration and continual agent improvement.

title: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference
comment: 4 pages, 5 tables
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made it exceptionally convenient for users to send their private data to model providers, which process them in plaintext. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) promises to secure remote inference by computing directly on encrypted data, yet it has remained prohibitively slow. The effort to make it practical remains fragmented, with most existing frameworks being closed-source, which keeps progress from compounding. We present Perseus, a free and open Python software library that supports the full stack of encrypted model inference, from the cryptographic backend and data packing, to encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution. Perseus ships with built-in novel optimizations, one at each level of the stack: in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the (i) backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the (ii) data level, and a state-of-the-art bootstrap placer that is both packing- and magnitude-aware at the (iii) model level. Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within $3\%$ of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity. Remarkably, it is $3.96\times$ faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B. We initiate, for the first time, a public speedrun on encrypted GPT-2, so that progress can compound.

AI.tldr: Perseus is an open-source Python library for the full stack of FHE-based encrypted model inference, with novel optimizations at the backend, data-packing, and model levels. It is 3.96x faster than other implementations at single-token decoding on Llama-3-8B and stays within 3% of plaintext accuracy and perplexity.
AI.motivation: Fully homomorphic encryption can secure remote LLM inference, but it has remained prohibitively slow, and most existing frameworks are closed-source, which prevents progress from compounding.
AI.method: Perseus adds in-kernel regeneration of key-switching keys at the backend level, a complex variant of Cachemir packing at the data level, and a packing- and magnitude-aware bootstrap placer at the model level, with encrypted nonlinearities and end-to-end model execution.
AI.result: Perseus achieves state-of-the-art latency across multiple models and modalities, within 3% of the plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity, and is 3.96x faster at single-token decoding than any other implementation on Llama-3-8B.
AI.conclusion: The open library and a public encrypted GPT-2 speedrun are intended to let progress in encrypted inference compound.

title: BtsPruner: Role-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) often process hundreds or thousands of visual tokens, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead during inference. Existing training-free pruning methods typically estimate token importance using language-model attention, visual attention, or feature similarity. However, these methods treat visual tokens with uniform criteria and overlook that tokens may serve different roles during visual encoding. In this work, we investigate the evolution of visual token roles in LVLMs and observe that tokens progressively transition from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives as encoding proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose BtsPruner, a training-free role-aware visual token pruning framework that preserves complementary token roles under a fixed budget. Specifically, BtsPruner first identifies the token-role transition point based on the evolution of attention concentration. It then discovers globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages to recover complementary fine-grained evidence. Extensive experiments across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM demonstrate that BtsPruner achieves superior performance retention under aggressive token reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, BtsPruner preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance using only 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). In the high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B setting, it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.

AI.tldr: BtsPruner is a training-free visual token pruning method for large vision-language models that uses the role transition of visual tokens across encoding stages to keep both global representatives and local detail tokens. On LLaVA-1.5-7B it keeps 91.6% of dense performance with 32 of 576 visual tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free pruning methods score visual tokens with uniform criteria, but tokens change role during visual encoding, from local detail carriers to globally referenced representatives, so a single criterion can discard complementary evidence.
AI.method: BtsPruner finds a token-role transition point from the evolution of attention concentration, selects globally referenced representatives from later encoding stages, and recursively retrieves local detail tokens from earlier stages under a fixed budget.
AI.result: Across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and CogVLM, BtsPruner retains performance under aggressive reduction. On LLaVA-1.5-7B it preserves 91.6% of the dense model's performance with 32 of 576 visual tokens (5.6%). On high-resolution LLaVA-NeXT-7B it achieves up to a 5.95x CUDA-latency speedup.
AI.conclusion: Role-aware pruning that preserves complementary token roles retains strong performance at large token reductions.

title: CANDO: Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization for Residual Reinforcement Learning
summary: Pretrained generative policies provide strong behavior priors for robot control, but adapting them efficiently with online reinforcement learning remains difficult. A central challenge is how to improve a frozen generative policy without destroying the structure learned from offline demonstrations. Noise-space residual methods address this by modifying the policy's input noise, but existing noise-space methods typically regulate adaptation through fixed latent feasible regions, which may exclude valuable noise edits. In contrast, action-space residual methods are more sample-efficient, but their efficiency can still be further improved. We propose Conservative Noise Directional Optimization (CNDO), a noise-space residual RL method that improves a frozen generative policy by learning state- and noise-conditioned directions around Gaussian latent samples. CNDO removes predefined latent feasible regions and instead regulates noise-space adaptation through the soft conservative constraint, which consists of conservative value estimation and gated execution. We further introduce Conservative Action-Noise Directional Optimization (CANDO), which adds an action-space residual, combining structured latent-space improvement with local action correction. Experiments show that, once CNDO narrows the gap between noise-space and action-space residual learning, CANDO further improves over single-space optimization, achieving 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, surpassing the best single-space results by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1% success rate. More demos and info are available on this https URL.

AI.tldr: CNDO improves a frozen generative robot policy with noise-space residual reinforcement learning by learning state- and noise-conditioned directions, and CANDO adds an action-space residual on top. CANDO reaches 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, beating the best single-space method by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1 points of success.
AI.motivation: Adapting a frozen pretrained generative policy with online RL risks destroying the structure learned from offline demonstrations, and existing noise-space methods use fixed latent feasible regions that may exclude valuable noise edits, while action-space residuals are sample-efficient but could be improved.
AI.method: CNDO learns state- and noise-conditioned directions around Gaussian latent samples, removes predefined latent feasible regions, and regulates adaptation through a soft conservative constraint made of conservative value estimation and gated execution; CANDO adds an action-space residual that combines latent-space improvement with local action correction.
AI.result: CANDO reaches 76.1 NAUC and a 91.4% final success rate, surpassing the best single-space results by 6.6 NAUC and 4.1 percentage points of success.
AI.conclusion: Combining structured latent-space improvement with local action correction improves over optimizing either space alone.

title: CosmosAlpha: Multi-Relational Graph Search with Pareto-Guided Exploration for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining
comment: 41 pages, 3 figures
summary: Discovering predictive alpha factors from noisy financial data is a fundamental yet challenging problem in quantitative finance. LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized. Consequently, information remains localized along parent--child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: CosmosAlpha is a graph-based framework for LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining that represents factors as a multi-relational graph and uses Graph Flow propagation and Pareto-guided selection over quality, fertility, and diversity. On CSI 300 and CSI 500 it achieves the best mean rank over seven metrics and beats its MCTS counterpart on every reported metric.
AI.motivation: Tree-based and generation-centric search organize factors by generation lineage, which leaves structural and statistical relations across branches unused and can confine exploration to redundant regions, and factor discovery involves several objectives that a single criterion cannot capture.
AI.method: Discovered factors form a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation; a Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, and Pareto-guided selection jointly weighs quality, fertility, and diversity.
AI.result: Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric.
AI.conclusion: Relational graph search shows a consistent advantage over tree search for LLM-driven factor mining.

title: Spectral Quantum Memory for Implicit Neural Representations
comment: Accepted to Neurips 2026
summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) model signals as continuous functions from coordinates to values, but their performance depends strongly on how spectral capacity is allocated. Yet most Quantum INR (QINR) architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks. We introduce the Spectral Quantum Memory Model (SQMM), a memory coupled quantum INR in which sequential hybrid data reuploading layers (bands) communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register. Each band reads the memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back, so later bands can build on the computation of earlier ones. When memory read and write layers are input independent, we prove that the memory state forms an operator valued Fourier series whose support is contained in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra. Downstream bands then condition their Fourier coefficients on the spectral content stored by earlier bands, and the memory coupling creates no new primitive frequencies. This theory motivates a spectral memory alignment loss that encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed prefix of the model. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.

AI.tldr: SQMM is a quantum implicit neural representation in which sequential data-reuploading bands communicate through a shared coherent quantum memory register, which the authors show creates no new primitive frequencies. Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks it improves over compact quantum and classical INR baselines.
AI.motivation: Most quantum INR architectures treat spectral components as independent outputs of separate quantum blocks, so later bands cannot build on the spectral content computed by earlier ones.
