AI.method: Each band reads a shared quantum memory, computes on its own coordinate upload, and writes part of its state back; when memory read and write layers are input independent, the memory state is proven to be an operator-valued Fourier series whose support lies in the Minkowski sum of the initial memory spectrum and the local band spectra; a spectral memory alignment loss encourages memory to encode the spectrum expressed by the deployed model prefix.
AI.result: Across audio and image reconstruction benchmarks, SQMM improves over compact QINR and INR baselines.
AI.conclusion: Coupling bands through shared quantum memory lets downstream bands condition on earlier spectral content without adding primitive frequencies.

title: Can Network Models of Science Do Without Pluralist Agents?
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Accepted at IWAI 2026 (International Workshop on Active Inference)
summary: Science is a process of useful models being proven wrong time and again, but despite its many flaws, it somehow works. Why is this? Paul Feyerabend argued that it works because people dare to hold and defend incompatible rival theories against the accepted one, since a theory's failures often lead to its abandonment in the presence of a more accurate or simpler alternative. He called this view theoretical pluralism. We introduce a theoretical and experimental model in which this can be examined. It compares communities of pluralist agents, which can hold rival theories side by side and maintain beliefs within and between those theories, with communities of monist agents, which can only incorporate what they hear or observe into a single model of their own. In a multi-agent variational inference setting, our experimental demonstrations illustrate how communities with rival theories can go through periods of uncertainty followed by a shift in the theories they hold true, how the information that is communicated between communities affects beliefs when those communities make different observations about the world, and how sharing support for theories and sharing beliefs within them contribute differently to collective belief dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a multi-agent variational inference model to examine Feyerabend's theoretical pluralism, comparing communities of pluralist agents that hold rival theories with communities of monist agents. Experiments show that pluralist communities go through periods of uncertainty followed by shifts in the theories they hold true.
AI.motivation: Feyerabend argued that science works because scientists hold and defend incompatible rival theories, but this claim had not been examined in a formal network model of science.
AI.method: The authors introduce a theoretical and experimental model in which pluralist agents hold rival theories side by side and keep beliefs within and between them, while monist agents incorporate observations into a single model; they study multi-agent variational inference with communities that observe different parts of the world and share information.
AI.result: Communities with rival theories go through periods of uncertainty followed by shifts in the theories they hold true. Information communicated between communities affects beliefs when they make different observations. Sharing support for theories and sharing beliefs within them contribute differently to collective belief dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The model gives a way to test whether pluralism shapes collective belief dynamics, and the results suggest that sharing theory support and sharing beliefs within theories play different roles.

title: Polyp Matching Using Deep Learning
summary: A key challenge in colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) analysis is accurately identifying whether multiple images depict the same polyp, which is critical to avoid over-counting and unnecessary clinical interventions. Additionally, this prevents prolonged follow-up colonoscopies where endoscopists search for duplicate polyps without precise localization. This study presents a novel contrastive learning-based approach to polyp matching using a Siamese neural network architecture. The model was trained on a dataset from the Danish CareForColon2015 trial. The dataset comprises 5,103 image pairs of confirmed same polyp and 5,103 pairs of different polyps, annotated by experienced clinicians. The proposed model employs ResNet variants (ResNet18, ResNet34, ResNet50), DenseNet121 and EfficientNet B0/B3 as backbones and utilizes contrastive learning with cosine vector distance metric for classification. Experimental results demonstrate high classification accuracies of up to 92% and AUC values close to 0.98. These results suggest that automated polyp matching has the potential to reduce polyp over-counting, improve patient risk stratification, and reduce unnecessary follow-up colonoscopies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Siamese contrastive-learning approach that decides whether two colon capsule endoscopy images show the same polyp, reaching accuracies up to 92% and AUC close to 0.98. The aim is to reduce polyp over-counting and unnecessary follow-up colonoscopies.
AI.motivation: In colon capsule endoscopy, identifying whether multiple images depict the same polyp is critical to avoid over-counting and unnecessary interventions, and manual matching without precise localization prolongs follow-up colonoscopies.
AI.method: A Siamese network with contrastive learning and a cosine distance metric is trained on 5,103 same-polyp pairs and 5,103 different-polyp pairs from the Danish CareForColon2015 trial, using ResNet18, ResNet34, ResNet50, DenseNet121, and EfficientNet B0 and B3 backbones.
AI.result: Classification accuracies of up to 92% and AUC values close to 0.98 are reported.
AI.conclusion: Automated polyp matching may reduce over-counting, improve risk stratification, and reduce unnecessary follow-up colonoscopies.

title: QueryFlow: Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval with Adaptive Query Evolution
summary: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supports Web information seeking and fact verification by recovering complementary evidence across related pages within a limited retrieval budget. Scoring evidence independently against the original question can miss supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts. Iterative retrieval incorporates these facts into subsequent queries, while graph retrieval explicitly models relations among evidence units. Yet fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query condition to accumulated relational context. We view multi-hop evidence recovery as the coupled evolution of evidence representations and query conditions, with accumulated context informing both what the retriever represents and how it searches for complementary evidence. QueryFlow realizes this perspective by recurrently integrating query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation. Across four representative multi-hop question answering (QA) datasets, QueryFlow achieves macro Recall@10 (R@10), Full Recall@10 (FR@10), and LLM-Acc gains of 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 percentage points over representative baselines, respectively.

AI.tldr: QueryFlow is a multi-hop graph retrieval method that recurrently integrates query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, so the query evolves with accumulated evidence. Across four multi-hop QA datasets it gains 4.98, 8.40, and 8.0 points in macro Recall@10, Full Recall@10, and LLM-Acc over representative baselines.
AI.motivation: Scoring evidence independently against the original question misses supporting units whose relevance emerges through intermediate facts, and fixed-query graph retrievers update entity representations without adapting the query to accumulated relational context.
AI.method: QueryFlow recurrently integrates query-conditioned summaries of graph context into a shared query state, which controls boundary inputs and relation features for subsequent propagation, so evidence representations and the query condition evolve together.
AI.result: Across four representative multi-hop QA datasets, QueryFlow achieves gains of 4.98 points in macro Recall@10, 8.40 points in Full Recall@10, and 8.0 points in LLM-Acc over representative baselines.
AI.conclusion: Coupling the evolution of the query with graph evidence improves multi-hop evidence recovery for retrieval-augmented generation.

title: Does LinUCB Need Valid Confidence Sets?
summary: We show that replacing LinUCB's usual confidence width $\beta$ by any fixed $\alpha>0$ preserves sublinear regret when the action set is $M$-smooth and $m$-strongly convex. Our high-probability regret bound for this generalisation, $\alpha$-LinUCB, establishes that valid confidence sets are not necessary for the success of LinUCB. We identify the mechanism behind this result: action-set curvature drives $\alpha$-LinUCB to explore every direction, even when optimism is not guaranteed. To analyse this mechanism, we introduce a logarithmically capped spectral potential that, unlike the standard log-determinant potential, caps contributions from well-explored directions. This yields lower bounds on the smallest eigenvalue of the design matrix. At the standard confidence width $\alpha=\beta\asymp\sqrt{d\log T}$, our $T$-round regret bound in $d$ dimensions is $O\bigl(\frac{M}{m}d\sqrt{T\log T}\bigr)$, up to iterated-logarithmic factors, improving the horizon dependence of the classical LinUCB guarantee by a factor of $\sqrt{\log T}$.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LinUCB keeps sublinear regret when its confidence width is replaced by any fixed alpha > 0, provided the action set is M-smooth and m-strongly convex, so valid confidence sets are not necessary. The resulting T-round bound is O((M/m) d sqrt(T log T)) up to iterated-logarithmic factors, improving the classical horizon dependence by a factor of sqrt(log T).
AI.motivation: Classical LinUCB analyses rely on valid confidence sets, and the authors ask whether these are necessary for its success.
AI.method: The authors analyse alpha-LinUCB, which uses a fixed alpha in place of the usual width beta, and introduce a logarithmically capped spectral potential that, unlike the log-determinant potential, caps contributions from well-explored directions, giving lower bounds on the smallest eigenvalue of the design matrix.
AI.result: The high-probability regret bound for alpha-LinUCB holds for any fixed alpha > 0 under the smoothness and strong-convexity assumptions. At the standard width alpha = beta of order sqrt(d log T), the T-round regret is O((M/m) d sqrt(T log T)) up to iterated-logarithmic factors, improving the horizon dependence of classical LinUCB by sqrt(log T).
AI.conclusion: Action-set curvature drives exploration in every direction, so valid optimism is not required for LinUCB's sublinear regret.

title: Therapy-FIS: A Dataset for Assessing Facilitative Interpersonal Skills in Psychotherapeutic Setting
summary: Facilitative Interpersonal Skills (FIS) is a performance-based assessment method that provides a structured framework for evaluating the interpersonal competencies of mental health professionals. However, existing FIS assessment relies heavily on human observer ratings, making the evaluation process labor-intensive, costly, and difficult to scale. Progress toward automated FIS assessment has also been constrained by the lack of publicly available professional data in psychotherapy settings. To address this limitation, we introduce Therapy-FIS, a dataset for automated FIS assessment in standardized psychotherapy tasks. To our knowledge, Therapy-FIS is the first publicly available dataset in this domain. It contains facial, acoustic, and textual signals derived from standardized therapist responses to standardized mock patient stimulus clips, based on 890 therapist video recordings and 8 patient videos, and is rated with eight FIS subscale ratings and an overall FIS score. Built on Therapy-FIS, we further establish a benchmark with two downstream tasks: Therapist Performance Rating and Joint Therapist--mock-Patient Performance Rating. We also introduce a competitive baseline, DyadicFIS, with gated fusion and routed readout under therapist-only and dyadic settings. DyadicFIS obtains the best macro CCC(Concordance Correlation Coefficient) scores on both tasks (0.2807 and 0.3299). Therapy-FIS offers a reproducible resource for data-driven automated assessment of therapeutic interpersonal skills in mental health.

AI.tldr: Therapy-FIS is a publicly available dataset for automated assessment of facilitative interpersonal skills (FIS) in standardized psychotherapy tasks, with facial, acoustic, and textual signals from 890 therapist recordings. The paper adds a benchmark and a baseline, DyadicFIS, which reaches macro CCC of 0.2807 and 0.3299 on the two tasks.
AI.motivation: FIS assessment relies on human observer ratings that are labor-intensive and costly to scale, and automated work has been limited by the lack of public professional psychotherapy data.
AI.method: The dataset contains facial, acoustic, and textual signals from standardized therapist responses to standardized mock patient stimulus clips, based on 890 therapist videos and 8 patient videos, rated with eight FIS subscale ratings and an overall score; two downstream tasks are defined, Therapist Performance Rating and Joint Therapist-mock-Patient Performance Rating; the DyadicFIS baseline uses gated fusion and routed readout under therapist-only and dyadic settings.
AI.result: DyadicFIS obtains the best macro CCC scores on both tasks, 0.2807 and 0.3299.
AI.conclusion: Therapy-FIS offers a reproducible resource for data-driven automated assessment of interpersonal skills in mental health.

title: Best-of-Depth: Learning Exploratory Dynamics in Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers extend inference-time computation through repeated latent-state updates, but final-depth training does not directly encourage useful intermediate alternatives. We introduce Best-of-Depth (BoD), which trains a recurrent trajectory as a candidate set by minimizing prediction loss across depths. Different valid targets can be matched at different depths without architectural changes or depth-specific labels. An exact-match analysis connects this objective to solution coverage. On N-Queens completion and graph coloring, BoD improves coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives. N-Queens coverage reaches 91.03%, versus 45.75% for final-depth training. Further experiments show discovery beyond the training depth and recovery of solutions withheld from teacher pools on familiar inputs. Fine-tuning a pretrained looped language model with BoD yields higher pooled code-generation success than final-depth training when programs are generated separately at evaluated fixed depths. These results support training recurrent computation for solution discovery along its trajectory.

AI.tldr: Best-of-Depth trains a looped Transformer's recurrent trajectory as a set of candidate solutions by minimizing prediction loss across depths, which improves solution coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives. On N-Queens completion coverage rises to 91.03%, versus 45.75% for final-depth training.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers extend inference-time computation through repeated latent updates, but final-depth training does not encourage useful intermediate alternatives.
AI.method: Best-of-Depth (BoD) matches valid targets to different depths of the recurrent trajectory by minimizing prediction loss across depths, without architectural changes or depth-specific labels, and an exact-match analysis links the objective to solution coverage.
AI.result: On N-Queens completion and graph coloring, BoD improves coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives; N-Queens coverage reaches 91.03% versus 45.75% for final-depth training. The method also finds solutions beyond the training depth and recovers solutions withheld from teacher pools. Fine-tuning a pretrained looped language model with BoD yields higher pooled code-generation success than final-depth training when programs are generated at evaluated fixed depths.
AI.conclusion: Training recurrent computation along its trajectory supports solution discovery.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Prototype Learning for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Open-set test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adapt source-trained models to unlabeled test streams where covariate-shifted in-distribution (csID) samples and covariate-shifted out-of-distribution (csOOD) samples may coexist. Existing TTA methods are typically designed under a closed-set assumption and therefore lack explicit mechanisms for reliably distinguishing csID from csOOD samples. Consequently, csOOD samples may be mistakenly included in confidence-enhancing adaptation, producing harmful gradients that degrade known-class performance. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Aware Prototype Learning for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (UAPA), a plug-and-play method for reliable open-set adaptation. Specifically, we first introduce Uncertainty-Driven ID/OOD Separation, which combines a classifier-prototype score with a mini-batch-normalized evidence-derived uncertainty score to distinguish csID from csOOD samples. We then propose a Dynamic Prototype Refinement strategy that periodically refines class-specific target prototypes using buffered csID features to progressively follow the estimated class directions. Lastly, we introduce Contrastive Prototype Entropy Adaptation, which applies entropy minimization to csID samples and entropy maximization to csOOD samples, while prototype-level contrastive learning aligns csID features with their corresponding target prototypes and reduces the maximum similarity between csOOD features and known-class prototypes. Empirically, UAPA outperforms the strongest baselines on the CIFAR benchmarks and Tiny-ImageNet-C, improving average OSCR by 2.08 and 1.28 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: UAPA is a plug-and-play open-set test-time adaptation method that separates covariate-shifted in-distribution from out-of-distribution samples using an uncertainty-aware score, then adapts with dynamic prototypes and contrastive prototype entropy. It improves average OSCR by 2.08 points on CIFAR benchmarks and 1.28 points on Tiny-ImageNet-C.
AI.motivation: Closed-set test-time adaptation methods lack a mechanism to tell covariate-shifted in-distribution samples from out-of-distribution ones, so OOD samples can enter confidence-enhancing adaptation and produce harmful gradients that degrade known-class performance.
AI.method: Uncertainty-Driven ID/OOD Separation combines a classifier-prototype score with a mini-batch-normalized evidence-derived uncertainty score; Dynamic Prototype Refinement periodically updates class-specific target prototypes from buffered in-distribution features; Contrastive Prototype Entropy Adaptation minimizes entropy on in-distribution samples, maximizes it on OOD samples, and uses prototype-level contrastive learning.
AI.result: UAPA outperforms the strongest baselines on the CIFAR benchmarks and Tiny-ImageNet-C, improving average OSCR by 2.08 and 1.28 percentage points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware separation of in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples makes open-set test-time adaptation more reliable.

title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
comment: 8 figures, 11 tables
summary: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that labelling hallucinations by thresholding similarity scores such as BLEURT is unreliable, because detector rankings change with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation finds that the judges differ widely in labelling error, with BLEURT-based judges misclassifying about 47%.
AI.motivation: Hallucination detectors are often evaluated on labels built by comparing generations to reference answers with similarity metrics such as BLEURT. That treats similarity as a proxy for factuality, although BLEURT is English-centric, has an unbounded score range, and was designed as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure.
AI.method: The authors compare 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets and five languages. They measure how detector performance changes with the judge and validate labelling reliability against human annotations.
AI.result: Detector performance varies substantially with the supervision judge. QGen-9B has the lowest overall misclassification rate at 12.86%, while BLEURT and BLEURT-n have rates of 47.23% and 47.32%.
AI.conclusion: Automatic similarity-based labelling is a limited basis for evaluating hallucination detectors, and the field needs judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

title: CLARA: A Cognitively-Driven Clarification Framework for Grounding Ambiguous Requests
comment: Work conducted in early 2025
summary: Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks. Yet, broad directives like "clean the room" or "organize the desk" frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome. Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details. In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans' clarification seeking behavior. Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user's preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene. This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system's understanding from the user. Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.

AI.tldr: CLARA is a clarification framework that lets a large vision-language model ask targeted questions about an ambiguous household or office instruction, refines the answer into a structured arrangement, and renders the result with a diffusion model as a visual check for the user.
AI.motivation: Broad instructions such as "clean the room" omit user preferences and object arrangements. Large vision-language models tend to overestimate how well they understand such instructions and rarely ask for the missing details.
AI.method: CLARA is a cognitively motivated conversational clarification framework. It asks targeted questions to turn an ambiguous request into a detailed description of the desired object arrangement, and a diffusion-based image generation pipeline then renders that scene.
AI.result: The abstract reports that CLARA gives more accurate and consistent outcomes than another state-of-the-art large vision-language model system, supported by experiments and user studies. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Interactive clarification, with a rendered scene as confirmation, helps bridge the gap between vague directives and fully specified task requirements.

title: DenseTwins: Dense Modality Decoupling for Multimodal Self-Supervision
summary: Multimodal perception is central to many computer vision applications, including robotics and autonomous driving, where different sensing modalities provide complementary cues. Self-supervised learning offers a scalable solution for exploiting large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. However, existing methods either neglect modality-specific information by enforcing feature-space alignment between modalities or learn only global representations without preserving spatial structure. We propose DenseTwins, a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by explicitly decoupling the dense feature space into shared and modality-specific components. The proposed approach combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives, enabling the model to capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues within a structured dense embedding space. DenseTwins jointly optimizes an intra-modal objective across augmented views and a cross-modal objective that aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific information. We evaluate DenseTwins across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multimodal self-supervised baselines. Code available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: DenseTwins is a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by splitting the feature space into shared and modality-specific parts. It reports state-of-the-art or competitive results on several multimodal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal self-supervised methods either force feature alignment across modalities, which discards modality-specific information, or learn only global representations that lose spatial structure.
AI.method: DenseTwins combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives. An intra-modal objective uses augmented views, and a cross-modal objective aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific features.
AI.result: The abstract reports state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, compared with multimodal self-supervised baselines. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly decoupling shared and modality-specific dense features is presented as a useful design for multimodal self-supervised learning in structured dense embedding spaces.

title: Cycle WAM: Coupling Action and Video through Cycle Consistency
summary: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.

AI.tldr: Cycle WAM couples video and action in world action models by adding bidirectional conversion and a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective. The authors report state-of-the-art results among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and a substantial improvement over DreamZero on DROID.
AI.motivation: Existing world action models use pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated video, but their training does not ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences agree.
AI.method: Cycle WAM treats video and action as paired modalities linked by a causal relation. It combines video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to learn forward and inverse dynamics, then adds a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective that couples the two mappings.
AI.result: The model achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM show sharper visual detail in forward-dynamics predictions and characterise its inverse-dynamics performance. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing cycle consistency between action and video is presented as a way to make better use of pretrained video priors in world action models, supporting both forward and inverse dynamics.

title: TAPES: Task-Aligned Joint Predictive Pretraining for Transaction Event Sequences
summary: Transaction event sequences support diverse prediction tasks in online commerce and digital financial services. The same transaction records can yield prediction targets with different semantics, including values, changes, and relations to past events. These targets impose different constraints on history representations, but their predictability alone does not establish the downstream utility of a target set. Moreover, target-wise prediction losses do not explicitly model conditional co-occurrence among targets. To address these challenges, we propose TAPES, a task-aligned joint predictive pretraining framework for transaction sequences. TAPES constructs a finite collection of candidate target sets from admissible field-operator combinations. It selects a target set according to the downstream utility of representations learned through short joint pretraining trials under matched budgets. It then reinitializes the encoder and pretrains it on the selected targets through a joint likelihood parameterized by a shared discrete latent variable, before downstream supervised adaptation. Experiments in a real-world transaction-risk setting and on multiple public financial benchmarks spanning diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that TAPES outperforms representative baselines. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of predictive target selection and joint modeling.

AI.tldr: TAPES is a pretraining framework for transaction event sequences that selects a set of predictive targets according to the downstream utility of short pretraining trials, then pretrains with a joint likelihood over those targets. It outperforms representative baselines on a real-world transaction-risk task and on several public financial benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Transaction targets can differ in semantics, such as values, changes and relations to past events, and predictability alone does not show that a target set is useful downstream. Target-wise losses also do not model conditional co-occurrence among targets.
AI.method: TAPES builds a finite set of candidate target sets from admissible field-operator combinations. It chooses a target set by running short joint pretraining trials under matched budgets, reinitialises the encoder, and pretrains it with a joint likelihood parameterised by a shared discrete latent variable before supervised adaptation.
AI.result: TAPES outperforms representative baselines in a real-world transaction-risk setting and on multiple public financial benchmarks spanning diverse downstream tasks. Ablations confirm the contributions of predictive target selection and joint modelling. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Task-aligned selection of pretraining targets, combined with joint modelling, is a useful approach for representation learning on transaction sequences.

title: Replica-Aware Split Inference for Edge IoT Systems
summary: Split Inference (SI) addresses the hardware resource limitations of Internet of Things (IoT) devices by distributing tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) model segments across multiple IoT devices. However, a device failure can interrupt the inference pipeline. This paper proposes a replica-aware recovery approach that deploys replicas of TinyML model segments originally hosted on failed devices onto surviving devices. We formulate the joint selection of replica hosts and communication protocols as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that minimizes post-reconfiguration inference latency, accounting for computation and transmission latencies, under flash memory and runtime memory constraints. Simulations using MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks compare the proposed approach with four baselines. We implement the model in a network of 15 IoT devices with a maximum link-rate reduction of 75%, and show that MILP approach achieves an average modeled end-to-end inference latency that is 6.8% lower than that of Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than that of Random. Index Terms TinyML, split inference, Internet of Things, fault tolerance, replica placement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a replica-aware recovery method for split inference on IoT devices. It places replicas of TinyML model segments on surviving devices, chosen by a MILP that minimises post-reconfiguration latency, and reports 6.8% lower latency than Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than Random.
AI.motivation: In split inference, a single device failure can interrupt the inference pipeline. Recovery must respect the flash and runtime memory limits of constrained IoT devices.
AI.method: The joint selection of replica hosts and communication protocols is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program. The objective is post-reconfiguration inference latency, including computation and transmission, under flash and runtime memory constraints. Simulations use MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks against four baselines, and the model is implemented on a network of 15 IoT devices with link-rate reductions of up to 75%.
AI.result: The MILP approach achieves an average modelled end-to-end inference latency 6.8% lower than Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than Random.
AI.conclusion: Joint replica placement and protocol selection with a latency-aware optimisation can keep split inference running after device failures on heterogeneous IoT networks.

title: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.

AI.tldr: ReSI-Math identifies recoverable capability frontiers, problems that a model fails to solve by direct decoding but can solve after trajectory-level search, and uses them as data-efficient RLVR supervision. On Qwen3-VL-8B it improves the MATH500 and WE-MATH average from 78.71 to 80.16.
AI.motivation: When a model fails a problem, it is unclear whether it lacks the capability or only fails to elicit it. Standard RLVR does not separate these cases.
AI.method: Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search finds recoverable failures under a fixed policy. Correct and incorrect trajectories are crossed over to produce new correct solutions, and frontier problems are selected adaptively for sequential one-shot RLVR as the policy evolves.
AI.result: On Qwen3-VL-8B, crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average rises from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches 53.31, against 54.16 for frontier-guided selection.
AI.conclusion: Failures that are recoverable by search are a useful source of training signal, and targeting them is more data-efficient than random problem selection.

title: Density-Aware Reward Scaling: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Reward-Proportional Sampling
summary: Reinforcement learning objectives that maximize expected return can concentrate probability mass on a small subset of high-reward outcomes, limiting diversity when multiple distinct solutions are desirable. We introduce Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a simple reward-processing mechanism that promotes reward-proportional sampling in continuous outcome spaces while retaining standard policy-gradient training. DARS estimates the local density of outcomes within each on-policy rollout group and inversely scales rewards by this density. The method requires no learned density model, auxiliary objective, critic, or modification to the underlying policy-gradient objective. In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO avoids the single-mode collapse exhibited by GRPO and closely recovers the target mode allocation. Applied to text-to-image prompt adaptation, DARS-GRPO consistently improves image and prompt diversity across datasets, Policy LMs, and reward settings while maintaining good semantic alignment. These results show that density-aware reward scaling provides a lightweight way to improve coverage of diverse high-reward outcomes within existing reinforcement-learning pipelines.

AI.tldr: DARS is a reward-processing method that scales each reward by the local density of outcomes in an on-policy rollout group, so that policy-gradient training samples in proportion to reward and keeps diverse high-reward outcomes. It avoids single-mode collapse in a navigation task and improves diversity in text-to-image prompt adaptation.
AI.motivation: Expected-return maximisation can concentrate probability on a few high-reward outcomes, which limits diversity when several distinct solutions are wanted.
AI.method: DARS estimates the local density of outcomes within each rollout group and scales rewards inversely by that density. It needs no learned density model, auxiliary objective or critic, and it leaves the policy-gradient objective unchanged. The method is applied as DARS-GRPO.
AI.result: In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO avoids the single-mode collapse shown by GRPO and closely recovers the target mode allocation. In text-to-image prompt adaptation, it consistently improves image and prompt diversity across datasets, policy language models and reward settings while keeping good semantic alignment.
AI.conclusion: Density-aware reward scaling is a lightweight way to improve coverage of diverse high-reward outcomes within existing reinforcement learning pipelines.

title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $c\mu$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $\mu$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

AI.tldr: The paper models LLM inference scheduling under KV-cache memory limits as a queueing problem and shows that a cμ priority rule, with an effective service rate set by compute, memory bandwidth and memory capacity, is optimal in a fluid model. It also reports lower average latency and high throughput on a real serving engine with H800 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing queueing models assume fixed service times. In LLM inference, the duration of a step depends on prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, and requests compete for limited KV-cache memory, so service capacity depends jointly on computation, memory access and memory occupancy.
AI.method: The authors develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates. This gives a cμ priority rule, and they prove that it minimises cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for finite workloads, minimises completion time and maximises full-run output-token throughput. They then construct a feasible policy for the finite system whose scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy.
AI.result: Experiments on a real LLM serving engine with an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: A memory-aware cμ priority rule gives a principled and practical scheduling policy for LLM inference under KV-cache constraints.

title: UniFlow: Unified Multi-Scale Flow Matching for Time Series Generation
summary: Real-world time series exhibit complex dynamics across multiple temporal resolutions, yet effectively incorporating multi-scale information into generative modeling remains challenging without increasing generative complexity. We propose UniFlow, a unified framework that integrates multi-scale representation learning with efficient non-autoregressive generation through a shared-semantic discrete interface. Specifically, a multi-scale tokenizer employs shared-index voting to consolidate complementary temporal information into a single public-ID sequence, while scale-specific codebooks preserve the information required for reconstruction. Building on this unified representation, we develop geometry-aware categorical flow matching, which initializes transport from learned low-rank anchors and generates public identities non-autoregressively. This design captures multi-scale temporal structure without requiring multiple generative token streams or sequential token decoding. Experiments across four benchmarks and both short- and long-term settings demonstrate improved generative fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency, and substantial inference speedups over representative autoregressive and diffusion-based baselines. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: UniFlow is a time series generator that combines multi-scale tokenisation with non-autoregressive categorical flow matching over a shared discrete index sequence. It reports better generative fidelity and cross-scale consistency than autoregressive and diffusion baselines, with substantial inference speedups.
AI.motivation: Real time series have dynamics at several temporal resolutions, but adding multi-scale information to generative models usually increases generative complexity, for example through multiple token streams or sequential token decoding.
AI.method: A multi-scale tokeniser uses shared-index voting to merge temporal information into one public-ID sequence, while scale-specific codebooks keep the information needed for reconstruction. On this representation, geometry-aware categorical flow matching starts transport from learned low-rank anchors and generates the public IDs non-autoregressively.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and both short- and long-term settings, UniFlow shows improved generative fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency and substantial inference speedups over representative autoregressive and diffusion-based baselines. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: A shared discrete interface with non-autoregressive flow matching captures multi-scale structure in time series without multiple generative streams.

title: Found by Search, Broken by a Shortcut: Transfer and Tampering of Searched Intrinsic Rewards
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Can a search over innate drives find intrinsic rewards that help a reinforcement-learning agent learn, transfer to a task it never saw, and resist an exploit that was absent during the search? Each candidate reward combines four generic events (a new view, a pickup, a drop and a toggle), each with a weight, a relief and a refill rate. We ran three pre-registered stages; the search protocol was locked in a public, timestamped commit before any search result existed. CMA-ES and an equal-budget random search used 1,560 PPO training runs, and the final evaluation and tamper test used 340. On the held-out task, KeyCorridorS3R2, the CMA-ES-selected reward (E) beat task-only PPO, episodic novelty and the random-search-selected reward (R) in all 3 registered comparisons, all of them meaningful by the registered size rule. Among these generic rewards E transferred best; the earlier paper's satiation reward, which on this task is given hand-wired key and locked-door events, did better (20 of 20 seeds solved against 4 of 20; descriptive). On UnlockPickup, where that reward uses generic events, E's mean area exceeded it by 0.276 (descriptive). On the training tasks there was no registered difference between E and R: both E-over-R tests missed. A free reset action, absent during the search, collapsed E's learning on DoorKey-8x8 (mean area 0.829 without it, 0.136 with it; registered) to below task-only PPO (descriptive). The searched drives helped on every task tested, but a reward given task-specific events did better on the held-out task, and selection gave E no protection against an exploit absent from the search.

AI.tldr: A pre-registered search over intrinsic reward candidates, built from four generic events with weights, relief and refill rates, finds a reward that helps an RL agent on a held-out task. The same reward is vulnerable to a free reset action that was absent during the search, which reduces its learning to below task-only PPO on DoorKey-8x8.
AI.motivation: The authors ask whether an innate-drive search can find intrinsic rewards that transfer to unseen tasks and resist exploits that the search did not contain.
AI.method: Three pre-registered stages were run, with the search protocol locked in a public, timestamped commit before any results existed. CMA-ES and an equal-budget random search used 1,560 PPO training runs, and the final evaluation and tamper test used 340 runs.
AI.result: On the held-out task KeyCorridorS3R2, the CMA-ES-selected reward beat task-only PPO, episodic novelty and the random-search reward in all three registered comparisons. A satiation reward from an earlier paper, which uses hand-wired task-specific events, did better (20 of 20 seeds solved against 4 of 20; descriptive). On UnlockPickup the CMA-ES reward's mean area exceeded the satiation reward by 0.276. With a free reset action, mean area on DoorKey-8x8 fell from 0.829 to 0.136, below task-only PPO.
AI.conclusion: Searched intrinsic rewards help on every task tested, but a reward with task-specific events does better on the held-out task, and the search gave no protection against an exploit absent from it.

title: One Assistant, Many Memories: Benchmarking Real-World Group Assistance When Recall Is Not Enough
comment: Project address: this https URL. Code address: this https URL
summary: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. Across evaluations of frontier models with full context, retrieval methods, and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, especially for distributed and conflicting memories. Together, two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints bring consistent gains, showing that group memory systems must improve use, not recall alone.

AI.tldr: GroupAssistBench is a memory benchmark built from 80,299 messages in 50 real group chats with a deployed assistant. It shows that the strongest memory system nearly matches full context on recall but falls far behind on using memory to assist, especially with distributed and conflicting memories.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and on recall against fixed answers. Group assistance needs integration across members, tracking of revisions and conflicts, and a single response for the group, which these benchmarks do not test.
AI.method: The benchmark evaluates memory recall (L1) against reference answers and memory use (L2) on service requests with no fixed answers, across single, distributed and conflicting memories (M1 to M3). Requests are verified to need group history, memories are anchored to sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback.
AI.result: Across frontier models with full context, retrieval methods and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, particularly for distributed and conflicting memories. Two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints give consistent gains. The benchmark cost over $53K to build.
AI.conclusion: Group memory systems must improve how they use memories, not only how they recall them.

title: Fault-tolerant shallow recurrent decoders for sparse sensing with missing sensor measurements
summary: Real-world sensing systems are inherently imperfect: sensors may fail, intermittently disconnect, operate with asynchronous sampling rates, and be subject to noise, leading to measurement streams that are irregular, incomplete, and heterogeneous. Nevertheless, sensing strategies for real-time state reconstruction typically assume synchronous and continuously active sensors, a constraint that substantially limits their applicability in operational environments. In this work, we introduce fault-tolerant sparse sensing strategies in the context of shallow recurrent decoders (SHRED) to enable high-dimensional state estimation from sparse, asynchronous, and missing sensor measurements. Specifically, we consider naive imputation strategies, fault-tolerant recurrent temporal encoders, and we introduce four different transformer-based masking mechanisms to make SHRED explicitly aware of sensor availability through the binary data-availability mask. Moreover, we further introduce a multi-step decoding training objective for SHRED, resulting in smoother latent trajectories and more robust predictions. Throughout a synthetic benchmark and three real-world problems in hydrodynamic and ocean modeling, we show that (i) transformer-based masking mechanisms outperform standard imputation techniques and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures, (ii) the multi-step decoding training objective enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness in the presence of heterogeneous missing-data patterns, while (iii) the computational efficiency of SHRED is preserved, with no additional inference-time overhead.

AI.tldr: The paper extends shallow recurrent decoders (SHRED) to sparse, asynchronous and missing sensor data. Transformer-based masking that makes the model aware of sensor availability outperforms imputation and fault-tolerant recurrent baselines, and a multi-step decoding objective improves robustness at no extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Sensing methods for state reconstruction usually assume synchronous, always-active sensors, which limits their use in operational settings where sensors fail, disconnect or sample at different rates.
AI.method: The authors test naive imputation, fault-tolerant recurrent temporal encoders and four transformer-based masking mechanisms that use the binary data-availability mask. They also add a multi-step decoding training objective to SHRED.
AI.result: Across a synthetic benchmark and three real-world hydrodynamic and ocean-modelling problems, transformer-based masking outperforms standard imputation and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures. The multi-step objective improves reconstruction fidelity and robustness to heterogeneous missing-data patterns, and computational efficiency is preserved with no added inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Making SHRED explicitly aware of sensor availability, together with multi-step decoding, enables reliable high-dimensional state estimation from imperfect sensor streams.

title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
comment: 41 pages, 22 figures
summary: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

AI.tldr: VisSearch-Bench is a benchmark of 204 human-written tasks for long-horizon visual search by multimodal agents, which require linking visual evidence across images and search steps. The best of 16 models fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools.
AI.motivation: Many existing search tasks use images only to identify an initial entity and then rely on text retrieval, which gives little insight into how agents organise and reuse visual information during search.
AI.method: The benchmark spans 7 main domains and 25 subdomains, with five task types: Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task has a reference answer, traceable evidence and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete success, and Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of intermediate results and subquestion answers.
AI.result: Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves 26.47% of tasks even with search tools.
AI.conclusion: Linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers remains a major challenge for multimodal agents.

title: Shuffled OPSD: When Semantic Consistency Hurts On-Policy Self-Distillation?
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables
summary: Knowledge distillation improves a student model's reasoning ability through supervision from a teacher. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as both teacher and student under different contexts: the student generates reasoning trajectories from the question alone, while the teacher additionally receives a complete worked example and provides token-level supervision along those trajectories. Because the problem statement is shared, its content and ordering shape both student generation and teacher feedback. Preserving its semantic structure therefore seems natural, but does it always improve learning? We introduce Shuffled OPSD, which shuffles the words of the shared problem statement while keeping the teacher-only worked example intact. Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 model scales, the method improves mean accuracy over both an intact-target control and Standard OPSD under matched training configurations. The largest gain over Standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B. Further controls show that preserving larger word blocks offers no advantage over word-level shuffling at the evaluated scales, whereas shuffling the teacher-only worked example reduces accuracy at every scale. Cross-problem mixing and target-removal experiments further distinguish the roles of problem content, word order, and teacher context. These results show that disrupting the shared problem statement can improve learning, while disrupting the teacher-only reference hurts performance. They challenge semantic coherence as a universally beneficial principle for OPSD and motivate closer study of how input structure shapes student generation and teacher supervision.

AI.tldr: Shuffled OPSD shuffles the words of the shared problem statement in on-policy self-distillation while keeping the teacher's worked example intact, and this improves mathematical reasoning accuracy across three Qwen3 scales. The largest gain over standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B.
AI.motivation: In on-policy self-distillation, the same model acts as student, which sees only the question, and as teacher, which also sees a worked example. Keeping the semantic structure of the shared problem seems natural, but the authors question whether it always helps learning.
AI.method: The shared problem statement's words are shuffled, while the teacher-only worked example is kept intact. Controls include an intact-target baseline, word-block shuffling with larger blocks, shuffling of the worked example, cross-problem mixing and target removal.
AI.result: Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 scales, the method improves mean accuracy over both an intact-target control and standard OPSD under matched training. Preserving larger word blocks offers no advantage over word-level shuffling at the scales tested. Shuffling the worked example reduces accuracy at every scale.
AI.conclusion: Disrupting the shared problem statement can improve learning, while disrupting the teacher-only reference hurts, so semantic coherence is not universally beneficial for OPSD.

title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
comment: Submitted to journal for publication, will be updated upon publication; figures are greyscale-compatible; raw data, fully reproducible code, and Quarto source in linked repository
summary: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

AI.tldr: A comparison of 73 human annotators and more than 40 LLM configurations on number-disambiguating 174 uses of "they" from Reddit finds that the best LLM, Kimi K3, reaches 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote of 86.2%. Qualitative analysis shows that human reasoning in low-agreement cases helps refine the annotation typology.
AI.motivation: Researchers need to know whether LLMs can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation, where cases such as innovative and context-sensitive uses of "they" are hard to classify.
AI.method: In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators, both students and crowdworkers with or without linguistics backgrounds, and more than 40 LLM configurations labelled 174 authentic uses of "they" from Reddit. Accuracy was compared against the human majority vote and the top half of human annotators, and cost and time were recorded. Error analysis was qualitative.
AI.result: The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%). Only the single best human annotator scored higher, at 95.7%. LLMs also offer substantial advantages in cost and speed.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but responsible use requires human oversight, because human reasoning in ambiguous cases exposes weaknesses in the annotation scheme.

title: LLMs as MDP Designers: A Dependency-Aware Agentic Framework for Automated Robot Policy Generation
comment: Accepted to the 40th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: We investigate the automated generation of executable robot reinforcement learning (RL) policies from natural-language task descriptions. Rather than using large language models (LLMs) as execution-time decision makers, we use them as designers that construct RL pipelines before deployment, including Markov decision process (MDP) formulation and simulator implementation. We identify a phase-wise structure in this problem: MDP formulation is dependency-structured and sequential, whereas simulator implementation becomes modular once the formulation is fixed. Based on this structure, we propose ARPG, a dependency-aware agentic framework that performs sequential MDP modeling, localized verification and correction, and simulator-structured implementation while externalizing intermediate artifacts. ARPG targets a key failure mode of automated policy generation: executable code may still yield non-learnable policies when state, action, reward, and termination artifacts are not semantically aligned. Experiments in Isaac Sim show that ARPG improves modeling correctness, environment executability, and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Additional demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL, and engineering-domain MDPs further suggest that the same modeling pipeline can be reused beyond the main benchmark suite.

AI.tldr: ARPG is an agentic framework in which an LLM designs an RL pipeline before deployment, formulating the MDP sequentially and then implementing the simulator in a modular way. It improves modelling correctness, environment executability and policy-generation success over monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems in Isaac Sim.
AI.motivation: Executable code can still yield non-learnable policies when the state, action, reward and termination artefacts are not semantically aligned. Monolithic LLM generation does not address this failure mode.
AI.method: ARPG uses dependency-aware sequential MDP modelling, localised verification and correction, and simulator implementation structured by the formulation, while externalising intermediate artefacts. The LLM is used as a designer of the pipeline rather than as a run-time decision maker.
AI.result: In Isaac Sim, ARPG improves modelling correctness, environment executability and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL and engineering-domain MDPs suggest the modelling pipeline can be reused. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Structuring LLM-driven policy generation around the dependency structure of MDP formulation and simulator implementation makes automated robot RL more reliable.

title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response
summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GeoFaham is a multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics, with specialist agents for vector, map, imagery and raster tasks coordinated by an orchestrator that uses a Response Store for large outputs. On the 40-task GeoFaham-Bench it scores 0.940 against 0.879 for the next-best coding agent, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Disaster-response questions combine spatial databases, map features, satellite imagery and raster products. LLM and coding-agent approaches struggle with large artefacts, choosing the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata and applying invalid geometric operations.
AI.method: The Orchestrator uses a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation and replanning. A Response Store keeps full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context, and agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. GeoFaham-Bench has 40 tasks grounded in 17 real disaster records.
AI.result: GeoFaham scores 0.940 against 0.879 for the next-best system, Codex, Claude Code or OpenCode, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. The abstract does not name which baseline scored 0.879.
AI.conclusion: Specialist agents with artefact-centric state management can outperform general-purpose coding agents on multi-source geospatial workflows.

title: Learned Smartphone ISP on Mobile GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
summary: With the increasing importance of mobile camera quality in modern smartphones, growing attention has been directed toward computational photography and advanced image signal processing (ISP) algorithms aimed at enhancing various perceptual attributes of captured images. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can reconstruct RGB photos from RAW Bayer camera data while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale Fujifilm UltraISP dataset consisting of RAW-RGB image pairs captured with the Sony IMX586 Quad Bayer mobile sensor and a professional 102MP medium format FujiFilm GFX100 camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to reconstruct high-quality 5MP RGB image from raw data on both platforms under 100 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

AI.tldr: This Mobile AI 2026 challenge report describes top solutions for learned smartphone ISP, which reconstruct RGB photos from RAW Bayer data using the Fujifilm UltraISP dataset. The best models produce 5MP images under 100 milliseconds on Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Mobile cameras need efficient deep learning ISP models that are accurate and can run on constrained smartphone GPUs.
AI.method: Participants designed fast RAW-to-RGB reconstruction models, trained on RAW-RGB pairs from a Sony IMX586 Quad Bayer sensor and a 102MP Fujifilm GFX100. Runtime is evaluated on Adreno and Mali GPUs.
AI.result: Top solutions reconstruct high-quality 5MP RGB images from RAW data on both platforms in under 100 milliseconds.
AI.conclusion: The challenge shows that high-quality learned ISP is feasible in real time on current mobile GPUs, and the report documents the models developed.

title: Rethinking GA2Ms: performance and out-of-distribution generalisation
summary: Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) are a cornerstone of interpretable machine learning, offering transparent predictions through structured additive decompositions. Despite advances from classical GAMs to modern neural and spline-based variants, two notable gaps remain. First, comprehensive benchmarking of spline-based GAMs on large-scale tabular learning tasks, the dominant modality in applied settings, is lacking. Second, their robustness under distribution shift, a setting where structured inductive biases should confer advantages, remains unexplored. We propose a multi-resolution, higher-order Composite Generalised Additive Model (CoGA2M) and evaluate it on the TALENT benchmark suite. CoGA2M ranks in the top third across all baselines (29 for regression, 32 for classification), establishing competitive performance with state-of-the-art tabular methods. We further extend TALENT with out-of-distribution (OOD) splits exhibiting train-test distributional shift and benchmark CoGA2M against LightGBM, a consistently top-performing model on TALENT. Under distribution shift, CoGA2M outperforms LightGBM, demonstrating a clear structural advantage. Our results position spline-based GAMs as strong contenders for tabular prediction and reveal a previously unrecognised benefit of additive structure in the OOD regime.

AI.tldr: CoGA2M is a multi-resolution, higher-order composite generalised additive model for tabular data. It ranks in the top third against baselines on TALENT and beats LightGBM under distribution shift, suggesting a structural advantage of additive models in the out-of-distribution regime.
AI.motivation: Spline-based GAMs lack comprehensive benchmarking on large-scale tabular tasks, and their robustness under distribution shift has not been studied, although structured inductive biases should help there.
AI.method: The authors propose CoGA2M and evaluate it on the TALENT benchmark suite. They extend TALENT with out-of-distribution splits that have train-test shift and compare CoGA2M with LightGBM on them.
AI.result: CoGA2M ranks in the top third of all baselines, at 29 for regression and 32 for classification. Under distribution shift it outperforms LightGBM.
AI.conclusion: Spline-based GAMs are strong contenders for tabular prediction, and additive structure offers a previously unrecognised benefit under distribution shift.

title: RGB Photo Enhancement with Deep Learning on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
summary: On-device RGB photo enhancement is a popular task that is needed for quality improvement of photos captured with mobile devices as well as for retouching of images acquired through other sources. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose participants to design fast solutions that can perform comprehensive enhancement of RGB photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale DPED dataset consisting of RGB image pairs captured with an old iPhone 3GS smartphone and a professional Canon 70D DSLR camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to enhance Full HD resolution RGB images on both platforms under 300 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

AI.tldr: This Mobile AI 2026 challenge report describes top solutions for on-device RGB photo enhancement, trained on DPED data, that run on Qualcomm and Arm smartphone GPUs. The best models enhance Full HD images in under 300 milliseconds.
AI.motivation: On-device photo enhancement is needed to improve mobile photos and to retouch images from other sources, which requires efficient models that run on constrained mobile hardware.
AI.method: Participants designed fast models for comprehensive RGB enhancement, trained on DPED image pairs captured with an iPhone 3GS and a Canon 70D DSLR. Runtime is evaluated on Adreno and Mali GPUs.
AI.result: Top solutions enhance Full HD RGB images on both platforms in under 300 milliseconds.
