AI.conclusion: The challenge shows that fast, comprehensive photo enhancement is feasible on current smartphone GPUs, and the report documents the models developed.

title: Do Agentic Policies Need to Look at Every Step? Geometric Abstraction for Reasoning and Action
comment: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Agentic Robotics. 13 pages, 8 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Recent multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they need to repeatedly reinterpret raw visual observations at every step of an interaction. We propose shifting routine spatial reasoning from images to text and symbols through a 3D geometric abstraction that is refreshed locally from observations and read directly by the language models. Specifically, our interface represents scene geometry via typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounds them from calibrated RGB-D, and returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals after each action. Symbolic task structure can thus be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene, with direct visual reasoning invoked only on demand. Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion while substantially reducing repeated multimodal queries, positioning explicit geometric state as an effective substrate for agentic robot policies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a 3D geometric abstraction that turns robot scene geometry into refreshed symbolic and textual checkpoints, so that multimodal models reason over text rather than repeatedly over images. The approach improves multi-step manipulation completion and substantially reduces repeated multimodal queries.
AI.motivation: Multimodal language models can reason directly about robot scenes, but it is unclear whether they must re-read raw visual observations at every step of an interaction.
AI.method: Scene geometry is represented as typed, evidence-aware symbolic references to object parts, grounded from calibrated RGB-D data. After each action, the interface returns compact textual checkpoints with metric residuals, and visual reasoning is invoked only on demand.
AI.result: Across offline policy synthesis and continuous online execution, reasoning over grounded text and symbols improves multi-step manipulation completion and substantially reduces repeated multimodal queries.
AI.conclusion: Explicit geometric state is an effective substrate for agentic robot policies, because symbolic task structure can be reused across decisions while metric values are rebound to the current scene.

title: FloMo: 3D Scene Flow as a World Action Model Intermediate for Learning from Human Video
summary: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at this http URL.

AI.tldr: FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene flow and action tokens, arguing that motion is a better intermediate than video for transferring video pretraining to robot actions. It generalises to unseen objects, motion primitives and tasks, and predicting video in addition to motion lowers policy success.
AI.motivation: Full video is a redundant signal for action prediction, and the authors argue that dense 3D motion better carries video pretraining into robot actions and gives better sample efficiency.
AI.method: Scene flow is rendered as RGB and encoded in the same latent space as video, so a pretrained video backbone can adapt to predict 3D scene flow. The model is co-trained on action-free human video and action-labelled robot teleoperation data.
AI.result: The model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalises to unseen objects, motion primitives and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with video prediction degrades out-of-distribution generalisation, and adding a video target alongside motion lowers policy success. Action tokens attend far more to motion than to video when all three are predicted jointly.
AI.conclusion: Motion mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action, and predicting video wastes model capacity.

title: VIGOR: Visual Gain Ordering for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Discrete Diffusion Language Models
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Multimodal discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate responses through iterative mask prediction and offer a promising alternative to autoregressive large vision-language models. However, they still suffer from hallucination, producing outputs that are plausible under language priors but insufficiently grounded in the image. We argue that hallucination in multimodal dLLMs is not only a token prediction problem, but also a premature commitment problem: during iterative denoising, some masked positions are unmasked too early because their confidence is driven more by language priors than by visual evidence, and these early commitments can bias later generation. To address this issue, we propose Visual Gain Ordering (VIGOR), a training-free and plug-and-play inference strategy that reorders masked positions according to counterfactual visual evidence. At each denoising step, VIGOR compares the confidence of each candidate token under the original image-conditioned pass and an additional visual-ablation pass, and prioritizes positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image. Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning performance across benchmarks. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: VIGOR is a training-free inference strategy for multimodal discrete diffusion language models that reorders masked positions by how strongly the image supports each prediction. It reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO.
AI.motivation: Multimodal discrete diffusion models can commit to tokens too early when language priors drive confidence more than visual evidence, and these early commitments then bias later generation.
AI.method: At each denoising step, VIGOR compares each candidate token's confidence under the image-conditioned pass and under an additional visual-ablation pass. It prioritises positions whose predictions are more strongly supported by the image.
AI.result: Experiments on LLaDA-V and Lumina-DiMOO show that VIGOR consistently reduces hallucination and improves multimodal reasoning across benchmarks. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination in multimodal diffusion language models is partly a premature-commitment problem, and visual-evidence-based ordering of unmasking addresses it without training.

title: Trajectory Evaluation via Rollout-Free World Model for End-to-end Autonomous Driving
summary: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: RFWorld is an end-to-end trajectory evaluator for autonomous driving that avoids recursive rollout by letting candidate trajectories query a shared scene memory. It achieves state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive while reducing computation roughly by the planning horizon times the number of candidates.
AI.motivation: Model-based trajectory evaluators predict candidate-conditioned future states, which is costly and accumulates prediction errors. The authors argue that planning needs only the future-relevant information for comparing candidates, not a full future scene.
AI.method: A shared scene memory is shaped into a future-readable representation by lightweight temporal readout with semantic supervision during training. At inference, each candidate trajectory performs a sparse spatial readout from this memory to get its score.
AI.result: RFWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive and learns a more planning-aligned world representation. The abstract reports that inference computation is reduced by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Rollout-free evaluation with a shared memory is a more efficient and error-resistant alternative to rollout-based trajectory scoring.

title: Molecular Prior Networks
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap
summary: Predicting affinity between small molecules and their protein targets remains one of the central problems in drug discovery. Due to the substantial cost of wet-lab experiments, machine learning models of drug-target affinity are usually trained on relatively small datasets, ranging from tens to hundreds of molecules. Given the inherent difficulty of generalization between different targets and chemical series, existing datasets of protein-ligand affinities are typically not used for new projects. At the same time, tabular foundation models, including Prior-data Fitted Networks, have recently shown how transformers can be used to solve machine learning problems in a single forward pass of the network, after being trained over a large corpus of, typically, synthetic datasets. Inspired by that line of work, we propose a novel affinity modelling approach, in which the labels of the query molecules are predicted from the labelled support molecules in a single forward pass of a transformer model. The model is trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets, enabling it to capture the general patterns of molecular activity across different targets, chemical series and dataset sizes. For the smallest support sets, our model matches the state of the art on the regression variant of the FS-Mol benchmark, while being faster than existing methods, thanks to the lack of task-specific training. A comparison against a reduced variant of our architecture, which amounts to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space, shows that the predictive performance of the transformer model is only partially explained by simple molecular similarity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a transformer that predicts drug-target affinity for query molecules from labelled support molecules in one forward pass, trained on thousands of affinity datasets. On the smallest support sets it matches the state of the art on the FS-Mol regression benchmark while avoiding task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Affinity datasets are small and do not generalise well across targets and chemical series, while tabular foundation models such as PFNs solve tasks in a single forward pass after pretraining on large corpora.
AI.method: A transformer predicts query labels from labelled support molecules in a single forward pass, trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets. An ablation that reduces the architecture to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space is used to test how much performance similarity alone explains.
AI.result: For the smallest support sets, the model matches the state of the art on the FS-Mol regression benchmark and is faster than existing methods. The reduced kernel-regression variant shows that the transformer's performance is only partly explained by simple molecular similarity.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining a transformer across many affinity datasets gives a fast, task-agnostic predictor for few-shot affinity modelling, with gains beyond simple similarity.

title: Workload-Static Optical Circuit Switching For Scalable LLM Inference Decode
comment: 39 pages, 10 main text, 29 appendix, 28 figures
summary: LLM inference decode executes fine-grained collectives whose latency directly limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are still built from electronic packet switches designed for training. We observe that, for a given model deployment and parallelization, the communication structure of decode is fixed, and propose workload-static optical circuit switching (OCS): circuits are configured once per deployment, co-designed with model parallelism and with topology-aware collective schedules that turn spare accelerator ports into fewer communication phases or higher bandwidth. We evaluate this design with GXNET, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements. In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.

AI.tldr: Workload-static optical circuit switching configures circuits once per LLM deployment, co-designed with parallelism and collective schedules, to speed up decode in scale-up fabrics. In a 576-accelerator domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.
AI.motivation: LLM decode runs fine-grained collectives whose latency limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are built from packet switches designed for training. For a given deployment, the decode communication structure is fixed.
AI.method: The authors propose workload-static optical circuit switching, in which circuits are set once per deployment and co-designed with model parallelism and topology-aware collective schedules. They evaluate it with GXNET, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements.
AI.result: In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.
AI.conclusion: Static optical circuits matched to a fixed decode workload are a promising interconnect design for scalable LLM inference.

title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
summary: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that irrelevant historical audio in speech LLMs can steer answers toward specific competing values, even when the queried event is still represented. Causal interventions show that source-role information alone does not control which historical values influence the answer.
AI.motivation: Speech LLMs keep audio history for multi-turn conversations, but remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. The authors ask why irrelevant history changes answers.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio measure how historical values direct errors. Causal interventions separate direct source access from the question-candidate pathway, and low-dimensional interventions separate source-role information from answer-value information.
AI.result: In open-ended question answering, most history-induced errors disappear when later computation cannot access the irrelevant source directly. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist because early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states. Strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers on naturally occurring errors, and combining them gives the greatest recovery.
AI.conclusion: Downstream evidence use can fail even when the right source is identified, so reliable conversational memory needs control over how retained information enters answer computation.

title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
comment: For code, checkpoints and more results, check out this https URL
summary: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

AI.tldr: Asynchronous Robot Policy decouples a slow vision-language model that updates a semantic memory from a lightweight vision-action expert that generates actions at a higher control frequency. It improves success rate by 18% on quasi-static Franka tasks and reaches 3 to 5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation, while running the VLM at 10 times lower frequency with no significant loss.
AI.motivation: Large vision-language-action models run semantic reasoning and action generation sequentially in one control loop, which creates latency that hurts real-time reactivity.
AI.method: A high-capacity vision-language model updates a semantic memory asynchronously at low frequency, and a lightweight vision-action expert conditioned on that memory generates actions at a much higher frequency. The expert is trained with the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observations across processes.
AI.result: On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less execution time in quasi-static setups, and 3 to 5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation. The VLM can run at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss.
AI.conclusion: Modelling robot policies as asynchronous processes allows fast reactive deployment while keeping the scale of foundation models.

title: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
comment: 29 pages, 15 figures, 13 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.

AI.tldr: RoboTryOn converts human videos into robot videos by treating human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on, and uses the resulting synthetic demonstrations to train policies. On novel tasks, including bimanual manipulation, policy success rises from 2% to 60% with no real robot demonstrations for those tasks.
AI.motivation: Egocentric human videos are a scalable source of demonstrations, but overlaying rendered robots or retargeting human poses leaves large visual or action gaps for high-DoF embodiments.
AI.method: Selected keyframes are translated autoregressively to keep visual consistency, and they guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. An inverse dynamics model that uses depth features infers action labels from the synthesised videos for policy learning.
AI.result: Policies trained on the synthetic data improve average success on novel tasks from 2% to 60% across several humanoid embodiments, without real robot demonstrations for those tasks. Training on the synthetic data matches policies trained only on teleoperated demonstrations at about a third of the collection cost.
AI.conclusion: Synthesising robot demonstrations from human videos is a cost-efficient alternative to teleoperation for training robot policies.

title: Basin2Vec: Learning Basin-Centric Embeddings for Scalable Hydrological Modeling
summary: Reliable streamflow prediction across time and in ungauged basins requires representations that capture hydrologically relevant basin characteristics. Existing methods rely on either fixed handcrafted attributes or general-purpose Earth observation embeddings not tailored to basin structure. We introduce \textbf{Basin2Vec}, a self-supervised framework that learns compact basin representations from hydroclimatic and physiographic data without observed streamflow. Basin2Vec organizes representation learning around basin scale and relationships across space and time. Across multiple forecasting architectures, it consistently outperforms predefined attributes and general-purpose geospatial embeddings in temporal generalization and zero-shot spatial transfer. Basin2Vec provides average relative gains of up to 8.3% temporally and achieves 3.5x the median predictive performance of the strongest baselines on unseen basins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of basin-centric pretraining for transferable hydrologic prediction. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Basin2Vec is a self-supervised method that learns compact basin representations from hydroclimatic and physiographic data, without observed streamflow. It outperforms predefined attributes and general-purpose geospatial embeddings for temporal generalisation and zero-shot spatial transfer.
AI.motivation: Streamflow prediction in time and in ungauged basins needs representations that capture hydrologically relevant basin characteristics, but existing methods use fixed handcrafted attributes or general Earth-observation embeddings not designed for basin structure.
AI.method: Representation learning is organised around basin scale and relationships across space and time, using hydroclimatic and physiographic inputs and no streamflow observations.
AI.result: Across several forecasting architectures, Basin2Vec gives average relative gains of up to 8.3% temporally and achieves 3.5 times the median predictive performance of the strongest baselines on unseen basins.
AI.conclusion: Basin-centric pretraining yields transferable representations for hydrological prediction.

title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
summary: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.

AI.tldr: OperAItor is an open-source framework for evaluating LLM agents that perform supervisory fault management in a simulated chemical plant. Without agent intervention, 18 of 20 scenarios cause plant stops, and validated agent configurations reduce stops to 5 to 8 for three of the four LLMs and recover $265,000 of the $399,000 loss.
AI.motivation: Supervisory fault management in chemical processes needs evaluation tools for LLM agents and for the methods that validate their actions, and a reproducible benchmark for comparing them is lacking.
AI.method: The plant is a 113-variable differential-algebraic model of isopropanol dehydrogenation in a reactor-distillation process, with 8 PI loops, 22 alarms, 5 pump trains and 11 safety instrumented functions. The agent combines multivariate statistical monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning and action generation. Five action-validation configurations are compared, across four LLMs and 20 single and multiple fault scenarios.
AI.result: Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, an economic loss of $399,000 under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce stops to 5 to 8 and recover $265,000 of the loss.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models and action-validation methods in chemical-process fault management.

title: Fairness Metrics based on the AUC in Clinical Predictive AI
summary: Fairness evaluation of clinical prediction models for binary outcomes often involves fairness metrics that compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC, or c-statistic) across subgroups. However, the AUC has been shown to be a non-collapsible metric, meaning that its subgroup specific and overall values are not directly comparable as often implicitly assumed. This raises important questions about how existing AUC-based fairness metrics should be used and interpreted. We examine eight AUC-based fairness metrics proposed in the literature, including: within-group AUC parity; cross-group AUC (xAUC) parity; gap-to-overall AUC; equity-scaled AUC; minimum-based metrics; $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$; $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$; and $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ or $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ parity. We characterise their estimands, relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC (into within- and cross-group components), and critically appraise them. We then illustrate their behaviour using simulations based on the EuroSCORE II, a clinical prediction model for in-hospital mortality. We recommend reporting an AUC matrix, containing the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group AUC components, alongside population characteristics. When fairness metrics are needed, we recommend reporting the within-group AUC parity, with cross-group AUC parity providing supplementary information but requiring caution due to its potential conflict with calibration. Metrics involving $\mathrm{xAUC}^1$ and $\mathrm{xAUC}^0$ have merit, summarising within- and cross-group AUCs into single values, but their interpretation is non-trivial, and they should be used with caution. Gap-to-overall AUC, equity-scaled AUC, and minimum-based metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and it is unclear how to operationalise them, making them not fit for purpose and generally not recommended.

AI.tldr: The paper examines eight AUC-based fairness metrics for clinical prediction models and finds that the AUC is non-collapsible, so subgroup and overall values are not directly comparable. It recommends reporting an AUC matrix and within-group AUC parity, and advises against gap-to-overall, equity-scaled and minimum-based metrics.
AI.motivation: AUC-based fairness metrics are widely used to compare subgroup performance, but the AUC is non-collapsible, so its subgroup and overall values are not directly comparable as often assumed.
AI.method: The authors characterise the estimands of eight AUC-based fairness metrics and relate them to the decomposition of overall AUC into within-group and cross-group components. They then illustrate their behaviour with simulations based on EuroSCORE II, a clinical model for in-hospital mortality.
AI.result: The abstract reports no new numerical results. It recommends reporting an AUC matrix with the overall AUC and all within- and cross-group components, alongside population characteristics. Within-group AUC parity is recommended, with cross-group AUC parity as supplementary information, and metrics based on xAUC1 and xAUC0 are considered to have merit but to need caution.
AI.conclusion: Gap-to-overall, equity-scaled and minimum-based AUC metrics compare quantities that should not be compared and are generally not recommended.

title: Going Deeper With Memories
summary: Byte level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and provide universal coverage, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive. We introduce DeepMem, a causal multiscale architecture that separates semantic compression from exact byte preservation. A learned invertible subband transform constructs a hierarchy of shorter sequences, while a lossless carrier and explicit detail sidebands preserve byte identity. Fast weight memory blocks operate along the encoder, with iterative shared state computation at the compressed bottleneck, while an attention based super resolution decoder restores byte resolution representations. DeepMem achieves stronger language modeling performance than a matched byte level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and obtains the best macro average performance across the evaluated FLORES languages. It also improves PIQA accuracy while remaining competitive on code modeling, multiple choice reasoning, and byte level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement requires approximately $7{,}600\times$ fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full resolution reasoning, while maintaining competitive evaluation throughput.

AI.tldr: DeepMem is a causal multiscale byte-level language model that compresses sequences with a learned invertible subband transform while keeping byte identity through a lossless carrier and detail sidebands. It outperforms a matched byte-level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19 and reduces counted FLOPs at the bottleneck by about 7,600 times.
AI.motivation: Byte-level language models avoid tokenizer dependence and cover all languages, but processing every byte at full resolution is expensive.
AI.method: Fast-weight memory blocks run along the encoder, with iterative shared-state computation at the compressed bottleneck, and an attention-based super-resolution decoder restores byte-resolution representations. Semantic compression is separated from exact byte preservation through the invertible transform, lossless carrier and detail sidebands.
AI.result: DeepMem achieves stronger language modelling than a matched byte-level Transformer on FineWeb-Edu and PG19, and the best macro average across the evaluated FLORES languages. It improves PIQA accuracy and remains competitive on code modelling, multiple-choice reasoning and byte-level corruption robustness. Bottleneck refinement needs about 7,600 times fewer counted FLOPs than equivalent full-resolution reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Multiscale compression with exact byte preservation can make byte-level language models far cheaper without giving up competitive quality.

title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
comment: Accepted in AACL-IJCNLP 2026 Workshop Multi-LLL
summary: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates language-subspace interventions for multilingual reasoning and finds that projecting out language subspaces does not remove language information. The intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, and the only one that improves joint accuracy does so by 1.60 points.
AI.motivation: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language components in mid-layer activations, but it is unclear whether the subspaces capture language information and whether accuracy gains come without cost.
AI.method: On MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, the authors build subspaces with the existing Mean-SVD method and their DiffPCA method. They then project out each subspace and train linear probes, and evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B.
AI.result: Both subspace methods capture substantial translation-associated variation. Linear probes still identify language almost perfectly after projection. The most accurate intervention on MGSM sacrifices response-language fidelity, and only one intervention improves joint accuracy, by 1.60 points. Subtle prompt changes alone reproduce the accuracy gains but seriously damage language fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, since they can trade accuracy for language substitution.

title: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
summary: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning on mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports answers that the model believes are false, with no harmful content, can induce broad misalignment, and the effect grows as the model disbelieves the answers more. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning on explicitly harmful narrow data is known to cause broad misalignment, but the authors ask whether training on believed-false yet harmless data can do the same, which bears on realistic model updates.
AI.method: The authors vary how strongly the model disbelieves its training answers across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, and then study a single-fact update as in knowledge editing or continual learning. They also compare framing the false fact as part of a coherent story with instructing the model to assert it, and test content filters and persona vectors.
AI.result: In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning the model states the wrong answers, yet its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones. In the single-fact setting the same relation holds. Framing the false fact as a story yields deeper belief and less misalignment than instructing assertion, and content filters and persona vectors cannot distinguish the two framings.
AI.conclusion: Updating a model toward facts it does not believe can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless, so model updates carry a risk that surface filters miss.

title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
comment: 7 pages, 3 tables. Dataset and code: this https URL
summary: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.

AI.tldr: The paper replays 117 frozen cases built from real NWS alerts through a Claude-based severe-weather pipeline and finds that a blind prompt gives 37.7% false reassurance, against 0.0% for the production pipeline. Real alerts remove false reassurance, but the disclosure instruction does not.
AI.motivation: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active, which the authors call false reassurance.
AI.method: The evaluation replays 117 frozen cases, including 69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls and 16 non-U.S. locations, under five conditions that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater labelled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which is disclosed. A preregistered single-sentence ablation tests one production instruction.
AI.result: False reassurance is 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0 to 5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69). It is 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69) and 44.9% when the blind prompt also asks the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Real alerts remove false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001), but the disclosure instruction does not (p = 0.40). With a neutral prompt the model raises alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt.
AI.conclusion: Alert data alone does not ensure safe behaviour, since prompt design also matters, and the released dataset, labels and code allow replication.

title: Personas Are Not People: Identity as State, Not Attribute
summary: Synthetic populations, large sets of simulated people, are increasingly used in place of real people to pretest surveys, simulate users and communities, and evaluate AI systems. Each simulated person is defined by a persona, a written profile of fixed traits, demographics, and attitudes that a language model is instructed to act out. Every such system assumes that a person's identity is a stable attribute that behaves the same way in every situation the simulation presents. We show that this assumption is not a harmless simplification. Three decades of personality research find the opposite. How a given person behaves varies more across contexts than people vary from one another. Drawing on identity economics, which describes how different situations activate different identities and norms within the same person, we separate behavior into three parts, which are stable traits, the identity a context calls up, and the situation itself. We then prove, under two stated assumptions, that any simulation built on fixed personas, no matter how detailed the personas or how large the underlying model, cannot reproduce the part of a population's behavior that is specific to it and its circumstances. We propose a new evaluation criterion based on this result and a person-in-context design that can meet it in principle. We test one version on a naturalistic Reddit personality corpus and on a published clinical-trial recruitment survey of a community with documented distrust of medical institutions. The design does produce context-dependent behavior when tested directly, but in neither setting does it fully match the real population, and we show where it falls short. The consequence for practice is a risk that synthetic-population evaluations misrepresent the groups whose behavior is most shaped by context, a distortion that richer personas cannot correct.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that synthetic populations built from fixed personas cannot reproduce behaviour that depends on context, because identity is a state activated by situations rather than a stable attribute. Under two stated assumptions it proves this limit, and a person-in-context design only partly matches real populations in tests on Reddit and clinical-trial recruitment data.
AI.motivation: Synthetic populations are increasingly used in place of real people for survey pretesting, user simulation and AI evaluation, and each persona assumes that identity is a stable attribute that behaves the same across situations. Personality research and identity economics suggest otherwise.
AI.method: Behaviour is separated into stable traits, the identity a context activates, and the situation itself, drawing on identity economics. The authors prove, under two stated assumptions, that fixed-persona simulations cannot reproduce the context-specific part of population behaviour. They propose a person-in-context design and test one version on a Reddit personality corpus and a published clinical-trial recruitment survey.
AI.result: The person-in-context design produces context-dependent behaviour when tested directly, but in neither setting does it fully match the real population. The abstract reports no numbers beyond this.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic-population evaluations risk misrepresenting groups whose behaviour is most shaped by context, a distortion that richer personas cannot correct.

title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

AI.tldr: LoopVQ is a KV-cache vector quantisation method for looped transformers that codes channels across loop steps jointly and fine-tunes codebooks to match full-precision outputs. At 0.5 bits per element it beats existing KV-cache quantisers, and in SGLang it nearly halves decode latency at 32K context and raises peak throughput by up to 4.3 times and 6.1 times on Ouro models.
AI.motivation: In looped transformers, each loop step stores its own keys and values, so the KV cache grows with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck, even though the parameters are shared.
AI.method: The authors observe that the KV cache is highly redundant along the loop axis and that loop steps differ in sensitivity to quantisation. LoopVQ codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the full-precision model's outputs. It is implemented in SGLang.
AI.result: At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV-cache vector quantisation methods on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Combined with TaSQ, it retains much of BF16 accuracy at 0.25 bits per element. In SGLang it nearly halves decode latency at 32K context and raises peak serving throughput by up to 4.3 times and 6.1 times on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models relative to BF16.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting redundancy across loop steps makes KV-cache quantisation practical for looped language models at very low bit rates.

title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HARP is a training-free method for LLM-based recommendation that adds symmetric item profiles, profile-level homophily used at retrieval time, and a single-pass reflective profile update to a frozen backbone. It lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9% to 24.0% on four benchmarks, with Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset.
AI.motivation: In memory-augmented LLM recommendation, only users receive structured profiles, items never produce comparable self-descriptions, profile signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt, and user profiles are frozen after warmup.
AI.method: The authors recast recommendation as an agentic communication process with BUILD, TRANSMIT, UNDERSTAND and SYNC stages. HARP instantiates the missing stages with a rule-extracted symmetric item profile needing no extra LLM calls, a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily consumed at retrieval time, and a single-pass reflective update that needs no gradient step.
AI.result: On Yelp, Books, MovieTV and Goodreads, HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9% to 24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations show complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source, and the reflective pass introduces a trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Treating recommendation as agentic communication, with a training-free instantiation, offers gains in Hit@1 across benchmarks.
